To the article "God is triune," to "the Church cannot err," and to every other principle of Christian doctrine, I assent by infused faith not because John said it, or any other man, but because God revealed it; and to "God has revealed" I believe at once, moved by God through a special instinct.

So on the object's side the formal moving reason is revealed divine truth; yet that does not move us unless an interior cause is also present — God himself moving by a free and special concurrence. Stapleton's third conclusion (question 1, article 2) says the same: God revealing is properly and absolutely the formal object of faith. He proves it from the Prophets and Apostles, who had no other formal object; therefore every believer's faith has that same object, for there is one faith of all. In reply to the third argument he writes: absolutely and of itself, the last resolution of things to be believed is the truthful God — or God revealing inwardly in the heart — after John the Baptist: "He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, and whoever receives his testimony has set his seal that God is true" (John 3).
Finally the scholastics commonly hold that the assent of our faith is at last resolved into the Holy Spirit's inward motion — as Thomas's commentators show on the Secunda secundae, question 1.
translator_notes: Pars III XVI. Canus interior efficient cause quotation; Stapleton Deus revelans; John 3 Baptist line restored from damaged italic.

title: The Church is a condition and medium, not the last ground of believing
english: Those doctors therefore treat the Church's voice and testimony as a cause without which we would not believe, and, in their terms, a condition of faith's object: the Church is the medium through which God reveals and proposes what is to be believed. Yet they refuse to reduce our faith to the Church's testimony as the supreme and last reason of believing. They reduce it to God revealing and the Holy Spirit illuminating — as Bañez teaches carefully in the place already cited.

Stapleton's words in the article we keep marking are the same: faith that begins from the Church's testimony, so far as that testimony proposes and leads to faith, ends in God revealing within and teaching within what the Church preached without. The Church's preaching teaches from outside; it proposes, leads, and helps. But the One who teaches within has his chair in heaven, as Augustine says. Once that inward teaching has come, the Samaritan line has its place: "Now we do not believe because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard, and we know that this is the Savior of the world" (John 4).
translator_notes: Pars III XVII. Stapleton definit in Deo intus revelante; Augustine cathedram in caelo; John 4 Samaritan line restored.

title: Faith is a prudent assent; certainty still rests on divine revelation alone
english: Nor do the scholastic doctors deny that the faith we give to divine revelation is a prudent assent: the one who believes God's Word is moved by arguments that can persuade a prudent mind that what is set before him as God's Word truly is. Faith's certainty does not hang on those arguments, nor properly lean on them. Gregory of Valencia makes the distinction sharpest in Analysis of Faith 1.1: because divine revelation is not evident to human reason, other arguments besides revelation are needed, so that men may prudently persuade themselves that Christian doctrine is true.

Yet those arguments are not required so that people believe properly, surely, and firmly because of them. The certainty and firmness of faith — and the assent itself — lean of themselves on divine revelation alone as their foundation. The arguments only supply clearer motives by which the mind may prudently will to believe surely and firmly because of divine revelation, with God's help. Two soul-motions must be told apart in those who take hold of faith. First, even under prudence's dictate, they judge Christ's doctrine worthy of sure and firm belief. Then, helped by God, they believe by faith's assent that it is true. That sure, firm, God-helped assent must be referred to the divine testimony alone contained in revelation, as the cause and reason of believing; and to the Church's proposing only as a condition without which Christian faith would scarcely be given. The first prudent judgment — that this doctrine may rightly be held as divine and true — is a judgment of prudence, and it properly leans on arguments other than revelation itself.

Canus teaches the same in Loci Theologici 2.8, reply to the fourth argument. It is not enough that the things of faith be simply proposed by a man to the one about to believe, as first principles to a pupil; some exterior persuasion and human inducement must also be used. He proves it from those moved to believe by miracles and other reasons. Once that is set out, he adds, what we said a little earlier is easy to see: certain human, outward supports must intervene for believing, yet they are not fit of themselves, and faith's resolution is not made into them, but into an interior divine cause that stirs and moves us to believe. That is the common teaching of the Roman school, so far as I know with no dissent — so further witnesses would be surplus.
translator_notes: Pars III XVIII. Valencia Analysis 1.1 long quotation and Canus exteriora adminicula restored; natural close before XIX (real controversy).

title: The real controversy is not a war of names
english: You will ask: what, then, is the real state of the controversy on Scripture's authority? In the heads reviewed so far the Orthodox and the Pontificii seem to agree. Is the fight only about a name? Not at all. The rift between the two sides is large and of the highest moment.

To see it clearly, note first that some revelations become known to us only through another revelation, and they borrow their authority for us from that other. Balaam's old revelation reached us through the revelation given to Moses. The same holds for that scrap of Enoch's prophecy to which Jude's letter lends authority.

Yet there cannot be an infinite regress here, and a circle — one revelation proved by another, and that other by the first — must not be allowed. So some revelation must be first for us: one that wins our faith by itself and for its own sake, not by help from a better-known revelation.
translator_notes: Pars III XIX. Status controversiae; Balaam via Moses; Jude/Enoch fragment; no infinite regress of revelations. Long-s OCR normalized.

title: Formal reason of faith versus the Church's public external rule
english: Speak carefully and you may also distinguish faith's proper formal reason — taken simply and absolutely, as the Schools put it — from an external principle of faith, an outward rule for what is to be believed.

Faith's proper formal reason was, is, and always will be the same for every believer: God's revelation, however it comes — by God's immediate breath, through men, through angels, through Scripture, or outside Scripture. For every believer the standing formal reason of religious belief is this: because God revealed such things.

Yet God did not judge it enough to reveal privately to each believer whatever that person needed for salvation. To keep unity and communion in the Church, and to meet Satan's tricks, he always willed a common, external, public revelation to stand in the Church as the rule of faith — the measure of every dogma, and the court that ends every dispute about faith.

Before the law was given, that rule was the Patriarchs' voices and God's living oracles. After Moses' law was given and written, the Church's rule was that written law, with the revelations later made to the Prophets and likewise written down. After Christ's coming the New Testament enlarged the rule. So now, in the Christian Church, the rule of our faith is the Scripture of both Testaments.
translator_notes: Pars III XX. Formal reason vs external rule; public revelation as fidei regula through Patriarchs / Moses / Prophets / both Testaments. Page-turn after Satanae praestigiis restored.

title: Faith resolves two ways: in the conscience, and before others
english: Third: our faith can be resolved in two ways — with respect to the object or the subject; with respect to ourselves or with respect to others.

With respect to ourselves and the subject, faith is resolved when we ask what the inward principle is, and where each conscience rests so that we may not press further. With respect to the object and to others, our faith is resolved when we ask for the last foundation we can show and name to someone else.
That last foundation we can show another must be some external principle of faith — an outward rule of faith — where we stop, with no further rule beyond it.
translator_notes: Pars III XXI. Duplex resolutio: respectu subjecti (conscientia) / objecti (externa regula).

title: Scripture is the first external principle; the Spirit seals within
english: Apply this to the present case. We and the Pontificii agree, as the earlier theses show, that faith's proper reason simply and of itself is divine revelation, however it comes; on that point there is no fight between us. We also agree that the last rest of each believer's conscience is the Holy Spirit's inward testimony.

What is not agreed is which revelation is today first and most known for us — the one we must receive by itself and for its own sake, not because of some other revelation better known to us and of higher authority; and so which is the first and most common external principle of faith, through which everything else is to be proved, while it itself has no prior.

We hold that this revelation is contained in sacred Scripture. God's Word in the books of both Testaments ought to win faith among us by itself — not by some other Word of God, some further divine revelation that would give it a public external witness better known and more certain to believers than Scripture is. No rule of faith, no external principle, stands prior to sacred Scripture so that Scripture could be proved from something earlier. Scripture is the first and most common rule of everything that belongs to faith, and it is not to be measured by another rule.

Ask why we believe this or that dogma — that God is triune and one, or that believers are to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — and we answer: because inspired Scripture holds it, and we point to the place. Press further why we take that Scripture as divine, and we do not offer another principle of faith to prove Scripture; we say one must stop there. We do offer arguments that Scripture is divine and deserves to be believed as divine. Those arguments are not, properly speaking, faith's principles, nor the foundation on which faith chiefly leans. We believe Scripture at once — God speaking in the Scriptures — moved by the Spirit's inward impulse.
translator_notes: Pars III XXII. Agreement on revelatio / Spiritus testimonium; disagreement on first external principle; Scripture stops the regress. Baptism formula named, no chapter:verse.

title: Rome makes the Church a superior revelation that proves Scripture
english: The Pontificii will not let sacred Scripture deserve and win our faith immediately and of itself. They teach another divine revelation by which Scripture must be proved, so that the Church may publicly settle its standing. For them that revelation is the Church's voice and testimony — the doctrine of her overseers. They want God to speak today through the Church's pastors as through organs infallible in the doctrine of faith, as he once spoke through Prophets and Apostles.

So they admit Scripture is a rule of faith, yet a subordinate and partial one that needs proving by a superior, fuller rule. When they prove dogmas they do cite sacred Scripture's authority. Asked why they trust sacred Scripture, they say: because of their Church's testimony — and in that testimony, as the supreme external principle of faith, they must rest if they mean to keep their own teachings.

We too bring the Church's constant testimony when we prove a sacred book's authority. But not as they do — not as a principle of faith to which our faith must be subjected. For us it is only an argument from the later effect: sound and strong, yet not wholly divine and infallible.
translator_notes: Pars III XXIII. Pontificii: Ecclesiae vox superior proof of Scripture; Reformed: Church testimony a posteriori only, not infallible principle.

title: The celebrated question: is Scripture's authority supreme or borrowed?
english: From this rises the famous question on Scripture's authority. We say Scripture's authority among us is supreme, not borrowed from elsewhere: above itself Scripture has no revelation, and no other principle of faith by which it can be proved.

The Pontificii say Scripture's authority hangs on the Church's: they take the Church's testimony for a principle of faith above Scripture, one by which Scripture must be proved so that the Church may publicly settle its standing.
translator_notes: Pars III XXIV. Celebris quaestio; mutuam sumptam restored across page-turn (PDF 49–50 / book pp. 37–38).

title: Their analogy: Scripture stands to the Church as a dogma stands to Scripture
english: To mark the difference between their sentence and ours, and where the hinge of the controversy sits, note how the Pontificii compare sacred Scripture with the Church's doctrine: as we compare a particular dogma of faith with sacred Scripture.

As an article of faith — for example that the dead will one day rise — has its truth and authority in itself from God alone, not from the Prophets' and Apostles' testimony as writers of Scripture, so they admit that sacred Scripture has its authority in itself from God alone, not from the Church's word.

And as the chief reason we embrace that dogma is not properly Peter's, Paul's, or Isaiah's authority, but the divine revelation brought to us by their pen — for the dogma was believed before Scripture, and can still be believed apart from it — so they confess that the Church's testimony is not the proper and chief reason of our faith about Scripture, but simply and absolutely divine revelation.

Yet again: as that dogma, or any like it, must not be publicly received in the Church or set forth for belief unless Scripture's testimonies prove it — since only from those can believers publicly know that something belongs to faith, so that any dogma's authority for us, and its public external certainty, hangs on sacred Scripture's testimony — so they want Scripture's authority for us to hang on the Church's testimony, and a book's divinity not to be publicly settled for believers except by the Church's approval and attestation.

Finally: even with that dependence of dogmas on Scripture, Christian dogmas can be proved and urged by many arguments besides Scripture's testimonies — motives that lead toward faith, not faith's reason and foundation. So the Pontificii also do not deny that sacred Scripture, besides the Church's testimony, has many notes and arguments of divinity by which it can be proved and urged — yet which cannot found public faith in the Church concerning Scripture's divinity.
translator_notes: Pars III XXV. Analogy dogma:Scripture :: Scripture:Church; public vs in-se authority; motives ≠ public foundation.

title: Controversy stated: first external rule — Scripture, or present pastors?
english: From all this the controversy between us and the Roman Church's doctors is plain enough. Is Scripture the first rule of faith and the first external principle of faith — so that no other principle can prove it, and it does not borrow its authority from elsewhere?

Or is the Church's doctrine and testimony the principle and rule of faith, better known and clearer to us than Scripture itself, and the means by which Scripture must be proved so that believers may publicly settle its standing? We assert the former. The Pontificii assert the latter — and by "Church," as already said, they mean the present pastors, above all the Roman Pontiff.
translator_notes: Pars III XXVI. Controversia stated; natural close before XXVII (Scripture better known than Church). Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus / Pontificem Romanum.

title: Scripture is better known among the faithful than the Church herself
english: Their error is answered from this: among believers Scripture is better known than the Church herself.

Every Christian body agrees, at least on the chief books, which writings are true Scripture. Greeks, Armenians, Ethiopians, Pontificii, Protestants, and whatever other Christian parties remain today all acknowledge as Canonical the books our churches hold Canonical. Rome adds certain Old Testament books to its Canon; on the books we count Canonical it still agrees with us.

Those who denied or despised Scripture outright — as the Libertines are remembered to have done in our fathers' day — were few, obscure, and soon gone. Which Church is the true one is not settled the same way: each party claims to be it. The Greek, Armenian, and Ethiopian churches neither take Rome for God's true Church nor bind themselves to its authority.
translator_notes: XXVII: Libertini / Graeci Armeni Aethiopes restored from damaged long-s OCR (PDF 50 / book p. 38).

title: No pope or council carries Scripture's notes of divinity
english: No pope, council, or gathering of pastors carries so many and so bright marks of its own authority as sacred Scripture carries of its divinity.

Earlier theses already listed what recommends Scripture: prophecies of things to come, the holiness, height, and force of its teaching, the majesty and plainness of its style, the harmony of Old and New Testament, miracles confirming it, the life of those who first handed it down, God's lasting care to keep it, the martyrs' constancy for its truth, the consent of peoples, and even hostile witnesses.

What council, or what crowd of pastors, presses its claim with notes so many and so strong? Ask the adversaries' own conscience: is it not plainer that Moses and Paul wrote divine, authentic books than that Florence, Trent, or the Lateran were legitimate councils led by the Spirit without fail?
translator_notes: XXVIII: notes-of-divinity list and Florentinum/Tridentinum/Lateranense conscience appeal restored across page-turn (PDF 50–51).

title: Scripture is more certain than living pastors; Peter's firmer prophetic word
english: Scripture is also more certain for believers than the word of those who preside in the Church — so it does not borrow its authority from them.

Pastors today are not more certain for the faithful than the Apostles were for the first Christians. Yet while the Apostles still lived and preached, their testimony weighed less among believers than Scripture's — as Peter shows in his second letter (2 Peter 1). Speaking to people who already believed, after he told how he heard the voice from heaven say of Christ, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," he adds that they have a firmer witness still: the Prophets in the holy Scriptures.

"We did not follow cleverly devised myths," he says, "when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. He received honor and glory from God the Father when that voice came to him from the Majestic Glory: 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.' We heard that voice from heaven while we were with him on the holy mountain. And we have the prophetic word made more sure, to which you do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place."
translator_notes: XXIX: 2 Peter 1 propheticum firmiorem quotation restored from damaged italic/long-s (PDF 51).

title: Scripture's witness outranks the Baptist's — and today's pastors
english: Sacred Scripture also has, on every side, greater authority among believers than the Church's pastors do.

Their testimony today is no greater than John the Baptist's once was. Yet Scripture's testimony was greater than the Baptist's — as Christ our Lord teaches plainly (John 5), where he sets Scripture's witness to himself above John's. "You sent to John," he says, "and he has borne witness to the truth; yet I have a testimony greater than John's."

He then names a threefold witness greater than John's: first the miracles he worked — "the works the Father gave me to accomplish testify that the Father has sent me"; next the Father's voice from heaven — "the Father who sent me has himself borne witness of me"; and last sacred Scripture. He adds: "Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me."
translator_notes: XXX: John 5 Misistis… Scrutamini Scripturas chain restored (PDF 51).

title: Councils and papal letters yield to Moses and Paul; the Bereans check preaching
english: On their own showing, no Church testimony is brighter or more solemn than what Councils and papal Decrees give. Yet common Christian sense says no council matches sacred Scripture's authority. No one dares set Nicea, Chalcedon, Trent, or any other beside Moses and the Prophets. Even Rome's warmest friends have not yet hardened their faces enough to level papal letters with Paul's epistles and the four Gospels.

Roman practice itself proves it. When they rank the sources of theological argument, Scripture always comes first; Councils and papal Decrees come later. They so honor Scripture, as they should, that they grant no error can be found in it, even the least. Councils they want infallible on dogmas of faith — yet they admit many other slips: conclusions may be of faith while the arguments are poor; they may hold the question of right and still err on the question of fact.

Pastors and doctors also use Scripture's witnesses to recommend their own teaching — and that teaching can and must be tried by Scripture. So the Bereans are praised: after hearing Paul preach, they searched the Scriptures to see whether those things were so (Acts 17). If Scripture carries more weight with believers than the Church's pastors, it plainly does not take its authority from their word. What is greater cannot draw its authority from what is less. Nothing can give an authority greater than its own.
translator_notes: XXXI: Beroenses / Ad. 17 and quaestione juris/facti restored; frontem perfricuerunt kept (PDF 51).

title: If the Church hangs on Scripture, Scripture cannot hang on the Church
english: How then could Scripture's authority for us hang on the Church's, when the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture?

From Scripture we learn which Church is true, and what force it has. That authority cannot be proved with certainty from anywhere else. So the fathers once sent heretics who denied Christ's true Church back to the Scriptures, and held that the true Church must be shown from them. Augustine tells the Donatists: if they hold the Church, let them show it only from the canonical books of divine Scripture.

Rome itself today tries to prove its Church and its infallible authority against us from sacred Scripture, and thinks the work well done when it cites places such as "I am with you to the end of the age," "I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail," "the Spirit will lead you into all truth," "Tell it to the Church," and the like, as foundations of the authority it gives the Church. Since, by their own confession, the Church's authority is known to us from Scripture, and no surer proof can be offered, it is clear the other way that our certainty about Scripture does not rest on the Church's testimony as its chief ground. Otherwise the circle is open: Scripture is proved by the Church, the Church by Scripture, and back again without end.
translator_notes: XXXII: Augustine–Donatist line and Ero vobiscum / Rogavi / Dic Ecclesiae cluster restored across G2 page-turn (PDF 51–52).

title: Rome's letters of credit cut the other way
english: Rome adds that Scripture in the Church's hands is like letters of credit: papers that accredit an envoy from a superior, and that send us back to that superior for a fuller account of his mind and will. So they want the Church to present Scripture as a diploma sealing its divine calling and authority, and remitting us to the Church to learn God's will more fully.

But letters of credit do not draw their force from the one who shows them. The opposite is true: the bearer's authority is known and confirmed by the letters. The one who brings the letters is not why we trust the letters; we trust him because of the letters that accredit him.
translator_notes: XXXIII: literae credentiae diploma analogy restored (PDF 52).

title: Stapleton's Baptist mutual-testimony fails; dependence cannot run both ways
english: Their reply to this argument is strange. Stapleton, who seems to have handled the controversy with the most care, grants that the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture's. He denies that Scripture's authority therefore fails to hang in turn on the Church's — and he tries to prove it by instances.

Christ's authority for us, he says, hung on John the Baptist's, for John was sent to witness to Christ so that all might believe through him; yet the Baptist's authority in turn hung on Christ's witness, for Christ attested John and confirmed his calling. The instance — and others like it — does not reach the point. Mutual testimony can prove two things to each other. It does not show that the first's authority hangs on the second's, and the second's on the first's, for the same people at once.

The Baptist did point men to Christ. Those who came to Christ that way did not believe in Christ chiefly on the Baptist's word, nor was John greater or surer for them than Christ. We grant that John's authority hung on Christ's; we deny outright that Christ's hung on John's. Two authorities cannot each hang on the other for the same persons at the same time. Whatever hangs on another is less certain and less known to us than that on which it hangs. If the Church's authority depends on Scripture's, Scripture is more certain and better known for us. If Scripture's hangs on the Church's, Scripture is less certain and less known. Then Scripture would be at once more and less certain, better and less known, than the Church — a contradiction.

The question here is not merely whether Scripture can be proved by the Church and the Church by Scripture. It is whether Scripture's authority, properly speaking, hangs on the Church's as on a principle of faith more certain and better known for us.
translator_notes: XXXIV: Stapleton Baptist mutual-testimony reductio and contradiction close restored; stops before XXXV Symbol reply (PDF 52–53).

title: Stapleton's Symbol reply fails; the Creed takes its authority from Scripture
english: Stapleton's second reply grants that the Church's authority for us hangs on Scripture's, yet denies that the Church can be known only through Scripture. Apart from Scripture, he says, the faithful learn from the Creed that the Church exists and must be believed.

The Creed has no authority of its own. It draws its whole force from sacred Scripture, from which it is taken. It is simply the faithful's confession of what they believe according to Scripture. That already makes the Creed's authority better known to us than the Church's — which cuts hard against those who say the Creed's authority, like every other article of belief, hangs on the Church as on a better-known principle of faith.

On their own showing the Church is the body that frames Creeds and confers that authority. Yet in the Creed we confess one holy Catholic Church, and the Creed never tells us which Church that is — Roman rather than Greek or Ethiopian. No proof from the Creed settles it. If Scripture's authority is to be confirmed to us through the Church's, as Rome wants, bare knowledge that some Church exists on earth is not enough. We must know determinately which Church is the true one, clothed with divine and infallible authority.
translator_notes: XXXV: Stapleton Symbol / Creed reply restored across page-turn after XXXIV (PDF 53 / book p. 41). Graeca / Aethiopica kept.

title: Faith received Scripture as Canon for centuries before any solemn Church decree
english: The certainty with which believers receive sacred Scripture as the rule of faith does not hang on some public, solemn Church decree that confirms Scripture's divinity like an oracle. For ages Scripture was publicly known and received as the Canon of faith with no such decree at all.

For several centuries after the Apostles, no council and no pope sealed a fixed Canon or drew up a catalogue of the sacred books. The first council to review the number of Canonical books was Laodicea — not before the three-hundredth year from Christ's birth, and still a particular council, not a general one. Yet before Laodicea the Canon was already certain, and Scripture's authority was certain to the faithful.
Neither Laodicea nor the later councils that listed the sacred books aimed to give those books some new authority. They only marked and declared which books were already Canonical.
translator_notes: XXXVI: pre-Laodicean Canon; Laodicenum as first numbered review, particular not general (PDF 53-54 / book pp. 41-42).

title: Pre-conciliar tradition cannot be the certain foundation of faith in Scripture
english: Nor may one fall back on some Church tradition, as if before the councils that fixed the number of sacred books tradition itself had been the foundation of faith concerning Scripture.

Rome grants that tradition is a means the Church uses in judging matters of faith. Yet on Rome's own terms tradition is as doubtful as the books of Scripture, and is no certain foundation of faith until a public Church judgment has proved it.
translator_notes: XXXVII: short tradition-before-councils reductio; tradition still doubtful until public judgment on Rome's own terms.

title: Stapleton's tacit Church testimony follows the faithful's belief; it cannot found it
english: Stapleton's further device helps no more. He distinguishes two kinds of Church testimony: one solemn and express, given in general councils and papal decrees; the other tacit and interpretative, by which the Church is said to approve whatever she lets her ministers teach and her people hold.

As if, before any council decided the Canon, the Church had already judged the Canonical books — not by a solemn sentence, but by this tacit reading: she let pastors hand the books to the faithful as Canonical, and did not reject the faith of those who received them.

That so-called interpretative judgment cannot found the faithful's belief, nor did Christian faith hang on it. It follows their faith; it does not precede it. What the Church allows to happen is already happening before she allows it. So I ask Rome: what grounded that early Christian faith which the Church merely tolerated and is said to have approved by her silence? A faith conceived as prior to that tolerance cannot rest on the tolerance and the tacit consent.
translator_notes: XXXVIII: Stapleton duplex testimonium (solemn/express vs tacit/interpretative) restored; tolerantia prior faith close (PDF 54 / book p. 42).

title: Disputed New Testament books were already received without a public Church determination
english: Whatever one makes of that tacit testimony, Rome herself teaches that for a time the Church gave no sentence on certain Canonical books. Some New Testament books were once doubted, they say, because the Church had not yet made her mind clear enough about them.

Even so, while some doubted, most churches already received those books publicly and held them divine and authentic. Public Church testimony is therefore not required before a book's divinity can stand publicly and believers be sure of it. Before any Church determination of the disputed books, their authority was already certain and publicly owned across the greater part of the Christian world.

Jude and James seemed disputed (ἀντιλεγόμεναι) to some, as Eusebius says; yet on his own witness others acknowledged them (ὁμολογούμεναι) and received them publicly. Some rejected John's Apocalypse, yet the churches John had nursed, as Tertullian puts it, defended its authority. Hebrews stood the same way: though long doubted in the Latin Church, Jerome tells Dardanus that the Eastern churches had venerated it as divine and Apostolic.
added_allusions: Eusebius on Jude/James as disputed yet acknowledged
Tertullian on churches nursed by John defending the Apocalypse
Jerome, Epistle to Dardanus, on Hebrews in the East
translator_notes: XXXIX: Eusebius ἀντιλεγόμεναι / ὁμολογούμεναι and Tertullian Johannis alumnae restored from damaged Greek/italic; Hieronymus ad Dardanum (PDF 54-55).

title: Old Testament prophets held divine authority before and against the priests who opposed them
english: Go back to Old Testament times. When the Prophets published their books, those books already had authority by right, and in fact held it among Israel's faithful, before the priests then ruling the Church had approved them or declared them divine.

Most of the Prophets were sent chiefly to rebuke the priests' vices and sloth, so the priests were usually their enemies. Even so, against that resistance the Prophets' books were held and acknowledged as divine and authentic. Jeremiah makes it plain. In chapter 8 he rebukes Judah's rulers: How can you say, We are wise, and the Lord's law is with us? The lying pen of the scribes has wrought a lie; the wise are shamed and taken; they have cast away the Lord's word, and there is no wisdom in them — from prophet to priest they all work a lie.

In chapter 18 those same rulers plot against him: Come, let us devise devices against Jeremiah. The law will not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and ignore all his words. Far from approving his prophecies, they fought him. Yet Jehoiakim is charged most heavily for rejecting the authority of those prophecies that Baruch had written out, and for cutting them with a scribe's knife and burning them (Jeremiah 36). On Rome's principles, what great crime was the king committing in refusing as divine a writing the Church's judgment had not yet approved — a writing her rulers were then attacking?
added_allusions: Jeremiah vs Jewish Church rulers; Jehoiakim and Baruch's scroll
translator_notes: XL: Jeremiah 8 / 18 / 36 Baruch-Jehoiakim against priestly opposition restored; OT prophets before priestly approval (PDF 55 / book p. 42-43).

title: Pastors cannot ground their own certainty about Scripture in the Church's judgment of themselves
english: Finally, since by the Church on which Scripture's authority for us is said to hang Rome means the pastors and bishops who rule the Church, we ask: whence does Scripture's authority hang for the pastors themselves, and how do they know these books are divine and God-inspired?

They cannot appeal here to a Church judgment that founds the pastors' own faith in Scripture. The pastors and bishops are that Church whose testimony is in question. They would then learn from themselves which writings are true Scripture, and their faith would rest on their own word. To leave no escape, take those who first gave such a judgment: they could not lean on other pastors' rulings.

Yet Rome will not have the Church's pastors driven by enthusiasms or taught Scripture by immediate revelation — for such enthusiasms and immediate revelations, they say, no longer have place in God's Church. Bishops and doctors reach that knowledge with the Holy Spirit teaching and leading, but also through their own study, diligence, careful reading of the books, and close weighing of the many arguments the Spirit uses to beget faith in Scripture in them. What absurdity is it, then, to say the faithful are led the same way by the Spirit into knowledge of sacred Scripture? At least this much follows plainly: Scripture can be established for us without enthusiasm or immediate revelation — and also without some authentic, infallible Church judgment.
translator_notes: XLI: pastors-as-Church circularity; Spirit-mediated study without authentic Church judgment; natural close before Pars IV (PDF 55-56 / book p. 43).

title: Pars IV opens: adversaries' arguments against the Reformed position remain to be answered
english: In the immediately preceding disputation we set out the state of this question and confirmed the true view with the arguments that seemed to us most fit. What remains is to sift the adversaries' arguments and show, as briefly and clearly as we can, how empty they are.
translator_notes: Pars IV Thesis I: open after Pars III XLI; adversaries' arguments remain (PDF 55 / book p. 43). Decorative initial D on DISPUTATIONE.

title: First adversary argument: Scripture cannot prove Scripture, so the Church's testimony must
english: Their first attempt is to prove that Scripture's authority hangs on the Church's. Scripture, they say, cannot be proved by Scripture. So for the faithful to be sure of Scripture, some divine and infallible testimony must prove it. That testimony, they claim, can only be the Church's — none more certain or august on earth.

If you answer that Scripture in many places asserts its own divinity, they retort that we would already have to be persuaded of that divinity from elsewhere before we could believe the assertion. Mere self-claim is not enough: most of the Apocrypha claimed to be divine and were rightly rejected.

And it seems plain that Scripture cannot prove Scripture, because every proof moves from what is better known — and the same thing cannot be both better and less known than itself. Nothing from Scripture proves anything to someone who does not yet grant Scripture's authority, or who still doubts it.
translator_notes: Pars IV II: first adversary argument — Scripture cannot prove Scripture; Church testimony required; Apocrypha self-claim (PDF 55 / book p. 43).

title: The argument is a fallacy that overturns every first rule of faith, including Rome's
english: I answer that this is a mere fallacy with which Rome can be pressed as hard as we can. Turn it back on them: the Church's voice and testimony is not the supreme rule of faith; its authority for us hangs on some other principle of faith better known and more certain.

There must be another divine testimony, clearer and surer than the Church's, by which the Church's testimony itself is established — because the Church's authority cannot be proved by the Church's own word. The same thing is not better known and less known than itself; nothing from the Church's testimony proves anything to someone ignorant of that authority, or still doubting it.
If the argument is worth anything, it overturns faith altogether. No rule of faith can be offered as first and supreme without leaving room for the same objection.
translator_notes: Pars IV III: retort — same fallacy topples Church-as-supreme-rule; OCR Uefpondeo/suprana/ridci restored (PDF 55).

title: Formalized, the major is false: a first principle need not prove itself or be evident
english: To expose the cheat, reduce the argument to form. They must argue: whatever is not evident of itself and cannot prove itself is not a first principle of faith or supreme rule whose authority does not hang elsewhere — it must be proved through something else. But Scripture is not evident, nor can it prove itself. Therefore, and so on.

The major is plainly false. On the contrary: what is a first principle of faith must neither prove itself nor be proved through another — and yet need not be something evident. In the human sciences some principles are first: the rest hang on them and are proved through them, while they hang on nothing else in that order, or they would not be first, and win assent of themselves. Faith is the same.

Either admit a circle, or an infinite regress — both absurd — or stop at some principle on which the rest of faith hangs, proved by no prior principle and not by itself either, since the same thing cannot prove itself, yet winning immediate belief and assent of itself.
translator_notes: Pars IV IV: reduce to form; major false; first principles neither self-proving nor evident; stop vs circle/regress (PDF 55-56 / book pp. 43-44).

title: Faith principles are not self-evident like science, yet we believe them immediately by the Spirit
english: Faith's principles and the sciences' differ here: the sciences' principles are self-known and evident, and by their own light compel the intellect to assent. Faith's principles, though they have some moral evidence, are — strictly and properly — inevident, and do not by their own light win the assent faith requires.

Yet they agree in this: as we assent to natural principles immediately by the natural light of the intellect, so we believe faith's principles immediately by the Spirit's illumination and impulse. And as nothing stops natural principles from sometimes being proved a posteriori, so faith's principles can be proved — but only a posteriori, and only ad hominem.
translator_notes: Pars IV V: faith vs science principles; moral evidence; immediate Spirit assent; a posteriori / ad hominem only (PDF 56 / book p. 44).

title: Scripture can still be the first principle of faith though it is neither evident nor self-proving
english: So in the matter of faith we must come down to some principle that is neither evident of itself nor able to prove itself, yet hangs on no prior principle and of itself deserves authority and belief. Though Scripture is neither evident of itself nor able to prove itself, it does not follow that Scripture is not that first principle of faith which borrows its authority from nowhere else.
translator_notes: Pars IV VI: first faith principle need not be evident or self-proving; Scripture still can be that principle (PDF 56).

title: Rome's Church-testimony claim collapses by the same standard they press against Scripture
english: Whichever way Rome turns, it must confess that the Church's testimony — which it offers as faith's first and supreme principle — is not evident of itself, and cannot well be proved by the Church's own voice. Yet they still want that testimony to hang on no prior authority and to hold among the faithful of itself. They fight themselves when, from Scripture's inability to prove Scripture, they conclude that Scripture's authority is not first and needs a superior testimony to establish it for us.

The sum of our reply comes to this: Scripture cannot indeed be proved by Scripture itself; yet it does not follow that its authority hangs elsewhere and must be proved to us by the Church as a principle prior and superior to Scripture. As faith's first principle, Scripture wins the faithful's belief and assent not by such a proof intervening, but immediately, by the Spirit's inward efficacy impressing a sure persuasion of it on our minds.
translator_notes: Pars IV VII: Church testimony under same standard; sum of reply — Spirit's inward efficacy, not Church as prior principle (PDF 56).

title: 'Scripture cannot prove Scripture' denies only bare self-assertion, not divinity's marks in the text
english: These points, though, must be taken carefully. When we grant that sacred Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture itself, we mean only that the places where Scripture proclaims itself divinely inspired are not fit arguments to convince and persuade someone who already denies sacred Scripture's authority.

That does not stop us saying, in another sense, that Scripture proves itself: as the preceding theses showed, sacred Scripture bears many marks and arguments of divinity by which it asserts itself true and divine — just as heaven and earth proclaim and show God as their author, not by a bare spoken claim, but by the excellence of their nature and the traces of divine power and wisdom visible in them.

Or as a book claims Aristotle or Euclid as its author not from the title alone, but from the genius of the teaching, the sharpness of style, and the manner of argument — the sort that can belong only to those rare minds.
translator_notes: Pars IV VIII: dextre — bare self-assertion vs divinity marks; heaven/earth; Aristotle/Euclid analogy (PDF 56 / book p. 44). IX+ remain.

title: Immediate belief is not blind persuasion; moral marks are helps, not de fide proofs
english: Next, when we say we believe Scripture immediately by the Spirit's inward efficacy, not by some proof stepping in between, we do not mean that our faith about sacred Scripture is a blind persuasion with no reason of its own.
Nor do we deny that the person who believes Scripture as he should is led there by arguments that can persuade a prudent mind that Scripture is true and comes from God.

By that word immediately we shut out only the proofs the schools call de fide — proofs drawn from some principle of faith, that make a matter of faith, and that can by themselves found an article of faith — not every kind of proof whatever.

The arguments that urge sacred Scripture's divinity are not of that kind. They are not taken from any principle or rule of faith, but only from various notes and signs, and they consist wholly of moral arguments that cannot of themselves yield the certainty faith requires — for the certainty owed to faith equals, if it does not surpass, every certainty demonstration can produce.

So although those proofs are helps to faith and motives for believing, the full certainty by which we ought to embrace the sacred books is not to be referred to them as its proper and chief foundation, but rather to the Spirit's inward persuasion.
translator_notes: Pars IV IX: immediate ≠ blind; scholae de fide vs moral notes/signs; certainty of faith vs demonstration (PDF 56–57 / book pp. 44–45). Page-turn after tantum restored.

title: Immediate excludes Church authority as faith's foundation, not the Church's teaching ministry
english: But when we say the certainty of our faith about Scripture's divinity is to be referred immediately to the Spirit's inward persuasion, the adversaries press hard: things that belong to faith — that this or that book was written by divine inspiration — are no longer had by immediate revelations, but by God's ordinance must be learned and received from the teaching Church; otherwise a window opens to fanatics and Enthusiasts.
Reply. Saying something is believed immediately by the Spirit's illumination and impulse can mean two things.

First, it can shut out the work and ministry of people who explain and commend what is to be believed — the way Paul received the Gospel not from a man nor through a man, but was taught immediately by the Holy Spirit. Immediate revelation of that kind no longer has a place in God's Church. Nor does the Spirit, in the common and ordinary way, reveal to the faithful which books were written by divine inspiration. Faith about Scripture is generated in us through the Church's work and ministry as she hands down and recommends the sacred books.

Yet in another sense Scripture can be said to be believed immediately by the Spirit's inward testimony: namely, so that any foreign authority is shut out — whether some unwritten word, or the teaching Church — that would be the properly so-called argument of our faith by which the Spirit founds that faith.

So we believe Scripture immediately because the faith we give it, and which God's Spirit impresses on us, does not properly rest on any external argument or medium, nor is it founded on a word in the Church's mouth.

Likewise, on the Roman Doctors' own view, the faith given to the teaching Church as she proposes God's word (which they believe is in her mouth) does not rest on some alien authority different from that word's authority, nor even take the Church's own testimony and voice as its argument — that would be an argument of itself — but is immediately from the Spirit's illumination and instinct. He still, they say, uses motives that dispose people to trust the Church, which they call the Church's notes.
So by immediately we exclude the Church's authority as faith's foundation, not simply the teaching Church's work and ministry.
translator_notes: Pars IV X: two senses of immediate — exclude enthusiasm (Paul) vs exclude Church as foundation not ministry; Roman notes analogy (PDF 57 / book p. 45). OCR: fenestram / disci / notas Ecclesiae restored.

title: Adversaries press recognition of books and Protestant discord as against immediate Spirit persuasion
english: But the adversaries keep pressing. If the faithful received Scripture immediately by the Spirit's inward illumination and persuasion, and not because of the Church's teaching and testimony as their rule of faith, then — they say — those who have God's Spirit could, without the Church's authority and testimony, infallibly and certainly tell divine books from ones that are not. Experience, they claim, says otherwise.

Before the Church judged and determined, many truly divine books were doubted — for example the Epistle to the Hebrews, John's Apocalypse, and several other New Testament books. Others that were not Canonical or divine were ignorantly taken as such even by pious people.

And to press harder: You Protestants, they say, who boast you have that Spirit of God by which sacred and divine books are told from the apocryphal, are not agreed among yourselves; Lutherans doubt the Epistle of James and some others that Calvinists admit.

To set the matter before the eyes and refute us among our own by experience, they read someone from our common people a chapter of an Apocryphal book and a chapter of a Canonical book with the author's and book's name hidden, then ask whether he can tell by the Spirit's help which is divine.

added_allusions.note: Named as disputed NT books in adversaries' objection

translator_notes: Pars IV XI: recognition objection; Hebrews / Apocalypse / James; Apocrypha–Canon blind test (PDF 57 / book p. 45). Adversaries' italic taunt kept as reported speech.

title: Reply: the Spirit's unction is real but unequal; Philippians 3 bears with the imperfect
english: Reply. It is true that God grants his Spirit to all the faithful and leads them into knowledge of his word, and that — as John says — they have an anointing from the Holy One that teaches them concerning all things.

Yet not all share that spirit of faith and wisdom equally. God does not dispense it to each by the same measure; he gives a greater supply to some and a lesser to others. Nor does that anointing teach every believer simply everything, but at least whatever suits each calling and is needed for each one's salvation and knowledge, according to state, condition, and place in God's Church.
So someone gifted with faith and knowledge of divine things enough for salvation may still err on some point of faith and fail to recognize some part of God's word.

That is why Paul in Philippians 3 wants those who are perfect to bear with those who think otherwise and keep brotherly communion while God reveals what they have not yet reached: As many of us as are perfect, let us think this; and if you think anything otherwise, God will also reveal this to you. Yet in what we have already reached, let us walk by the same rule and think the same.
translator_notes: Pars IV XII: 1 John unction; unequal measure; Philippians 3:15–16 (PDF 57–58 / book pp. 45–46). Joannes unctionem / Quotquot perfecti restored.

title: Salvation does not require knowing every canonical book; reception may still be immediate
english: It is not necessary for anyone's salvation to receive and acknowledge every book of Scripture and every part of them.

So it is no wonder if all who have received the spirit of faith and revelation, even in some measure, still miss certain parts of Scripture — taking a truly divine book for human, or conversely taking a mere product of human wit for something written by divine inspiration.

It is plainly unjust, and against reason, to demand that any ordinary believer be able at once by himself to tell any scrap of a Canonical book from a scrap of an Apocryphal one. Salvation does not require that.

Yet it does not follow that those who embrace books some have rejected or not known, and take them on faith, do so only through the Church's testimony and authority as faith's foundation, and not immediately by the Spirit's inward testimony and illumination — with which they have been given a greater supply in this part.
translator_notes: Pars IV XIII: salvation need not know every book; injustice of particle test; reception may still be immediate by Spirit (PDF 58 / book p. 46).

title: Retorsion: Rome's faithful cannot better tell true councils from false than our people tell canon from apocrypha
english: Plenty of people Rome itself counts as true believers are no better at spotting a forged church-testimony, an unlawful council, or adulterated canons than our ordinary hearers are at spotting Apocrypha next to Canon.
Even their own learned men quarrel over whether some councils bind, and they do not settle the question among themselves.
Still they insist their church's teaching and witness is faith's supreme rule, depending on no higher authority, and that the faithful must submit to it at once under the Spirit's impulse.
translator_notes: Pars IV XIV: retorsion — germanum testimonium / Councils / Canons; Rome's own discord (PDF 58 / book p. 46). XV+ (Scripture doubtful without Church) remains.

title: Adversaries: without the Church Scripture is doubtful and uncertain
english: The Roman doctors next try to prove that Scripture's authority for us hangs on the Church's.
Without the Church's authority and witness, they say, Scripture is doubtful and uncertain for us, and must be confirmed by that authority and witness.

They argue that without it we cannot know for certain which books are holy and divine: heretics and idle men have forged many writings under the Prophets' and Apostles' names; not everything Prophets and Apostles wrote earned divine authority (Solomon and others wrote things never numbered among the sacred letters); and scarcely any biblical book has escaped doubt or outright denial from professing Christians.

The Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament; the Ptolemaeans Moses; the Marcionites the Gospels except Luke alone — and so on. We still contest Rome over certain books they force into the Old Testament canon as Apocrypha. Even among the orthodox there was once doubt about many New Testament books, and there is still doubt among those who have left Rome in these later centuries — Jude, James, and some letters of John and Peter.
Add corruption, depravation, and interpolation by heretics, with additions and omissions; some still suspect the first part of John 8 and the story of the adulterous woman.

In so great a clash of opinions about the sacred books and their parts, they ask, how can truth be found without the Church's authority and judgment? How do you know those books are truly the Prophets' and Apostles'? And even if they are, how do you know they were written by divine inspiration rather than human care, and have reached us whole rather than variously corrupted?

They conclude that for faith about Scripture to rest on a firm base we must turn to the Church, which by a certain and infallible judgment tells divine books from Apocrypha and forgeries — a judgment the faithful may safely trust.
translator_notes: Pars IV XV: adversaries' second argument — Scripture doubtful without Church; forged books; Manichaeans/Ptolemaeans/Marcionites; Apocrypha; Jude/James/John/Peter; John 8 adulteress (PDF 58 / book p. 46).

title: Reply: the argument is a sophism; retorsion on doubtful Church authority
english: They press and inflate this with a fine show; yet anyone who looks into the argument and weighs it carefully will see it is a mere sophism on a false presupposition.
To make that plain even to them, we can argue the same way against them and overturn the foundation they put under their own faith.
The Church's authority is doubtful and uncertain. Therefore its teaching is not faith's supreme rule, nor does the Church hold first authority for us.

That doubt is plain: people dispute what authority the Church has — whether some infallible divine authority, as Rome wants, or, as we hold, great yet human and open to error. Among Christians it is not even settled which church is true; Christianity is split into many parties, and each claims to be the true Church.

So we ask them: amid so many Christian sects, by what argument do you prove that yours is the true Church and its authority infallible? They cannot fall back on Scripture, whose authority they also put in doubt and make to hang on the Church as better known and higher. Still less can they plead their own church's witness, which is the very thing under dispute.

They must either fall silent, or turn to those marks of the true Church by which they think it only probable that Rome is the true Church. But what we need here is not mere probability — it is a lawful foundation for faith that proves the matter to be of faith.

Scripture, moreover, bears far clearer and brighter marks of divinity than the Church does, and there is no lack of strong persuasive arguments — short of strict demonstration — many of which were already set out in the first part of these Theses.
translator_notes: Pars IV XVI: sophisma / false presupposition; retorsion — Church authority doubtful; sects; marks of true Church only probable; Scripture clearer notas (PDF 59 / book p. 47). OCR illustiores/argumenta restored.

title: Retorsion on popes and councils: their authority is likewise doubtful
english: When Rome's doctors locate that church authority chiefly in councils and popes, the same argument turns on them.
I prove that papal and conciliar authority is not first and supreme by the same token: it is doubtful and uncertain.

Some popes were intruders, irregularly created. Often several antipopes excommunicated one another and branded one another Antichrists. Councils that called themselves ecumenical and gathered in Christ's name favored heretics and were not lawful — Ariminum for the Arians; the second Ephesine for the Eutychians.
Second Nicaea and Frankfurt under Charlemagne cannot both be lawful: one banned the worship of images, the other commanded it under anathema — so one of them erred.

In the later Roman Church of these past centuries many councils have each styled themselves ecumenical, yet some were rejected, some approved, some half accepted and half refused. Their own doctors quarrel sharply over certain ones.

Bellarmine signs the Lateran under Leo X; the Gallican Church refuses its decisions, because it set the Roman pontiff above the whole Church and a universal council. Constance, which many in France receive whole, Bellarmine and others reject as to its first canons, because it set the council above the pope. Some Roman doctors revere Basel; others brand it a mere conciliabulum.
translator_notes: Pars IV XVII: retorsion on Pontiffs/Councils — Antipopes; Ariminum; Ephesus II; Nicaea II vs Frankfurt; Lateran Leo X / Gallican; Constance; Basel conciliabulum (PDF 59 / book p. 47). Tess misnumbered XVII as XVI restored.

title: How do you know Trent is lawful, or papal acts uncorrupted?
english: We may fairly ask them in turn: how do you know this or that council is lawful, or that this pope is not an intruder created by defect — like many others whose successors cancelled their acts and stained their memory?

By what certain argument do you prove Trent was truly gathered in Christ's name? Because it says so? Nothing proves itself; and many wicked councils have boasted the same Spirit. Because the Roman pope approved it? He also approved that Lateran whose authority not all Romanists will bind themselves to.

By what certain argument of faith can you prove the approving popes were lawful and did not seize the see by force or simony? At best you have historical and moral certainty, which does not suffice for faith.

How will anyone trust that copies of councils and papal decrees are uncorrupted, with nothing added or cut, when it is certain many decrees were fastened on popes and many councils' acts corrupted and spoiled?
A fresh papal or conciliar declaration will not end the doubt: the same difficulties rise against the latest council as against the earlier one, and so without end.
If their case against Scripture's certainty and authority stands, the authority of church, councils, and popes falls with it — and no foundation of faith is left.
translator_notes: Pars IV XVIII: Trent self-witness; Lateran approval; historical/moral certainty insufficient; corrupted decrees; infinite regress (PDF 59-60 / book pp. 47-48).

title: Any first rule of faith is logically indemonstrable
english: I dare say one cannot even imagine a foundation of faith against which the same cavils would not be lawful.

Whatever is offered as faith's first rule must be something logically inevident and not properly demonstrable. Theologians and scholastics agree: the principles of faith are inevident and indemonstrable.
Nor can it be proved from other, prior, better-known principles of faith — or it would not be first, and some earlier rule would take its place.

So the first rule of faith, whose authority for us is supreme, cannot be proved by arguments of faith a priori, nor can the questions of irreligious men be met about it by demonstrations and strictly necessary, evident reasons.
translator_notes: Pars IV XIX: any first fidei regula logically inevidens / indemonstrabilia (PDF 60 / book p. 48). OCR X/xl restored to XIX.

title: False presupposition: what many deny is not thereby uncertain for the sound
english: To see the sophism's emptiness more clearly, note how many false things it assumes.

First it assumes that whatever many deny, or many doubt, is doubtful and uncertain for us. Admit that, and nothing certain remains. Almost nothing so certain and evident has escaped doubt — or flat denial — from many.

Then it would not be certain from the sight of heaven and earth that God is, because Epicureans and atheists deny it. First principles of the sciences would not be certain, because Pyrrhonians who suspended all assent doubted them too. And Rome's own church authority would not be certain for Romanists, because the rest of Christians deny it.

What is doubted without desert, and denied without reason, does not cease to be certain for those who judge rightly. The error and doubt of idle, perverse, foolish people about things certain in themselves do not touch the certainty of sound minds rightly disposed.
translator_notes: Pars IV XX: first false presupposition — denial by many does not make uncertainty for the sound; Epicureans/Atheists; Pyrrhonii (PDF 60 / book p. 48).

title: What cannot be demonstrated can still be a sure rule of faith
english: Next the argument assumes that what cannot be demonstrated by necessary and evident proofs cannot be certain for faith, or a sure rule and foundation of faith among believers. That is utterly false.
Whatever first rule of faith you set must be something that cannot be proved by evident — and, speaking logically, strictly necessary — arguments.

Such proofs would have to come from its own testimony, from other principles of faith, or from human reason. It cannot prove itself from its own witness. It cannot be proved from other faith-principles, because as first rule it is already supposed the best-known principle — so weaker ones would be useless except perhaps ad hominem. And it cannot be proved from human reason: a rule of faith is properly inevident, and so can only be urged by moral arguments, not demonstrated by necessary ones.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXI: second false presupposition — indemonstrable can still be certain rule of faith; self-proof / ad hominem / moral suasions (PDF 60-61 / book pp. 48-49).

title: Church authority does not remove the same inquisitive doubts
english: Third, the argument assumes that doubts human reason can raise against Scripture are cleared by the Church's authority. That too is false.

To someone asking how we know circulating books are the Apostles' and Prophets', or that there ever were Apostles and Prophets, it is not enough to say the Church so teaches — he will ask with equal right how we know the Church speaks truth and is led by the Spirit.

With so many Christian sects, how do we know this rather than that is the true Church — or that any Church of God is on earth at all? Then they have nothing left against such an inquirer but those marks and prejudices that make Rome's authority look credible to them.

But what we need here is not that kind of probability — it is what proves the matter to be of faith and can bear faith as its foundation. And if we did have to go there, we are ready to show that Scripture's authority is recommended by far more and surer arguments and marks than any Christian church's.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXII: third false presupposition — Church does not remove the same doubts; percunctator; notae/praejudicia only credible. XXIII+ (pressius application) remains.

title: Closer application: the doubt syllogism and two senses of uncertainty
english: But to deal more closely now, apply this to the argument on the table. It runs like this: what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly believed unless some higher authority confirms it; Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us; therefore some higher authority must confirm it — and that can only be the Church.
I answer that something can be called doubtful and uncertain to us in two respects: with respect to faith, and with respect to human reason.

Uncertain for faith is what God has not revealed and inspired. Uncertain for human reason is what cannot be shown by necessary and evident proofs. So distinguish the minor: Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us. Said of human reason, that can be granted; said of faith, it must be denied.

Scripture can of course be urged on human reason with many good, weighty arguments. Because those arguments are not logical or mathematical demonstrations, we allow that Scripture may be called uncertain to human reason. But it is false that what reason finds uncertain and indemonstrable cannot be certain for faith. What can be demonstrated is, to that extent, not a matter of faith at all.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXIII: pressius application of the doubt syllogism; duplex respectus fidei / rationis humanae. OCR page-turn canda→applicanda; long-s normalized (PDF 61 / book p. 49).

title: Reply to the major: what cannot be demonstrated can still be faith's first rule
english: As for the major — that what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly grasped or stand as a sure rule of faith unless a higher authority confirms it — the reply is that this is utterly false if "uncertain to us" means "what cannot be demonstrated and confirmed by wholly necessary arguments."

What cannot be proved by necessary and evident arguments in the philosophical sense can still be firmly believed and be a sure rule of faith, even without confirmation from an authority prior and superior for us.

As we have just shown, the first rule of faith must be something non-evident that cannot be demonstrated — and that neither can nor should be confirmed by a higher authority. Otherwise it would not be, as supposed, faith's first and supreme rule, but only a subordinate, inferior one.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXIV: major premise falsissima if incertum = indemonstrable; prima fidei regula must be inevidens. OCR restorations from tess+pdftotext.

title: Reply to the minor's confirmation: rash doubt does not unsettle the instructed
english: As for the confirmation of the minor — that Scripture's books are doubtful apart from the Church because many books were foisted on the Apostles and genuine writings were doubted — the reply is that what is doubtful to the ignorant, the perverse, or the poorly taught can still be certain for the faithful and devout who are well taught and enlightened by the Holy Spirit.
Rash, unjust doubt from some people does nothing to shake the certainty of those with sound judgment.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXV: minor confirmation — forgery/doubt among the uninstructed vs certainty for Spirit-taught faithful; sani judicii.

title: Importunate questions demand demonstration of the indemonstrable
english: As for those importunate questions — How do you prove the Apostles existed and wrote by divine impulse, and that the circulating books are truly theirs? — something unjust is being demanded of us: that we demonstrate what is indemonstrable.

We freely admit that we cannot demonstrate those things mathematically or logically. We deny that it follows that those books cannot be faith's certain first rule. It belongs to faith's principles to be non-evident and not provable by philosophically necessary and evident arguments.

That does not mean we have nothing to answer profane objectors. We have arguments enough for a prudent person — that the Apostles and Prophets wrote by divine impulse, and that we hold their genuine books — many of which we already set out in Part I of these theses; there is no need to repeat them here.

We only grant that those arguments lack logical or mathematical evidence, and so leave the matter "uncertain" if one chooses to call the non-evident and undemonstrable (anapodeikton) uncertain. Even so, whatever uncertainty they leave cannot be cleared by some church judgment or determination — as we have just proved.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXVI: importunate Unde probatis…; indemonstrabile; Greek anapodeikton (ἀναπόδεικτον) in Latin lock. Part I motives recalled; Church judgment cannot clear leftover uncertainty.

title: Next argument from Church practice: rejection of Apocrypha
english: Enough on that argument. On to another. The Roman doctors also try to prove that Scripture's authority for us hangs on the Church's from the Church's use and practice.

Apocryphal books, they say, which impostors published under Prophets' and Apostles' names and tried to pass off as sacred, were rejected and exploded by the faithful — and that was by the Church's authority and judgment, which wisely separated those forgeries from the divine books and struck them from the Canon, or at least never judged them receivable.

They pile up Fathers for this. The synopsis attributed to Athanasius, explaining why the Gospels of Thomas, Peter, according to the Hebrews, and the like are not approved, says the Canons of the holy Catholic Church sanctioned four Gospel books for us; besides those it is not safe to have another.

Augustine likewise rejects a Gospel of Thomas the Manichees were offering: We need not believe this Scripture, because it is not in the Catholic Canon; and again, The ecclesiastical Canon rejects these Scriptures. They add Eusebius, who in the Ecclesiastical History often calls such writings Apocrypha because the ancients never mention them, and no church writer cites them or bothers to record them.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXVII: close prior argument; new praxis/usus argument — Apocrypha rejected by Church; Athanasius synopsis / Augustine on Gospel of Thomas / Eusebius. OCR page-turn into book p. 50.

title: Disputed New Testament books said to wait on Church determination
english: When even among the orthodox some truly divine and Apostolic books were sometimes doubted — Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, and the Apocalypse — they claim this was because the Church had not yet given its judgment, and that the doubt was finally lifted by church determination: at Laodicea, the third council of Carthage, and the decrees of Popes Innocent and Gelasius.
By those, they say, not only the New Testament books just named, but also the Old Testament books still disputed between us and Rome, were received into the Canon — as they would have it.

For confirmation they cite Jerome on James: though it was being put about as written by someone else under his name, little by little it gained authority. On Jude: though most rejected it, antiquity and use earned it authority.

In the same vein Jerome writes to Dardanus on Hebrews and John's Apocalypse: We receive both, following not present custom but the authority of the ancient writers, who usually cite both not as they sometimes do the Apocrypha, but as Canonical and Ecclesiastical.
added_allusions: Jerome to Dardanus on Hebrews and Apocalypse
translator_notes: Pars IV XXVIII: disputed NT books (Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Apocalypse); Laodicea / III Carthage / Innocent & Gelasius; Jerome to Dardanus. OT deuterocanon still litigated.

title: Fathers alleged to refute heretics from Church authority alone
english: Finally, when heretics rejected or doubted many books whose authority was always sure among the Orthodox, many Roman doctors try to show that the Fathers refuted them from the Church's authority, consent, and testimony, by which they vindicated those books' divinity and authority.

So Augustine on Acts, which the Manichees denied: I must believe this book if I believe the Gospel, since Catholic authority recommends both Scriptures to us alike. And against the same: The authority of our books, strengthened by so many nations' confession through the successions of Apostles, bishops, and councils, stands against you; yours has none, being put forward by so few.

From this and the like they conclude that our faith about sacred Scripture hangs on the Church's judgment, and that its authority, testimony, and consent are the rule and plumbline by which all Scripture must be tested so we can be sure of it — citing Augustine's famous line, I would not believe the Gospel unless the Catholic Church's authority moved me.

And elsewhere the same holy man: The faithful mind will keep this measure in the Canonical Scriptures — prefer what all Catholic churches receive to what some refuse; and among books not received by all, prefer what more and weightier churches receive to what fewer churches of lesser standing hold.
added_allusions: Augustine Contra epistolam Manichaei (Ego vero Evangelio…)
Augustine De doctrina Christiana on canonical reception
translator_notes: Pars IV XXIX: Fathers vs heretics from Church testimony; Augustine on Acts vs Manichees; Ego vero Evangelio non crederem; De doctrina measure for disputed books. amussim = plumbline.

title: First clarify what adversaries mean by Church
english: To answer all this, first recall what the adversaries mean by "Church." That is essential for the real state of the question and for clearing away the ambiguity of the name.
Church is not here taken collectively for the whole multitude of the faithful who are and ever have been. The debate is not properly about that Church's authority.

Even though sacred Scripture's authority does not depend on the authority of the Church so taken, it is still certain that from that Church's testimony and consent one can draw a divine, infallible argument for Scripture's authority that binds our faith — because that Church includes the Apostolic and primitive Church, whose role it was to confirm Scripture's Canon by a sure divine reason and hand it to the faithful as what would thereafter be faith's unique rule.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXX: clarify Ecclesiae nomen — not collective faithful; Apostolic/primitive consent can yield divine argument without making present Church the formal ground. Natural close before XXXI present pastors.

title: Present Church means present pastors
english: But by "present Church" the Pontificians mean the Church of each age.
Even then they do not mean the community of the faithful living in one and the same age. They restrict the name "Church" to the overseers and pastors of the Church.

So when they claim that the authority of Scripture depends on the authority of the Church, they mean that the faith by which the faithful people receive the books of Scripture as true and divine rests on the testimony of the pastors then in office, and settles on that testimony.

Why? Because in the pastors and prelates of the Church there always resides a certain infallible, divine authority by which they can decide the truth and divinity of a book, so that their sentence and judgment bind our faith.

They even hold that those pastors have power to make authentic a book that until then was of doubtful authority, and about which either side might be held, so that after their determination it must be ranked with the other sacred and canonical books.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXI: adversaries mean by Ecclesia praesens the overseers/pastors of each age, not the collective faithful; popular faith in Scripture is said to rest on those pastors' infallible determination.

title: Older scholastics vs today's schools
english: Among the older scholastics some did restrict that power of deciding Scripture infallibly and with certainty to the Apostolic Church. They taught that it belongs to the present Church only insofar as that Church is counted one body with the Apostolic — as an old man truly did what he did as a boy, though as an old man he can no longer do those same acts.

That was the view of Durandus, of Thomas Netter of Walden, and in the previous age of Driedo. Today that view is commonly judged wrong, and the doctors of the present Roman schools yield to the earlier opinion instead.

So the question is whether from the Church's practice, and from the ancient Fathers' arguments recited above, one may conclude that the pastors who govern the Church in each age have authority so great that it is our rule of faith about Scripture — more certain and better known to us than Scripture itself — and the chief foundation of our faith in sacred Scripture.
That is what we deny. The proofs already brought do nothing to establish it.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXII: Durandus / Waldensis / Driedo limited infallible canon-decision to Apostolic Church; modern Roman schools reject that and claim present pastors as rule. We deny.

title: Apocrypha rejected for never being in the Canon
english: We gladly grant that the doctors of the ancient Church rejected the apocryphal books heretics had forged and pushed as divine on this ground: those books were never in the Church's Canon, nor acknowledged, held, and cited as divine by the Church's doctors.

We treat that argument as sound, and we use the same kind of argument against the books Rome adds to the Old Testament beyond the Jewish Canon — because the Jewish Church never acknowledged them, even while it was still God's true and only Church.

Nor did the primitive Christian Church: its doctors, by common consent (a very few perhaps excepted), remove those books from the Canon, though they allow them to be read in churches as useful for the people's edification.

Many apocryphal books do carry marks of vanity and traces of human weakness that show they are not God-inspired. Still, speaking absolutely and in general, we judge no argument more fit to break their authority than this: the true Church of God never held them as divine.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXIII: concede Fathers rejected forged Apocrypha as never-canonical; same ground against Roman OT additions above Jewish/primitive Canon.

title: The argument needs no present infallibility
english: For that argument to stand, the pastors of the present Church need not have a divine, infallible authority better known to us and superior to Scripture itself.

The argument does not simply rest on their authority.
