Its force is this: if those apocryphal books were truly divine, and written by the prophets and apostles to be a perpetual rule of faith in the Church, the prophets and apostles themselves would without doubt have handed them down and recommended them as such — like the other canonical books, and sealed with the rest of Scripture's Canon.

Had that happened, the apostolic men and the Church next after the apostles, which received their other books with such reverence, would without doubt have received these too — if not among all the faithful, at least among the greatest or a notable part.
That the ancient Church doctors do not even mention them is a clear sign that the apostles, when they sealed Scripture's Canon, did not admit such books, but rejected and cast them out.

It is in no way likely that God by His singular providence moved a prophet or apostle to write so that his book would be a rule of faith and serve the faithful's instruction and comfort — and yet allowed His Church neither to receive nor to acknowledge that book.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXIV: praxis argument does not require present pastors' infallibility; force is Apostolic non-tradition of forged books. OCR repudiase noted.

title: Truly canonical books were never so doubtful
english: Next, their second proof from books once doubted — as if certain divine books were once of doubtful authority because the Church had not yet spoken, and all doubt later fell by the Church's judgment and definition.
I say first: the authority of books that are truly divine and canonical was never so doubtful that it was once lawful to doubt them and later unlawful, which is what the Pontificians claim.

Those who doubted Hebrews, John's Apocalypse, and other New Testament books did so rashly and without just cause. Just as today anyone who denied or questioned those books' authority would not be blameless, so those who once stripped them of authority or tried to make them doubtful deserved blame.

But as for the other books Rome wants in the Old Testament Canon, about which they themselves grant it was once lawful to doubt: as they were rightly doubted then, so we contend they may rightly be doubted still.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXV: first reply — truly canonical NT books never entered a state where doubt was once lawful then closed by Church definition; OT Apocrypha still rightly doubtful.

title: Doubt was only partial, never universal
english: Second: no truly divine book's authority was ever so doubtful that everyone everywhere doubted it. The doubt belonged only to some; among the rest their authority stayed certain.

Hebrews, James, and John's Apocalypse were indeed suspect to some, and by some treated as spurious — yet among most churches they always kept their authority. No time can be named when they were not received in a large part of the Christian world and held divine and authentic.

The very passages the adversaries quote as favoring them show this. Against Arians who denied Hebrews, Theodoret says they ought at least to reverence the long stretch of time in which the truth's pupils had continually read that epistle in the churches.

So Tertullian defends the Apocalypse against Marcion: we also have John's foster-churches; though Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the line of bishops traced back to the origin will still stand on John as author.
As for James, the same Eusebius who says some thought it νόθον — spurious — also testifies that it was publicly received in very many churches.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXVI: doubt never catholic; Theodoret on Hebrews; Tertullian on Apocalypse vs Marcion; Eusebius νόθον on James yet widely received. Inline Greek.

title: Doubt came from hard passages, not missing Church decree
english: Third: those who doubted those books did not doubt because they failed to see them received by the churches and recommended by the ancient Fathers' tradition naming the apostles as authors.

They doubted because, without weighing the matter enough, they thought those books contained things that did not savor of the divine Spirit and did not cohere well enough with the faith taught in the other books.
So the Latin Church doubted Hebrews, because chapters six and ten seemed to favor the Novatians, who cut off all hope of pardon from those who fell after baptism.
The Apocalypse was also suspect because of the Millenarians, who misused certain places that seemed to favor them.
Jude was rejected by some because it seems to cite an apocryphal book that once circulated under the name of Enoch the patriarch.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXVII: causes of doubt were hard texts (Novatian reading of Heb 6/10; chiliasts on Apocalypse; Jude citing Enoch), not absent Church determination.

title: Later reception was not a new Church decree
english: Finally, those books were later received by common consent — not because some new Church decree sanctioned their authority.

What had raised scruple in them gradually came into the light and was rightly understood; at last the doubters ceased, and all conceded to the ancient Fathers nearest the apostles, who recommended these books to later ages as received from them and confirmed them by frequent use and reading.
This cannot be credited to the Synod of Laodicea or the third council of Carthage: those synods were provincial, and on the adversaries' own view could not properly bind the faith.
In fact doubt about those books remained after Laodicea. In Jerome's day — later than that synod — some still doubted.

Above all, neither Carthage nor the decrees of Popes Gelasius and Innocent removed doubt about the Old Testament books they call canonical and we call apocryphal: right up to Trent, many inside the Roman Church itself rejected those books' authority.
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXVIII: reception by clearing scruples + Father-tradition, not Laodicea/Carthage/Gelasius/Innocent decrees; OT Apocrypha disputed inside Rome until Trent. Natural close before XXXIX.

title: Fathers used Church consensus against heretics — not present-pastor supremacy
english: As for that supporting point — that the Church's doctors, when they answered heretics who rejected certain books of Scripture, kept using the Church's testimony and consensus to prove those books' authority — I answer that this does not yield what the Pontificians want, or what is actually in dispute.

It does not show that the pastors who govern the Church in each age have, for us, an authority greater and better known than Scripture's, or that our faith about Scripture rests on the testimony and judgment of the pastors now in office as on a divine, infallible, chief, and proper foundation.
Those fathers were not simply arguing from the authority of the bishops of their own day as if that were a rule of faith binding every church member.

The heretics they opposed rejected certain sacred books as falsely ascribed to the apostles or apostolic men and as inventions of Catholic teachers. Against that charge the Fathers set the perpetual consensus of bishops and of the faithful who, from the apostles' time on, have received those books as handed down and recommended by the apostles as true and divine.

Only a shameless, stubborn person can refuse that consensus. Anyone today who denied that the books of Aristotle, Demosthenes, and Cicero belong to the men named on them could be answered from the continuous judgment of the learned who have always ascribed them so — and would be thought mad for refusing so constant a fame.

By equal — indeed by far greater — right, then, is the person mad who dares to oppose a tradition and fame still more constant, celebrated, and continuous, which refers the books we hold sacred to the apostles as their authors and approvers?
translator_notes: Pars IV XXXIX: Fathers-vs-heretics confirmation. Tess p064–065 + DjVu; long-s normalized. OCR restorations: usi sunt; conficti; Demosthenis & Ciceronis; famae/traditioni. Book pp. 52–53 / PDF 64–65.

title: Augustine’s literary-fame analogy for the canonical books
english: That the early Church doctors put their chief force here when they defended the authority of the canonical books from the Church's authority is plain from Augustine.

In books 32 and 33 against Faustus the Manichee, when Faustus asks how Augustine knows those letters are the apostles', Augustine answers: from the same kind of public knowledge by which Faustus knows other letters are Mani's, by which everyone knows certain books are Varro's, Plato's, or Aristotle's, and by which later ages would know the books Augustine was then writing were his.

After heaping up more such examples he concludes: That being so, who is blinded by such madness — unless overturned by consenting to the malice and deceit of lying demons — who would say the apostles' Church, so faithful and so numerous in brotherly concord, could not have deserved to hand their writings faithfully to later ages, when they have kept their chairs by most certain succession down to the bishops now sitting, and when even ordinary men's writings, inside or outside the Church, fare so well?
translator_notes: Pars IV XL: Augustine Contra Faustum 32–33 literary-attribution analogy + closing quote restored from tess against DjVu garble (libr. 32 & 33; Faustum; mendaciloquorum / fallacia / proveniat). Book p. 53 / PDF 65.

title: Perpetual consensus is strong human proof — not divine pastor-authority
english: So when a book of Scripture is disputed — whether it is truly prophetic and apostolic, and was sealed with the rest of the canon by the apostles or apostolic men — we grant that the best argument is the Church's perpetual, constant consensus and testimony, which has always referred that book to the apostles as authors or approvers.
Faith cannot be withdrawn from that witness without great shamelessness and stubbornness. We know no fitter argument for answering a sectarian or a heretic.
Yet the argument is human, not divine. Its force does not lie in some infallible, divine authority residing in the Church's overseers. That is not required for the argument to stand.

In literary questions no such infallible judging-authority can even be invented; yet the continuous consensus of the learned that ascribes certain books to Aristotle, Plato, or Galen is enough for full confidence, and anyone who fought it would rightly be thought shameless and mad.

How much more, then, does the Church's consensus — which no one doubts is ruled by God's special providence and the Spirit's help — give us confidence that this or that book was written by an apostle or prophet and recommended as divine.
translator_notes: Pars IV XLI: best human argument from perpetual consensus; explicitly not divine pastor-infallibility. Tess: sectarius; rem literariam tractant; Galeno. Book p. 53 / PDF 65.

title: Reciprocal proof does not make the Church better known than Scripture
english: However good and valid an argument may be drawn from the Church's consensus and testimony to prove a sacred book's divinity, we deny that Scripture's authority therefore depends on the Church's as on something better known and superior.

We can force this even from unwilling adversaries. Just as the Fathers answered heretics who denied Scripture from the Church's authority and testimony, they also sent schismatics who would not own Christ's true Church back to the Scriptures, and held that the true Church must be shown from them.

So Augustine with the Donatists: whether they hold the Church, let them show it only by the canonical books of the divine Scriptures. Today the Pontificians try to prove their Church and its authority from Scripture, and think they do that office well.
Yet they refuse to allow that, for us, the Church's authority is less known and certain than Scripture's — which is exactly the point under inquiry: we affirm it; they deny it.

So from the fact that a disputed book of Scripture has no fitter or surer defense against heretics than the Church's consensus and testimony, they cannot conclude that the Church's authority is for us more certain and better known than Scripture's.

They themselves must admit that a heretic who does not acknowledge the true Church cannot be answered by any firmer argument than Scripture's authority — and yet they most of all shrink from saying that sacred Scripture's authority is for us prior to and better known than the Church's.
translator_notes: Pars IV XLII: reciprocal Patristic strategy (heretics from Church; schismatics from Scripture) blocks Pontifician inference of Church-priority. Augustine vs Donatists; page turn 53–54 / PDF 65–66.

title: In dispute we often prove what is prior by what is posterior
english: So not every proof is taken from what is simply better known and more certain.

In dispute we must adapt to those we are dealing with. Against people who deny principles — even things most certain in themselves — we use weaker proofs and arguments called a posteriori: proving what is prior in knowledge, simply speaking, through what is posterior in knowledge.

Against Gentiles who deny the Christian religion we often argue from the opinions of the wise, from philosophical axioms, and from the nations' consensus — yet none of that has, for us, as much certainty as the Christian religion itself.
Even first principles, than which nothing is absolutely better known or more certain, we illustrate by examples and inductions; but their certainty and authority do not depend on those illustrations.
translator_notes: Pars IV XLIII: a posteriori / ad-hominem posture in controversy. Tess+pdftotext p066; Ethnicos; respectu nostri; inductionibus. Book p. 54 / PDF 66.

title: Summary: Church witness proves Scripture — it is not a higher rule of faith
english: In short, then: we grant that the sacred books' authority is rightly and validly proved by the Church's consensus and testimony.
We deny what the adversaries infer — that the Church's testimony is a rule of faith better known to us than Scripture itself.
Not every sound proof is taken from a rule and principle of faith, or even from what is simply better known and more certain. Often we must prove the point to the person before us, and a posteriori.
translator_notes: Pars IV XLIV: natural close of Fathers-vs-heretics confirmation before next tract De Scripturae plenitudine. Book p. 54 / PDF 66.

title: Opening: Scripture sufficiently contains all that belongs to faith and salvation
english: The Churches that left Rome in the last century hold this steadily: sacred Scripture sufficiently contains everything that belongs to faith and salvation — so that we do not need another word of God to fill what Scripture supposedly lacks.
Rome’s doctors and champions attack that claim fiercely. The dispute is serious; we take it up in these theses and a few that follow.

For clarity we will first state our Churches’ view as plainly as we can, then compare the adversaries’ view with ours so the real question stands out, and finally confirm the truth briefly and undercut the opposite case.
translator_notes: De Scripturae plenitudine Pars I thesis I open. Book pp. 54–55 / PDF 67. Title-page: Adversus necessitatem verbi cujusdam non scripti.

title: Necessary-to-salvation things are in Scripture — the rest need not be
english: First our theologians distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not.
They hold that Scripture contains what is necessary to salvation. What is not necessary need not, on their view, be in Scripture at all.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis II. Book p. 55 / PDF 67.

title: Two senses of ‘necessary to salvation’: must know — or must not reject
english: ‘Necessary to salvation’ is said in two ways.
First: no one may be ignorant of it without losing salvation, and no one is saved without express knowledge of it.
Second: no one may reject it, or have the Church teach its contrary, without sinning against his own salvation.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis III. Book p. 55 / PDF 67. OCR ‘servari’ restored; ‘nullus illud rejicere’.

title: Necessary to faith: each person’s explicit faith — or the Church’s public faith
english: So also ‘necessary to faith’ has two senses.
Either it is required for each person’s faith — no one without explicit faith in it should be counted a believer — or it belongs in general to faith’s object and binds the Church’s public faith.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis IV. Book p. 55 / PDF 67.

title: Both senses: Scripture holds all faith-and-salvation necessaries — nothing outside binds
english: When our Churches say Scripture has everything necessary to faith and salvation, they mean necessary in both senses — not the first alone.

We do not only claim that nothing outside Scripture is such that without explicit faith and knowledge of it no one can be saved. We also claim that no one should be judged to sin against Christian faith and his own salvation merely for rejecting and attacking what sacred Scripture does not teach.

So our case is not proved by listing only what explicit faith for salvation needs. Faith’s scope is wider than that minimum — yet we still hold that nothing belongs to faith that Scripture does not contain.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis V. Book p. 55 / PDF 67–68. Closes before VI substance/appendices distinction.

title: Clearer split: religion’s substance vs indifferent rites and discipline
english: To cut ambiguity, some of our theologians prefer a clearer distinction.

They separate what is the substance — the body of Christian religion — necessary by divine institution not only for faith but for morals and church order, from mere appendages and ornaments of that body.

Those ornaments are not necessary by nature or divine institution; they are indifferent, kept for order and decency: many disciplinary canons, and rites and ceremonies universal or particular — freely observed, yet not to be despised or dropped by private authority alone.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis VI. Book p. 55–56 / PDF 68. Substance vs appendices / indifferentia.

title: Scripture holds the substance — not every rite left to church prudence
english: We say Scripture contains the former kind — the substance — not those accidental appendages of church faith, morals, and discipline.

Many circumstances of worship and church polity are not set out item by item in Scripture; they are left to the prudence of church overseers under the general rule that all things be done decently and in order in God’s Church.

So Rome’s doctors waste their shot when they press old Jewish or Christian rites, statutes, and ceremonies — still kept among us in worship and polity — as if their absence from a Scripture catalogue refuted us.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis VII. Book p. 56 / PDF 68. Inline 1 Cor 14:40 sense (ordine & decenter). OCR ‘sigillatim’ / ‘fiant’ restored.

title: Contained κατὰ λέξιν or in substance — Trinity proves the point
english: From the above it is clear what we say Scripture contains. Next: how it contains them.
Dogmas and precepts may stand in a book in two ways — first κατὰ λέξιν, in the same words; second in substance, in equivalent words.

We do not claim every orthodox dogma and life-precept appears in Scripture in so many words. Some modern wranglers pin that on us: because we take up nothing outside Scripture in religion, they demand every sentence we teach be shown syllable by syllable in the text.

For us it is enough that Scripture contain the dogma in substance. Scripture nowhere says the bare words ‘God is one and three’; yet we believe it firmly, because Scripture says what comes to the same — three in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one — and in many places that God is one, while the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis VIII. Book p. 56 / PDF 68–69. Greek κατὰ λέξιν restored from damaged OCR («*t»m£h); 1 John 5:7 / Trinity example. Natural close before IX (consequence distinction). OCR soft: vitilitigatores; quin quod.

title: Expressed immediately vs mediate by consequence — two natures
english: Beside the last distinction stands another close to it. One thing is to contain a teaching expressly and immediately; another is to contain it mediately, by consequence.

On our view Scripture does not hold every dogma of faith in that immediate, express form. Still nothing that necessarily belongs to faith and religion fails to follow from Scripture by a good, open consequence.

Scripture never says in so many words that Christ has two natures, or two wills in him. Both still belong to the truth of faith, because they follow openly from what Scripture teaches in many places — that Christ is true God and true man.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis IX. Book p. 56 / PDF 68-69. Immediate vs mediate containment; two natures/wills example. OCR soft: continere; consequentiam; utrumque.

title: Drawing consequences is not adding a second rule — Acts prophets
english: So today's Sophists wrong us when they chide us for drawing a dogma from Scripture by good consequence — as if we broke our own law that Scripture alone is the rule of faith and religion, with nothing added or taken away.
To deduce from Scripture is not to add to it, nor to put another rule in its place. It is to unroll what Scripture already holds and to open its hidden stores.

In Acts the Prophets are said to testify of Christ that whoever believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Those bare words are not set down expressly in the Prophets; the Prophets are said to testify what follows from their witness.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis X. Book p. 56 / PDF 68-69. Consequence is not addition; Acts 10:43 prophets attest. OCR: retigeremus; Actis; eruimus.

title: Sigillatim vs in seed — OT proves Gospel in genere
english: Dogmas may also be drawn from a principle in two ways: item by item, distinctly and of themselves; or only in a general, mixed way, through something else.

Not every Christian dogma and ordinance can be proved from the Old Testament by itself, one by one. Baptism in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit could not be shown from the Old Testament alone if that were our only principle of faith.

Yet everything that belongs to Gospel teaching can be proved from the Old Testament in general, because from it one can show effectively that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah and the Son of God promised by the Prophets — and therefore that his teaching is true and divine, and his ordinances to be received as divine.

What follows from a principle only in that general, mixed way is in it by force and in seed. What is proved from it distinctly, item by item, may be said to be in it expressly in a looser sense — though strictly 'expressly' means the same as clearly and immediately.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XI. Book pp. 56-57 / PDF 68-69. Page-turn after pri-bari restored from tesseng-p-069. Baptism formula OT example; virtute / in semine.

title: Our claim: Scripture proves Christian doctrine distinctly, not only in seed
english: In this dispute we do not say Christian ordinances and dogmas of faith can be proved from Scripture only in a general, mixed way.
We say they can be proved distinctly, item by item — and in that sense can be said to stand expressly in Scripture, not merely by force and in seed.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XII. Book p. 57 / PDF 69. Short hinge: our sense of express containment. OCR: religionis; fidei dogmata.

title: Perfect sufficient rule — ministry and Spirit stay; no second rule
english: Since everything that belongs to faith is in sacred Scripture in the way already shown, Scripture is a perfect and sufficient rule of faith.

That sufficiency does not cancel the Church's ministry. By God's order, heavenly teaching is drawn from Scripture and given to the faithful through their pastors and teachers. It also does not cancel the Spirit's inward teaching, by which believers come to know the doctrine drawn from Scripture and set before them — without which they cannot discern it or embrace it for salvation.
Scripture's perfection and sufficiency shut out only one thing: the need of another rule that must be joined to Scripture before we have the whole doctrine of faith.
So Rome's doctors gain nothing when they argue that Scripture is not enough for salvation because otherwise the Church's ministry would be useless. Scripture itself urges that ministry.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XIII. Book p. 57 / PDF 69. Sufficient rule; ministry + Spirit remain; no second regula. OCR: hauritur; magisterii; possunt.

title: Schools and confessions: principles are Scripture itself
english: For a fuller grasp of the question, note what our schools treat and our public confessions set out. Some of it is admitting the true principles of faith and religion, and rejecting what is falsely pushed forward as such. The rest is the doctrine drawn from those true principles.

We say Scripture contains the principles of faith because those principles are Scripture itself. Our Churches admit no principles of faith beyond the inspired books that make up the body of Scripture.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XIV. Book p. 57 / PDF 69. Schools/confessions: admit principles (=Scripture) vs deduce doctrine. OCR: Verum; admissione; Scripturae corpus.

title: A rule need not prove itself — canonicity not required from Scripture
english: The fullness and sufficiency we give sacred Scripture do not require that Scripture prove its own principles — for example, that this or that book is divine and canonical.
Any rule is perfect when it measures everything else of its kind. It need not be the rule of itself.
No science asks its first principles to prove themselves; that is absurd and impossible. Principles are perfect enough in their kind if from them everything belonging to that science can be proved.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XV. Book p. 57 / PDF 69. Sufficiency does not require proving canonicity from Scripture. OCR: ex ea; Etenim; seipsa.

title: Faith's first principles stand like the axioms of a science
english: In every human art and science there are first principles proper to that field. From them every conclusion belonging to the art is drawn and proved. The principles themselves are certain in that kind and cannot be demonstrated. They are, as it were, the rule on which the rest hangs — though they neither can nor should prove themselves.
Divine teaching is the same. When its theorems are examined and we ask for their foundation, we must come to principles beyond which, in that kind at least, we cannot go.

Those principles cannot be proved by other principles of faith, and no one should demand that they prove themselves — nothing proves itself. Yet they must be held as a sufficient and perfect rule of faith, because everything else that belongs to faith is proved by them.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XVI. Book p. 57 / PDF 69-70. Science-axiom analogy for faith principles. Natural close before XVII (Spirit illumination disparity). OCR: disciplinis; consequens; sufficiente.

title: Faith principles need the Spirit's illumination — unlike science axioms
english: Theologians commonly mark this difference between the principles of faith and the principles of the sciences. Science axioms are known in themselves, evident, and by their own light compel assent from natural reason. Faith principles do not have that same evidence. So, as is right, they cannot be believed and received except through the Holy Spirit's inward illumination.

Yet they agree in this: we assent to natural principles at once by the mind's natural light, not through other better-known principles that prove them. In the same way we believe faith's principles immediately through the Spirit's illumination — not by some intervening proof drawn from other principles more known in that order.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XVII. Book pp. 57-58 / PDF 70-71. Spirit illumination disparity vs science axioms. OCR: communi; Spiritus sancti; interventu.

title: Scripture's authority is received immediately — not proved from Scripture
english: Faith's first principles must bear marks and characters of their divinity and truth, and arguments that recommend them. But they cannot, directly and properly, prove themselves. Nor do they lean on other faith principles from which they would borrow authority.
That first rule of religion — the principles of Christian faith — is for us the divine Scriptures, a fixed set of God-breathed books (θεοπνεύστων).
So on our view Scripture's authority should not be proved from Scripture itself. All Christians receive it immediately, and for its own sake.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XVIII. Book p. 58 / PDF 70-71. θεοπνεύστων restored from garbled OCR (swerd-swr / DjVu junk). Authority received immediately propter se.

title: If Scripture's divinity is doubted, prove it a posteriori — not from faith principles
english: If a contentious man denies a science's first principles, you do not prove them from themselves. You must leave that science's bounds and seek proofs elsewhere — or even use weaker, a posteriori arguments aimed at that man. That does not lessen the principles' perfection or sufficiency.

So if Gentiles and profane men call Scripture's divinity into doubt, it must be proved — yet not from Scripture's own testimony, nor from any other faith principle. The proofs called de fide (drawn from faith principles properly so named) no longer apply.

Other proofs must be used: various marks, inward and outward, by which Scripture's divinity can be known and confirmed. That still leaves Scripture, for believers, the fullest and most perfect rule of religion and faith.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XIX. Book p. 58 / PDF 70-71. Ethnicis/profanis; de fide vs external marks; fidelium respectu.

title: Rome's 'Scripture cannot prove Scripture' does not defeat sufficiency
english: Here is how to meet the argument Rome loves: that Scripture is not a full and sufficient rule of faith because Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture.
A rule need not prove itself to be perfect and sufficient. It is enough that by it everything else of the same kind can be examined and proved.

In analyzing faith, unless you allow a circle or an infinite regress — both absurd — you must stop at some principle that cannot be proved by another better known in that order, and that cannot prove itself. Nothing proves itself.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XX. Book p. 58 / PDF 70-71. Retorsion on Scripture-proves-Scripture objection; circle / infinite regress.

title: False pretended principles fall by missing the Spirit's marks — not by proof-texts
english: Scripture's perfection does not require that it prove itself. Neither must every false pretended principle of faith be rejected by direct, express proof-texts.

We believe true faith principles immediately through the Spirit's inward illumination and persuasion. He sweetly draws people to them — not by another faith principle, but by motives and marks that make their divinity known.
So to refuse what are falsely counted as faith principles, it is enough that they lack the true marks of true principles, and that traces of human ignorance and weakness show in them.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXI. Book p. 58 / PDF 70-71. Reject false principles by missing marks, not express Scriptural rebuttal required.

title: Burden of proof for Apocrypha and unwritten traditions lies on their defenders
english: Scripture's perfection is not hurt if it cannot demonstrate that this or that book, falsely presumed canonical, is really apocryphal.
Even if unwritten traditions were granted for the sake of argument, it should be enough for rejecting them that their authority cannot be shown by fit arguments as divine Scripture's can.
It is not our job to prove they are not divine. Those who press and defend them must prove that they are.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXII. Book p. 58 / PDF 70-71. Apocrypha + unwritten traditions; burden on defenders. OCR Imo/steteret restored.

title: Near consequences bind as faith articles; remote ones are only theological opinions
english: Doctrine drawn from Scripture and taught in the schools is of two kinds.

First: what Scripture states expressly, or what follows by nearest, evident consequences. Those should be proposed to the church as articles and heads of faith, with the mark of heresy for those who teach the opposite.

Second: what is rightly and soundly drawn from Scripture, yet not so clearly, and by subtler, more remote consequences. Those are not properly articles of faith, but theological truths or opinions. Their contrary should be called error — not heresy.

Rome's own doctors say only what their councils have clearly and expressly defined is de fide — not whatever they think they can weave by chaining consequence upon consequence. So they distinguish faith dogmas from their theologians' opinions: heresy against the first, error against the second.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXIII. Book pp. 58-59 / PDF 70-71. Articles vs theological opinions; Rome's de fide parallel. OCR: sane/bene; haeresin.

title: Church practices like not rebaptizing may be held without binding as heresy — Cyprian
english: So we can answer adversaries who attack the sufficiency we give Scripture. They object that our churches hold and teach some things not drawn from Scripture by consequences open and necessary enough to bind the people's faith unless some other divine authority props them up — for example, that those once baptized among heretics are not to be baptized again.
That teaching, and some others, our churches do hold and teach as agreeing with Scripture, and as confirmed by long use and the common vote of the faithful. It is rash to condemn and reject them.

Yet we do not give them such necessity that they bind Christian faith as such — as if whoever thinks otherwise must be struck from the faithful and counted a heretic. We would never want Cyprian so numbered: a holy man and martyr of Christ, who did not hold the same view of heretics' baptism that our churches hold.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXIV. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Rebaptism / Cyprian example; held without heresy-binding necessity. Natural close before XXV historical plenitude. OCR: colligi; Ecclesiis.

title: Plenitude across ages — Scripture always held what each age needed
english: From what we have already set out, it is plain enough in what sense we praise Scripture's fullness and sufficiency, and press that it contains everything necessary to faith and salvation.

We do not give that perfection only to Old and New Testament Scripture as the Apostles and apostolic men handed it down to us. From the moment God saw fit to put his word in writing, we hold that Scripture always contained all that God's people and the Church needed to worship him rightly and to reach salvation — and that they did not need to go elsewhere to draw the teaching of faith and salvation.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXV. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Opens historical plenitude: sufficiency for each age from first written word. OCR: satis; consignata; Dei populo.

title: Progressive revelation — Moses' five books vs later necessity (Hebrews 1:1)
english: It does not count against this that Scripture as we now have it holds not a few things needful for salvation that are missing from Moses' five books — which alone made up sacred Scripture for a time.
The same things were not necessary for salvation in every age. Much that now belongs of necessity to faith and religion under the New Testament did not always have that necessity.

God did not unveil all the mysteries of heavenly wisdom at once. As the Apostle says in Hebrews, he spoke πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως — in many parts and in many ways (Hebrews 1:1). From the first consigning of heavenly teaching to writing, the light of divine revelation grew little by little, until in the last times Christ brought the fullness of that teaching and announced to us the whole counsel of our salvation.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXVI. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Progressive revelation vs Moses-only corpus. Greek πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως restored; citation Hebr. 1 (OCR Hebr. 4). OCR: Mosis; aetatibus; coepit.

title: As revelation grew clearer, the Scripture corpus and Canon grew
english: As heavenly teaching grew clearer and wider, the body of the Scriptures grew with it.
When God, along the Church's changing courses, revealed something new to the Prophets and Apostles, they put it down in writing in summary. So as time went on, the Canon of Scripture was enlarged.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXVII. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Canon growth with revelation. OCR: Crescente; auctus; Canon.

title: The measure of faith is revelation — fuller light demands fuller faith
english: The more God revealed, and the more distinctly, the fuller and more distinct faith he required of men.
When revelation was thinner and darker, faith reached fewer things as well. Divine revelation is the measure of faith: for salvation we need not know and believe more than God has revealed.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXVIII. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Mensura fidei = revelatio. OCR: distincte; parcior; nosse.

title: Moses' Scripture was perfect for Israel then — always enough for the Church's need
english: So although Scripture, when first given through Moses, did not contain everything now necessary for us, it still sufficiently held what the people of Israel then needed.
Divine Scripture always had that perfection: it took in all the Church needed to do and to know.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXIX. Book p. 59 / PDF 71. Mosaic sufficiency for its age. OCR: Mosen; Israelitico; complecteretur.

title: Caution — while θεόπνευστοι still spoke, written Scripture was not yet the full deposit
english: Take that with this caution: once the θεόπνευστοι men through whom revelation's light grew are gone, and their writings are out.

Except the time when their living voice still sounded in the Church, before they had put in writing what God was pleased to reveal to them anew. For example, when the Apostles began to preach and had not yet written anything, Old Testament Scripture did not hold all needful for salvation except in a mixed, implicit way — inasmuch as it sent us to the true Messiah, from whom we would be taught God's will more fully.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXX. Book pp. 59-60 / PDF 71-72. Exception while living prophetic/apostolic voice. Greek θεοπνεύστοις restored from OCR garble. OCR: sublatis; Messiam; edoceremur.

title: After the inspired writers were taken up — nothing outside their writings for faith
english: But after those men were taken from the earth and translated into heaven — whose mouth and pen God was pleased to use to hand his mysteries to the Church — nothing is to be counted as belonging to faith and salvation that is not found in the writings they left and entrusted to the faithful as the Church's norm and rule of faith.
Their teaching cannot be sought or found safely and certainly anywhere but in their writings.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXXI. Book p. 60 / PDF 71-72. Post-apostolic closed deposit. OCR: postquam; calamo; quaeri.

title: Oral teaching and unwritten polity admitted — yet outside the written deposit
english: We freely admit that the Prophets and Apostles and other men inspired by God said and taught many things by living voice that are not found set down word for word in sacred Scripture.

Nor do we deny that the Apostles and θεόπνευστοι men may once have ordered many things in the Church about the form of divine worship and various circumstances of church polity that are not written out in Scripture. Some historical items received from them may also have been kept among the faithful and handed on to later ages.
translator_notes: Pars I thesis XXXII. Book p. 60 / PDF 72. Oral / polity / historia admitted; natural close before XXXIII sum-in-Scripture. Greek θεόπνευστοι restored. OCR: fatemur; politiae; posteros.

title: Sum of inspired oral teaching — as to faith and salvation — is in Scripture
english: Yet we hold this tightly: the sum of what holy men, moved by the divine Spirit, taught and spoke — so far as suffices for salvation and faith — is contained in sacred Scripture.
They taught nothing of any weight for religion that has not been handed down abundantly in the sacred letters.
translator_notes: OCR: furamam/summam, hotnincs/homines, Hdem/fidem, Scriptufa/Scriptura restored from tess+DjVu (PDF 72 / book p. 60).

title: Apostolic rite and polity left to the Church — under order and decency
english: We also assert that what the Apostles instituted about rites of divine worship and circumstances of church government — where sacred Scripture is silent — was left to the Church's power.
She may change those things variously for times and places, under this general rule alone: that all things be done in order and decently in the Church of God (1 Cor. 14:40).
translator_notes: Inline sense of 1 Cor. 14:40 (omnia fiant ordine & decenter) as in earlier plenitudine theses.
OCR: rrmdivmtcuhus to ritus divini cultus; legiminis to regiminis restored.

title: After the Apostles — certainty only from what is written; no more ἀδιάπτωτοι
english: The chief point — from which the rest follow — is this: of what the Apostles taught or instituted, we hold nothing as fully certain except what is handed down and set in sacred Scripture.

After the Apostles and apostolic men, the Church had no more ἀδιάπτωτοι men set beyond every danger of error. So whatever of their sayings and deeds reaches us outside the Canonical writings comes only on the credit of weak men, who could both err and deceive.
translator_notes: Greek ἀδιάπτωτοι restored (OCR aube-yeisui / broken forms).

title: No unwritten tradition equals Scripture — sole rule of faith
english: So there is no unwritten tradition that should be matched in authority with the divine and Apostolic writings.

Scripture is the sole rule of faith; nothing else can be joined to it with the same power to bind conscience and constrain faith. If Scripture were not enough and did not hold all that belongs to faith, the Church would lack a sufficient rule, and her salvation would not have been adequately provided for.
translator_notes: OCR: rtullsm/nullam; Hdej/fidei restored.

title: Negative argument from Scripture — reject what lacks Scriptural foundation
english: Hence we argue negatively from Scripture's authority.

Of what God revealed through the Prophets and Apostles, nothing certain has reached us except what they themselves divinely committed to writing. To reject something as not belonging to faith, it is enough that it has no foundation in Scripture and cannot be proved or drawn from it.
translator_notes: OCR: nrnceft/hinc est; ntgati ve/negative restored.

title: Historical and polity traditions admitted — none for faith dogmas or morals
english: We do not wholly despise or reject unwritten traditions about historical matters and the Churches' rites, order, and polity.

But we admit none for the dogmas of faith, or for what belongs to morals. What the Spirit did not judge needful to put in writing through his amanuenses the Apostles and Evangelists cannot be known by us with equal certainty, or hold equal authority in the Church, as what he willed to consign in writing to have the force of an eternal law there.
translator_notes: OCR: contemnimus; historicas; aeternae; sentence close haberent restored from tess (PDF page break into Pars II title).
Natural close of Plenitudine Pars I before PARS SECUNDA.

title: Pars II open — summary of our churches' plenitude teaching
english: From the preceding theses on Scripture's plenitude and sufficiency — as clearly as we could — we have set out our Churches' teaching.

In short: once God willed his word consigned in writing, the Church in the sacred books had all that each age and God's varied dispensation made so needful to salvation that no one could teach, defend, or hold the contrary without loss of salvation.

Or the same point: sacred Scripture has always held all that belongs to the body and substance of religion and is necessary by God's institution — though many circumstances of worship and church discipline were left to the Church's power, not prescribed one by one in Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: THEISIBUS; aetatibus; sigillatim; salutis dispendium restored from tess+pdftotext (PDF 73 / book p. 61).
Pars II title: Pontificiorum sententia exponitur.

title: Not word-for-word — equipollent wording or necessary consequence
english: We do not claim every necessary point stands in Scripture word for word.

It may stand in equivalent words, or at least so that each item can be drawn from Scripture by a necessary and clear consequence — without needing another principle of faith to which Scripture would send us for fuller knowledge.
translator_notes: OCR: Non tamen; aequipollentibus; singula; hauriamus restored (PDF 73 / p. 61).

title: Faith principles are Scripture itself — dogmas vs school theological truths
english: The principles of faith are contained in Scripture because they are Scripture itself — not something outside it — and not because they must or can be proved from Scripture.

Everything else in religion and sacred doctrine either is proved by express texts, or drawn from Scripture by open, near consequences (what properly count as dogmas of faith), or only fetched by more remote, less plain consequences from Scripture's deeper store (many theological truths taught in the Orthodox schools).
translator_notes: OCR: sacra; depromi; Theologicae veritates; Scholis Orthodoxis restored (PDF 73 / p. 61).

title: Sole rule — nothing of equal authority beside Scripture
english: Our Churches also hold tightly: what is necessary to salvation cannot be sought elsewhere than from Scripture — with certainty and without fail.
Besides Scripture there is no word of God by which the things of faith can be confirmed. Sacred Scripture is the sole rule of faith; nothing of equal authority can be joined to it.
translator_notes: OCR: Ecclesias; salutem; infallibiliter; paris authoritatis restored; V begins mid-line on page break (PDF 73-74).

title: Roman doctors — Scripture not given as sole rule; Bellarmine on Augustine
english: We turn next to the Roman doctors on this question.

First they teach that Scripture was not given so the Church would have it as the sole rule of faith, or so that religion's institutes and the dogmas of faith would have to be sought from it alone. So not everything that belongs to faith and morals need be proved from sacred Scripture.

They do not deny that what is simply necessary to each person's salvation is found in Scripture — see Bellarmine, De verbo Dei 4.11 (last section). Answering Augustine's line our side cites (In what is openly set down in Scripture are found all things that contain faith and the way of life), he limits it to dogmas simply necessary for all, such as the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue, and presses Augustine's further point about ignorance that would cost promised salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: De verbo Dei; ultimo; Limitat; Symbolo Apostolico; Credo quod authoritas restored from tess (PDF 74 / book p. 62).
Inline Bellarmine De verbo Dei 4.11; Augustine quotation kept in sense.

title: Roman concession — contained for the whole Church, not expressly; Stapleton modes
english: Roman doctors do not deny that Scripture contains the whole necessary doctrine of faith or morals — not simply for each person, but somehow for the whole Church. They only deny that it is contained expressly (Bellarmine, De Verbo Dei 4.3 section 2).

Stapleton (Controv. 5 q.5 art.1) offers modes by which the whole saving doctrine is in Scripture: first, Scripture points to the true Church and through that Church teaches all that is needed; second, from dogmas openly set in Scripture the rest can be firmly drawn — as two natures in Christ from the Son's incarnation. Even in that sense, he says, the Fathers teach that all faith needs is comprehended in Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: Porro etiam totam doctrinam; Bellarminum 4 de Verbo Dei cap. 3; Stapletonus Controv. 5; Patres docent restored (PDF 74 / p. 62).

title: Roman consensus — all needed for eternal salvation in Scripture explicitly or in seed
english: Roman doctors do not all speak alike here — some seem to grant Scripture more, some less.

Yet they all agree: everything necessarily required for eternal salvation is in sacred Scripture explicitly or implicitly, expressly or by virtue, and as in seed — if Scripture is read in the sense the Holy Spirit intends.
translator_notes: OCR: aeternam salutem; investigantur; Spiritus sanctus restored (PDF 74 / p. 62).

title: Roman denial — tradition and unwritten word still needed beside Scripture
english: Yet they all deny that everything the Church needs for the doctrine of faith and morals is so contained in Scripture that it can be sufficiently sought and drawn from there alone.
They still require the help of tradition and of an unwritten word deposited in the Church's heart.
translator_notes: OCR: sine ope traditionis; non scripti; Ecclesiae corde depositum restored (PDF 74 / p. 62).
Natural close before IX (Christ and Apostles taught unwritten matters).

title: Roman consensus — Christ and Apostles taught unwritten faith and worship matters
english: Roman doctors agree: Christ and the Apostles taught and set up many points of faith and worship that sacred Scripture neither states expressly nor yields sufficiently when mined alone.
Christian and Apostolic doctrine, on their view, rests partly on Scripture and partly on an unwritten word passed along by mouth.
translator_notes: OCR: Doctores Ecclesiae; Dominum nostrum; Apostolos; ore tenus; Scriptura restored (PDF 74 / book p. 62).
Opens unwritten-dogma claim after VIII (tradition still required).

title: Unwritten word — committed to pastors; succession keeps it pure
english: That unwritten word, they say, was placed in the charge of the churches' rectors and overseers.
Hand to hand it was then passed down, and through unbroken succession of bishops and pastors it has reached us pure and unspoiled.
translator_notes: OCR: Istud; rectoribus & praepositis; successione; sincerum & incorruptum restored (PDF 74 / p. 62).

title: Unwritten traditions named — general sense vs viva voce; not in Canonical books
english: What they label unwritten traditions are dogmas and religious institutes never lodged in the canonical books.
Even Pontificians grant that tradition as a word is broad: any teaching one person communicates to another, in writing or outside Scripture. Handing on equals teaching; tradition equals a teaching.
Church writers, however, usually narrow the term to teaching given by living voice rather than writing — and that is how the Pontifician schools use it.
They do not mean a doctrine that exists nowhere in writing, but one the first author never wrote — or, more carefully, one absent from the Canonical books of Prophets and Apostles.
translator_notes: OCR: traditiones non scriptas; fatentibus ipsis Pontificiis; viva voce; Canonicis Prophetarum & Apostolorum restored (PDF 74 / pp. 62-63).

title: Tradition kinds — Divine, Apostolic, Ecclesiastical; confirmation chrism as Divine
english: Traditions get many partitions. The one that matters here turns on the authors to whom each kind is traced.
Roman doctors name three: Divine, Apostolic, and Ecclesiastical.
Divine are those Christ himself taught and instituted ἀγράφως (without writing), yet nowhere appear in sacred Scripture.
Their stock case is the oil-and-balsam anointing in confirmation, counted among the new-law Sacraments — for they grant every new-law Sacrament must come immediately from Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: Divinas / Apostolicas / Ecclesiasticas; Greek agraphos restored; unctio oleo & balsamo; confirmatione (PDF 74-75 / pp. 62-63).

title: Apostolic Lent; terms confused with Divine; Ecclesiastical customs by consent
english: Apostolic traditions, in the proper sense, are commands and institutes they ascribe to the Apostles even when the Apostolic writings are silent.
Under that head they place the Quadragesima (Lent) fast, which they claim the Apostles founded.

Often they blur the labels: what only the Apostles (not Christ) instituted they still call Divine, because those institutes came with the Spirit's breath; and what they tie to Christ they also call Apostolic, since nothing of Christ's teaching reaches us except through Apostolic writing and preaching.
Ecclesiastical traditions are old customs begun by prelates or peoples that, by gradual tacit consent, took on the force of law.
translator_notes: OCR: Apostolicae; mentio nulla fiat; Quadragesimae; contundunt; tacito populorum consensu restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).

title: Authority grades — Divine equals Gospels; Apostolic equals Apostolic writings; Ecclesiastical equals canons
english: Authority is not equal across these kinds.
What they call Divine is given the same force as precepts and dogmas written in the Gospels.
What they call Apostolic is ranked with the Apostolic writings themselves.
Ecclesiastical traditions sit lower — on a level with the Church's written canons and laws.
translator_notes: OCR: Caeterum; eandem vim; scriptis Apostolicis; Canones & Leges Ecclesiae scriptae restored (PDF 75 / p. 63).

title: Trent Session 4 — equal piety for unwritten traditions restricted to first two kinds
english: They therefore confine Trent's Session 4 rule — receive unwritten traditions with the same piety as the Canonical books — to the first two kinds alone (Divine and Apostolic).

The Council says: seeing Gospel truth and discipline live in written books and in unwritten traditions received from Christ's mouth by the Apostles, or passed from the Apostles under the Spirit's dictation as if by hand down to us, the Synod, following the orthodox Fathers, receives and venerates with equal piety and reverence every Old and New Testament book (one God their author) and those faith-and-morals traditions spoken by Christ or the Spirit and kept by continual succession in the Catholic Church.
translator_notes: OCR: Decretum Concilii Tridentini; Sessione quarta; pari pietatis affectu; Synodus perspiciens restored (PDF 75 / p. 63).
Natural close before XVI (three rules for discerning true Divine/Apostolic traditions).

title: Three Roman rules for discerning Divine and Apostolic traditions — first rule
english: Roman doctors offer several tests for sorting true Divine and Apostolic traditions from fakes; they boil down to three.

First: whatever Rome believes as de fide, yet is not clearly in Scripture, must itself be a Divine or Apostolic tradition — because Rome cannot err, and because she is not ruled by fresh revelation but only by what she learned from Apostles and Prophets.
translator_notes: OCR: Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae; discerni possint; de fide; revelationibus; Apostolis & Prophetis restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).
Opens discernment-rules slice after XV (Trent Session 4).

title: Second rule — rites only God could institute, absent from Scripture, must be Apostolic
english: Second rule, on the same two foundations: what Rome keeps that only God could lawfully institute, yet Scripture never shows God instituting, must have come from the Apostles.
translator_notes: OCR: Secunda regula; iisdem fundamentis; legitime; Scripturis; Apostolis restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).

title: Third rule — common Roman consensus as Apostolic tradition; Lenten fast example
english: Third rule: whatever Roman doctors by common consent say descends from Apostolic tradition is to be treated as Apostolic — even when the Church herself could have set it up.
They class the Quadragesimal (Lenten) fast under this head.
translator_notes: OCR: Tertia regula; communi consensu; Quadragesimale restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).
Links back to XIII Lent as Apostolic tradition example.

title: Three rules collapse to one — present Roman Church judgment alone discerns
english: The three rules fold into one: whatever Rome proposes as Divine or Apostolic tradition must be taken as such without doubt.

As they hang the authority of long-known books on the present Church's witness, so they will have true traditions sorted from false ones only by that same judgment — and that with certainty and infallibility.
translator_notes: OCR: tres regulae; unicam contrahi; indubitato; praesentis testimonio; infallibiliter restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).
Closes the discernment-rules cluster; XX+ turns to controversy status.

title: Controversy status — Reformed concede polity and external ceremonies to Church prudence
english: From the foregoing, the controversy's state is clear: where Reformed churches agree with Rome, and where they do not.
First concession: polity and public external-worship ceremonies need not be fetched from Scripture; they are left to Church power and her overseers' prudence.
translator_notes: OCR: Ecclesiae nostrae; politiam; ceremonias; praepositorum restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).
Opens agreement/disagreement after the three rules.

title: Further Reformed concession — substance of faith not always verbatim, often by consequence
english: Further concession: the substance and body of faith and religion are not always in Scripture verbatim, expressly, or immediately.
Many faith dogmas come only by good and lawful consequence from Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: Ultro; substantiam & corpus; verbatim & expresse; consequentiam restored (PDF 75 / book p. 63).

title: Roman concessions — necessary-to-salvation truths clear in Scripture; rest at least virtually
english: Rome concedes in turn: whatever is simply necessary for every person's salvation, and whose explicit faith each believer must hold, stands clear and open in Scripture.
They also grant that whatever is needed for faith-and-morals doctrine is at least in Scripture virtually and implicitly, and can be drawn by good consequence.
translator_notes: OCR: Vicissim; simpliciter ad salutem; fides explicita; virtute & implicite restored (PDF 76 / book p. 64).

title: The real difference — sola Scriptura vs tradition as a second equal divine word
english: The real split: Reformed hold that everything needed for faith and religion can be drawn and proved from Scripture alone — no second faith-principle to which Scripture remits us for fuller teaching, and no rule of faith outside Scripture.

Roman doctors deny that faith dogmas and religion's institutes can be proved sufficiently from Scripture without intervening Church doctrine and tradition, which they take as another part of the divine word equal in authority with sacred Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: discrimen; alio fidei principio; interveniente; alteram verbi divini partem; paris ... authoritatis restored (PDF 76 / book p. 64).
Closes status slice before XXIV (two-point question).

title: The two-point question — unwritten apostolic necessities vs equal-authority tradition
english: The whole question therefore turns on two points.
First: Did the Apostles teach or institute necessary things not sufficiently contained in sacred Scripture?

Second: Can apostolic teaching and institutes be had with certainty and infallibility from somewhere other than Scripture — namely from the tradition of post-apostolic Church doctors, owed equal faith-obedience with Scripture itself?
Rome affirms both. All Orthodox (Reformed) theologians deny both.
translator_notes: OCR: Adeoque; in duobus versatur; aliunde; par obsequium fidei; Utrumque ... utrumque restored (PDF 76 / book p. 64).
Opens Reformed affirmative case after controversy-status XXIII.

title: Two Reformed affirmations — Scripture's full substance; no equal unwritten word
english: Two affirmations follow.
First: everything belonging to the substance of faith and religion is fully and sufficiently in sacred Scripture.

Second: besides Scripture there is no word of God that is our faith's principle and rule — so no unwritten traditions equal Scripture's authority, and least of all Rome's so-called Apostolic and divine traditions.

The first follows from the second: if there is no divine word outside Scripture, Scripture must hold all that faith and salvation require, or we already lack necessities and have no sure path of salvation.
So, without rehearsing Scripture's own fullness-texts, the main proof target is this: no living-voice-only word of God stands as a certain faith-rule alongside Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: Duo igitur affirmamus; plene & sufficienter; aequalis ... authoritatis; viva voce tantum restored (PDF 76 / book p. 64).
Sets proof program for XXVI+.

title: A fortiori from the Jewish Church — Christ and Paul reject extra-Scriptural traditions
english: First argument: when Jewish Scripture was only the Old Testament, the whole salvation-doctrine was in Scripture, with no unwritten traditions equal to it.
A fortiori today: Scripture now includes the New Testament books that set out Christ's and the Apostles' teaching, so all the more must salvation-doctrine be contained in Scripture.

That Judaism had no equal-authority unwritten traditions follows because any such would have been the very traditions the Jewish teachers pressed — yet Christ shows those empty human inventions (Matthew 15; Mark 7).

When scribes and Pharisees (then the Jewish Church's doctors) charged the disciples with breaking the elders' tradition by unwashed hands (Matthew 15:2; Mark 7:5), Christ answered that they break God's commandment by their tradition and make God's word void (Matthew 15:3, 6; Mark 7:8-13).

He does not merely rebuke hypocrisy; He rejects their traditions as vain in general and draws no line between true and false extra-Scriptural traditions — citing Isaiah: This people honors Me with lips while the heart is far; in vain they worship Me, teaching human commandments (Isaiah 29:13 via Matthew 15:8-9; Mark 7:6-7).
Paul likewise warns against human tradition (Colossians 2:8) and recalls his own former zeal for ancestral traditions (Galatians 1:14).
So if Christ and the Apostles treat Jewish extra-Scriptural traditions as human doctrines, Rome's traditions fall the same way — they come with no greater authority.
translator_notes: OCR: Primum ergo sic; Atqui multo magis; Matthaeum 15; Marcum 7; Isaias; Coloss. 2; Galat. 1 (OCR Galat. 4) restored (PDF 76 / book p. 64).
Inline scripture beside quoted clauses in Pass B.
Long-s / quote lines repaired from tess + pdftotext.

title: Adversaries' Mosaic-tradition reply — oral law claim still falls under Christ's verdict
english: Rome replies: Christ condemned only later, empty, or Scripture-contradicting Jewish traditions — not Mosaic/Prophetic ones — and Rome's traditions come from Christ and the Apostles.

Counter: the traditions Christ attacks as human doctrines were sold as Mosaic and Prophetic. Rabbis call them thorah shebbal peh (oral law), claiming Moses received them viva voce on Sinai equal in authority with the written law.
In Christ's day those Jewish doctors were the Church's only teachers — there was no true Church of God except among the Jews.

Yet Christ still rejects their extra-Scriptural traditions as human doctrines despite ancient/Mosaic pedigree. So why trust today's Roman doctors when they claim hand-to-hand receipt from Christ and the Apostles?

Church teachers can err and push merely human dogmas as divine; therefore no certain word of God stands outside sacred Scripture — for any such word would still have to come through fallible overseers, with no greater warrant.
translator_notes: OCR: Respondunt adversarii; Mosaicis & Propheticis; thorah shebbal peh (oral law); mere humana restored (PDF 77 / book p. 65).
Hebrew oral-law name normalized from tess garble.

title: Extra-Scriptural teaching is rejectable as human — Scripture the examination rule
english: Church teachers' delivery can be rejected as human tradition only because it stands outside Scripture.

If God's word were not bounded by Scripture and an unwritten divine word also existed, teachers could rightly claim their teaching is that word — and if we needed an unwritten word, where else would we take it?
Yet Christ shows Church doctors can propose mere human invention as God's word.

Therefore whatever can be proposed outside Scripture's substance counts as human doctrine, and Scripture is the rule for examining all things — otherwise magisterial precepts could never be rejected as human traditions.
translator_notes: OCR: Denique; determinatum; obtendere; teste Christo; Scripturae substantiam restored (PDF 77 / book p. 65).

title: Ecclesiastical traditions fall under Isaiah — later pastors' human precepts
english: Note Rome's own concession: Christ rebuked traditions from teachers later than Moses and the Prophets.

By the same right, so-called Ecclesiastical traditions fall — rites and worship practices invented by later pastors and doctors, not by Christ or the Apostles — and those make up much of Rome's system.
They are no less human commandments than the Jewish elders' once were.
Isaiah's words, cited and confirmed by Christ, fit them equally: In vain they worship Me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:9; Mark 7:7).
translator_notes: OCR: Praeterea valde notandum; Ecclesiasticas; posteriorum saeculorum; Isaiae verba restored (PDF 77 / book p. 65).
Inline Isaiah/Matthew/Mark beside the Frustra colunt clause.

title: Not only Scripture-contrary traditions — Christ damns human precepts as such
english: Rome says Jewish traditions contradicted Scripture, but theirs do not.
Many Jewish traditions were not evil or directly anti-Scripture by nature — only unlawful as additions, since divine law forbids adding to itself.
Hand-washing before meals looks harmless and not directly against Scripture — yet that is the very tradition Christ specially targets.
Calling it empty helps Rome nothing: their traditions are no less empty, and by mere human wisdom Jewish washings look no less wise than most Roman institutes.
Christ's verdict is broader: He damns them not only as empty or contrary, but in general as human commandments and doctrines — and that charge fits Rome's traditions equally.
translator_notes: OCR: directe; legis additamenta; nec quod sit directe; speciatim carpit; in genere restored (PDF 77 / book p. 65).
Hand-washing tradition pointed via Matthew 15 / Mark 7 context.

title: Many Roman traditions directly conflict Scripture — cup, images, Mass sacrifice
english: Most Roman traditions are not only beside Scripture (already a kind of conflict as unlawful additions) but often fight Scripture directly.

Example — communion in one kind: Rome says it is lawful and expedient to give the Eucharist under bread alone; yet Christ instituting the sacrament said of the cup, Drink from this, all of you (Matthew 26:27).

Example — images: the second commandment forbids religious worship of any image, and Scripture often forbids fashioning a likeness of God; Rome teaches placing and religiously venerating images of God, angels, and the dead in churches.

Example — the Mass: Rome holds Christ is offered daily as a true and proper sacrifice though He suffers nothing there; Hebrews teaches Christ's offering is once for all and He does not offer Himself repeatedly, because He cannot suffer repeatedly (Hebrews 9:25-28; 10:10-14).

Therefore Rome's supposedly Apostolic and divine traditions are not God's word or a certain faith-rule: God's word cannot contradict itself, and what contradicts undisputed Scripture must not be held as God's word.
translator_notes: OCR: plerisque; sub sola specie panis; Bibite ex hoc omnes; secundo Decalogi praecepto; Hebraeos; unicam ... oblationem restored (PDF 77-78 / book pp. 65-66).
Inline cup, Decalogue, and Hebrews refs beside the conflict examples.
Closes affirmative-case slice before XXXII (memory/corruption of viva-voce deposit).

title: Unwritten viva-voce deposit would corrupt — Scripture alone a certain rule
english: Scripture alone is a certain rule of faith; traditions proposed outside it are doubtful and uncertain.

If any part of Christian doctrine had been left by the Apostles only viva voce, committed to memory and never written, it either would not have reached us, or would have reached us thick with corruptions — so that pure truth could hardly be separated from human inventions.
Men's perversity, ignorance, and negligence easily bury, erase, or adulterate what is trusted only to care and memory. Writing is needed for a sure and accurate record.
What is not written soon vanishes from memory or is tangled in fables until true and false cannot be told apart.

Philosophers' opinions and commonwealth institutes left only to memory have perished, except scraps someone happened to write. Of past deeds and sayings we have nothing certain except what books kept as faithful custodians.
If writing is needed anywhere, it is needed most in religion and worship — where people are by nature forgetful and quick to invent.

Ask Rome where the Jews' alleged Mosaic and prophetic oral traditions are now: even Rome cannot say what they contained. Of Jewish religion and worship we know nothing certain except from Moses and the Prophets in writing.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXII heading restored from spaced X X X 1 1 (PDF 78 / book p. 66); dubias & incertas; germanaque ac sincera; figmentis; Mosis & Prophetarum.
Opens memory/corruption argument against viva-voce deposit after XXIV-XXXI Jewish-Church slice.

title: Pre-Mosaic oral survival was brief — and extraordinary revelation filled the gap
english: Rome replies: from creation to Moses, heavenly doctrine was kept by oral tradition alone — so why not apostolic traditions for sixteen hundred years?
Answer: before Moses sacred teaching did survive unwritten for a while — but only among very few.

Among most it was soon corrupted and wrapped in absurd fables; God's covenant and saving doctrine nearly remained in Abraham's family alone while the rest of humankind turned to idolatry and invented cults.

What Scripture later supplied was then filled by frequent divine appearances and familiar talk with the Patriarchs, by which God repeatedly restored the viva-voce teaching and called it back to purity.
Those extraordinary appearances and conversations have long ceased in the Church.
translator_notes: OCR: foedus; fere Abrahami; instauravit & renovavit; Ecclesia pridem (PDF 78 / p. 66).
Replies to Rome's creation-to-Moses oral-survival objection.

title: Why God had the law written — then why leave any equal part unwritten?
english: Press harder: why did God finally will His law written, and the rest of sacred Scripture composed?

Rome cannot deny the twin aims — to help human weakness and to block the frauds of the ungodly — and that God's counsel was to rescue the doctrine in those books from oblivion and corruption, and keep it safe against negligence and imposture.
Then why not the same care for the whole of sacred doctrine? Why write one part and leave another equal part unwritten?
Is the unwritten part somehow less open to diabolical fraud and forgetfulness than the written part?
Worldwide experience says otherwise: where Scripture was missing, Father-handed vestiges remained, but ruined by fables, foreign sacrilegious rites, and idolatry.

Rome itself counts later doctors' writings among providence's means of keeping traditions. If traditions needed writing to survive, why leave that writing to fallible common authors instead of Prophets and Apostles — and why seal Scripture on authentic tables while parking equal-weight traditions in ordinary men's books?
translator_notes: OCR: page-break after dicant adversarii restored; consultum noluit; vestigia; sacrilegos; relinquere close (PDF 78-79 / pp. 66-67).

title: Continuous use does not freeze tradition — vernacular languages keep changing
english: Rome adds: their traditions survived intact by continuous use among Christians — like vernacular languages, which endure even without grammars because a people keeps speaking them.
Experience says the opposite. People are inconstant; whatever lives only in use keeps changing, often slowly and unnoticed — unless something else holds it fast.
Their own analogy proves it: vernaculars continually shift until, after centuries, they look like another dialect. Ancient customs diverge from today's for the same reason.
Church history shows the same: set the second- and third-century Church beside Rome's present rites and discipline, and the gap is obvious.

So the Church needs a firm, stable rule that does not hang merely on memory and good faith — a rule by which creeping abuses can be corrected. That rule is sacred Scripture alone, not unwritten tradition.
translator_notes: OCR: Addunt Pontificii; grammaticae; sensim & sine sensu; enascentes (PDF 79 / p. 67).

title: Fathers are fallible witnesses — their consensus cannot equal inspired Scripture
english: Unwritten traditions are wrongly leveled with Scripture: Scripture's inspired writers, beyond error's reach, tell us what Christ taught and instituted.
Outside Scripture, sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles reach us only through early post-apostolic witnesses — the Fathers whose monuments remain.
Those Fathers were fallible, confessed it, and asked that their writings be measured by Scripture — not received ἀθεωρήτως and without examination.
Roman doctors themselves mark many errors and blemishes in the Fathers — not only in lone opinions, but even where many agree.

Examples Sixtus of Siena collects: most Fathers denied the saints the beatific vision before the resurrection; ancients held no creature incorporeal as a received Catholic rule; many forbade all oaths; chiliast hope of an earthly fleshly reign (Papias, Irenaeus, and others); and a purifying world-fire for all except Christ on judgment day — which even Jerome and Augustine hesitate to condemn outright.

If early doctors could hug false dogma as divine truth, later-age traditions learned only from their witness cannot stand as certain beside what God consigned in the Prophets' and Apostles' books — nor can fallible men's testimony claim equal Church authority with God's own.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVI heading from XXXVLE; Greek ἀθεωρήτως restored from @feovicws; Sixtus Senensis Bibliothecae sanctae; naevos; urendos igne; page-break after Hieronymus Ezechielem (PDF 79-80 / pp. 67-68).
Pass A spells Greek sense in English (unexamined) to keep check_pass_ab lemma-friendly; Latin lock keeps Greek.

title: Even the earliest unwritten traditions were already uncertain and contested
english: If unwritten apostolic traditions ever had certainty, it should have been strongest while apostolic memory was still fresh.
Yet already in the first centuries they were so uncertain and various that Church doctors fought over them, and good men were taken in by the name of tradition.
Eusebius: Papias, living next after the Apostles, leaned hard on traditions and wrote five books of the Lord's sayings from unwritten tradition — stuffed with fables.

Pascha dispute: Asian bishops (Polycrates) alleged John and Philip's tradition for Nisan 14; Victor of Rome and the West claimed Peter and Paul for the Sunday after — Eusebius and Socrates record the clash.
On fixed apostolic fasts, ancients disagreed; Augustine to Casulanus and Socrates deny the Apostles fixed fasting rules at all.
Augustine on Sabbath fasting: Rome alleged Peter's tradition; other churches alleged other apostles — an interminable fight proving unwritten tradition yields no certainty on fasting.
Tertullian and Basil list standing prayer, no Sunday fasts, Pascha-to-Pentecost customs as apostolic — later ages dropped them even while still calling them apostolic.
translator_notes: OCR: Eusebius Historiae; Polycrates; Victor Romanus; Augustinus epist. 86 ad Casulanum; Tertullianus de corona militis; Basilius de Spiritu sancto; Nicena Synodus (PDF 80 / p. 68).
Closing clause keeps Le Blanc's irony: later non-observance of what was still labeled apostolic.

title: Infant communion once treated as apostolic — later abrogated by Rome herself
english: Still stronger: for many ages, especially in the Roman and African churches, infants received the Eucharist as soon as they were baptized, and it was held necessary to their salvation.

Witnesses: Cyprian On the Lapsed; Innocent I to Milevis; Gelasius to the Picene bishops; Augustine in many places — not as a private whim but as the common Church view descending from apostolic tradition, and used as conceded ground against the Pelagians.
No contemporary writer objects. Roman doctors admit it: Vasquez and Maldonatus note Augustine's and Innocent's view held about six hundred years.
Yet Rome long ago abolished the custom, and Trent condemned it.
If unwritten traditions were already so uncertain and various in the first Christian centuries — and often deceived even good doctors — what certainty can sixteen later centuries add?
How unsafe, then, to take them as a rule of faith and set them equal in authority with sacred Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: Cypriano de lapsis; Innocentio; Gelasio per Picenum; peccati meritis & remissione cap. 24; Vasquez; Maldonat.; Tridentino damnata page-break join (PDF 80-81 / pp. 68-69).
Closes memory/corruption slice before XXXIX (spurious apostolic writings objection).

title: Forged or doubted apostolic writings do not level Scripture with oral tradition
english: Rome objects: forged 'apostolic' writings once circulated, and even true apostolic books were doubted among the faithful — so if that undercuts unwritten tradition, Scripture's authority falls too.

The objection fails on our side. We do not hang Scripture's authority on Church doctors' testimony. The faithful receive Scripture immediately, for its own sake, because it carries the marks of its divinity in itself.
Old doubts about certain books therefore do not prejudice Scripture among us.
We reject Rome's traditions not merely because some doubted them, but because they fight Scripture and have nothing in them that can claim divine authority.

Rome, by contrast, makes both written and unwritten 'word of God' hang on doctors' testimony. If those early doctors — the only chain by which later ages learned 'apostolic' traditions — were themselves uncertain, various, and often deceived, then on Rome's own principles those traditions have no certain authority.
translator_notes: OCR: falso supposita; immediate & propter se; notas insitas; prisci Ecclesiae Doctores (PDF 81 / p. 69).
Opens spurious-vs-true writings reply; closes memory-corruption arc into discernment authority.

title: Rome's living judge — Pope or Council — is not even certain inside Rome
english: Rome replies: when ancients disagree and apostolic tradition looks uncertain, the Church has a living authority that can settle true vs false traditions for the faithful, certainly and infallibly.
Ask who holds that authority now that prophets and apostles are gone, and Rome splits.
Most say the Roman Pontiff is Christ's infallible faith-judge — yet even inside Rome that claim is not a settled de fide dogma; many Catholics in communion deny it.
Others put infallibility in a general Council of overseers — still less settled; many Roman doctors, and the popes themselves, fight it, and denying it is not treated as heresy.

The fallback — Councils safe once the Pope confirms them — collapses into a circle: if Councils can err before confirmation and the Pope is not infallible, how can he infallibly judge whether the Council erred?
