translator_notes: OCR: spaced X L.; dissentientes; Pontifice Romano; Concilio; confirmationem (PDF 81 / p. 69).

title: Neither Pope nor Council can show a real title — proof-texts are twisted
english: Neither Pope nor Council can show a lawful title-deed for the authority they claim.
What they offer with any color is Scripture twisted off its sense.

Example — Luke 22:32 ('I have prayed for you… that your faith may not fail'): Christ promises Peter, about to deny Him, that heart-faith would not be snuffed out and he would rise again — not Roman episcopal infallibility.

Councils lean on Matthew 18:20 ('two or three… in my name'): Christ does not absolutely underwrite every general pastors' council; He promises Spirit-help to any council that uses His means, seeks God's and Christ's glory and the Church's building up, and is not dragged by its own passions.
No pastors' meeting can be known infallibly to have met that condition.
translator_notes: OCR: spaced X L I.; Rogavi pro te; duo vel tres / in medio eorum; assistentiam (PDF 81–82 / pp. 69–70).

title: Infallible Church-judge is a circle — prove it without Scripture and tradition
english: If only a present, infallible Church authority can certify true Scripture and tradition against the false and apocryphal, that authority must be known first — before Scripture and tradition, and without leaning on their witness.
So ask Rome to prove papal or conciliar authority from somewhere other than Scripture and tradition.

They say they defer to Scripture and traditions as divine because Pope or Council so moves them — which leaves the question: what finally makes them believe the Church is infallible when it judges Scripture and tradition?
translator_notes: OCR: XLII from X L 1 1; Ecclesia praesenti; seposita; aliunde (PDF 82 / p. 70).

title: No new revelation — only a fallible hand-to-hand chain Augustine calls interminable
english: Even Rome's best grant: the Church is not run by new revelations, and neither Pope nor Council learns immediately from God what the Apostles taught.
Their only remaining answer: hand-to-hand testimony of doctors back to hearers of the Apostles.
But we have already shown — and Rome's own history admits — that the earliest doctors often erred in receiving 'apostolic' traditions, and by common consent held as apostolic what Rome now condemns.
How then can that chain give later Councils and popes certain faith, or serve as a rule equal to Scripture for settling controversies?

The uncertainty of conflicting Father-witness is exactly what still needs removing. Augustine, in the place already cited: when the fight turns on apostolic tradition itself, the contention is interminable — it breeds quarrels and does not end questions.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIII from XLlll; novis revelationibus; de manu in manum; Interminabilis quote (PDF 82 / p. 70).
Augustine quote continues Casulanus locus from XXXVII.

title: Only perpetual Christian consensus could count — Rome's traditions fail that test
english: If any tradition deserves to be true, it is one marked by the perpetual, constant consensus of Christians.
Rome's traditions fail that test: they stand outside Scripture, often against it, and many were unknown in the ancient Church and contrary to its faith and practice.

Examples: papal indulgences; saint-canonization; public worship in a tongue the people do not share; bans on vernacular Scripture without special leave; communion in one kind; and religious image-making and image-worship — easy to show absent, even opposed, in the primitive Church.
So they are human inventions, and it is impious to set them equal in authority with the writings of Apostles and Prophets.
Pars II closes here; Pars III opens next.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIV closes Pars II before PARS TERTIA title page (PDF 82–83 / pp. 70–71).
Honest partial: Plenitudine Pars II complete through XLIV.

title: Pars III opens: two questions Rome still presses against Scripture sufficiency
english: Pars III opens by splitting the fight into two questions that travel together but are not the same.
First: are all things necessary to faith and religion fully and sufficiently in Scripture?
Second: is there, beside Scripture, another word of God in the Church, equal in authority, handed down only by unwritten tradition?
Rome denies the first and affirms the second, and piles arguments on both.
translator_notes: OCR: PARS TERTIA title + Thesis I on PDF 83 / book p. 72; long-s normalized.

title: Rome's first sufficiency attack: lost canonical books would leave doctrine incomplete
english: Rome's opening move: if Scripture were enough, either the whole Canon together would be enough, or each book by itself would be enough.
Neither works. Single books, cut off from the rest, do not hold every saving dogma — not every OT prophecy, not every NT epistle.
So sufficiency would have to belong to the whole Canon. Missing books would mean missing doctrine.
They claim many sacred books have perished: Nathan and Gad, Ahijah and Iddo, Solomon's songs and parables, plus a Laodicean letter and perhaps another Corinthian letter.
From today's incomplete Canon, they say, salvation's doctrine cannot be drawn sufficiently.
translator_notes: OCR: II spans PDF 83-84; Ahiae/Addo = Ahijah/Iddo; Colos. = Colossians.

title: Reply: sufficiency is of Scripture's body taken indefinitely, not of every booklet
english: We never meant: every single biblical booklet by itself teaches every dogma.
Sufficiency belongs to Scripture's body taken as a whole — indefinitely, and at least in its chief parts.
Rome assumes that dropping any one book instantly guts doctrine. That is not our claim.
Today's corpus holds salvation's teaching not only enough, but richly; many books only explain or apply what others already teach.
Even if some authentic divine writings had perished, the remaining Scripture could still hold the full saving doctrine — those lost books need not have carried any dogma missing from what survives.
translator_notes: OCR: III begins after Respondeo on PDF 83; continues PDF 84 / p. 72.

title: Unlikely that any properly divine authentic writing truly perished
english: We also doubt the premise: it is not likely any properly divine, authentic writing has truly vanished.
Providence is injured if God had a book written only to let it vanish useless to the Church.
Among books providence did keep, some are tiny and of no obvious necessity — so why invent larger lost equals?
Rome, which credits the Church with ἀδιαπτωσία and exalts her, still shames her if she let many God-given norm-books perish through neglect.
translator_notes: OCR: Greek ἀδιαπτωσίαν restored from tess garble on PDF 84.

title: Gad and Nathan's lost books are Samuel / Kings still extant
english: For the cited lost books: either they did not perish, or they were never canonical immediate inspiration.
Gad and Nathan we count prophetic and canonical — but still extant as Samuel, Vulgate 1-2 Kings.
Samuel alone cannot be full author: his death falls mid-1 Samuel, so he stops around chapter 16.
The rest, and 2 Samuel, fit Gad and Nathan, who lived the story and are named beside Samuel as its writers and continuators.
translator_notes: OCR: V on PDF 84-85; Regum = Kings in Vulgate numbering.

title: Hiddo and Ahijah likewise wrote what remains as 1 Kings
english: Same move for Iddo and Ahijah in 2 Chron. 9: Solomon's acts credited to Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo's vision.
Those writings look like 1 Kings, Vulgate 3 Kings — anonymous, yet best ascribed to the prophets of that age.
So again: not vanished canonical books, but books we still read under other titles.
translator_notes: OCR: VI on PDF 85; Hiddo = Iddo.

title: Solomon's lost songs and sayings need not have been inspired Scripture
english: Yes, much of Solomon's writing is gone — but not everything a God-breathed man writes is divine Scripture.
Augustine in City of God 18: prophets can write as historians by human diligence, or as prophets by inspiration; only the latter bind as God's word.
Solomon's inspired share is what entered the Canon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs.
The rest — plant-lore from cedar to hyssop, extra parables, five thousand songs — can be brilliant human work without being lost canonical revelation.
translator_notes: OCR: VII PDF 85-86; Greek restored; Augustine Civ. Dei 18.

title: Apostles too may have written pious letters beneath canonical authority — 1 Cor. 5
english: Apostles could write other pious letters that never rose to canonical, immediately inspired authority.
1 Cor. 5 may point to an earlier Corinthian letter — if so, a holy but non-canonical piece, not a lost rule of faith.
Many Reformed and Roman scholars instead read 'in this epistle,' pointing back to Paul's words already in the same letter about the incestuous man.
Either way, Rome gains no vanished second Canon equal to Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: VIII PDF 86; closes lost-books slice before IX Laodiceans.

title: No lost Pauline letter to the Laodiceans — Col. 4 ambiguity
english: Rome's 'lost letter to Laodicea' rests on a Latin ambiguity in Col. 4, not on a vanished Canon.
The Vulgate's 'epistle of the Laodiceans' is read as a letter to them; the Greek says a letter from Laodicea.
τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας means written from Laodicea — anyone with a little Greek can see it.
So the lost-Laodiceans proof for an incomplete Canon falls with the mistranslation.
translator_notes: OCR: IX PDF 86 / book p. 73; Greek τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας restored from context + tess.

title: Roman argument: Christ would have expressly commanded writing
english: Rome's next move: if Scripture alone were the Word, Christ would have plainly ordered writing.
They want an explicit 'write this' parallel to the explicit 'teach the nations' mandate.
Because they find no such vocal command on the page, they say the Word outruns the book.
The claim sets up the reply: inspiration itself is the stronger mandate.
translator_notes: OCR: X PDF 86 / book p. 73; command-to-write opening.

title: Reply: internal inspiration is a stronger writing mandate than vocal order
english: Agreed: they would not make writings the rule of faith without a divine mandate.
Denied: that they lacked one — Augustine says Christ ordered the Apostles to write what we should read.
Even without a spoken 'Write!', inspiration and the Spirit's extraordinary impulse are the stronger command.
2 Tim. 3: all Scripture is God-breathed — once that stands, a further vocal warrant is needless.
translator_notes: OCR: XI PDF 86; 2 Tim 3 restored from Omnis Scriptura quote (print/OCR 1. Tim. 5). Augustine de consensu Evang. 1 ult.

title: John had an external write-command; Teach all nations includes the pen
english: John's Apocalypse repeatedly records a heavenly order to write — including the seven Asian letters.
Bellarmine's split between 'teach' and 'write' fails: teaching includes the pen.
Matthew's closing 'Teach all nations' is not viva-voce-only; writing is one teaching mode.
Christ wants the nations filled with the Gospel by speech or by calamus.
translator_notes: OCR: XII PDF 86-87 / pp. 73-74; calamo line straddles page break.

title: Occasions of writing do not cancel the divine mandate to write
english: Bellarmine lists occasions: Matthew's memorial, John's anti-Ebionite request, Luke vs uncertain tales.
He infers they wrote casually, not by office or divine order.
Occasions do not cancel mandate — inspiration is the strongest mandate of all.
They seized those occasions for the Church's perpetual use, not for one private fix.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII PDF 87 / book p. 74; Bellarmine occasion-arguments.

title: No scholastic catechism required — God wrote by their hands
english: Bellarmine wants a catechism; he finds only Gospels and letters that touch dogma in passing.
Reply: God wrote through their hands — not bound to school method.
Pious readers can still gather faith and life-precepts from the books as written.
Moses had an express write-order yet left precepts scattered in narrative — same pattern.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV PDF 87 / book p. 74; Moses counterexample.

title: Not every Apostle need write — a few inspired books serve the whole Church
english: Bellarmine: if God meant a written Gospel, every Apostle — or a joint council — would have issued a full body of doctrine.
Reply: a few inspired writers suffice for the whole Church's use.
No need for an Apostles' committee — God inspires persons as well as assemblies.
Sacred books arise from God's immediate breath, not from human planning.
translator_notes: OCR: XV PDF 87 / book p. 74; closes command-to-write cluster before XVI third argument.

title: Third attack: many needful things missing from Scripture — OT remedies for women and day-eight males
english: Rome's third attack: many things we must know are missing from Scripture.
Under the Old Testament women needed a cleansing from original sin as much as men — yet circumcision is only for males, and Scripture names no parallel rite for women.
Nor is it believable that males who died before the eighth day had no remedy, though circumcision could not yet be given — and Scripture is silent here too.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI PDF 86 / book p. 74; long-s/ligatures normalized; foeminae/masculis restored.

title: Reply: tradition is as silent — lost-tradition retorsion mirrors the lost-books attack
english: If the silence proves Scripture incomplete, it equally proves Scripture-plus-tradition incomplete — tradition is silent too.
Let Rome name the Old-Testament remedy for women and for boys who died before day eight from her unwritten word.
If she says the tradition perished, her own lost-books attack against the Canon rebounds on her.
One could as easily stash the missing remedy in the prophetic books she claims are gone.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII PDF 86–87; scitu necessaria / intercidisse restored.

title: False hinge: grace need not hang on external signs — OT rites lacked NT sacramental force on Rome's own view
english: The whole attack hangs on a false hinge: that grace must ride on outward signs.
On that hinge Rome wonders how women were saved without circumcision — yet she forgets her own teaching.
She grants New-Testament sacraments alone that grace-working force; Old-Testament rites she calls shadows without power to work grace.
Stand by that, and circumcision itself was no remedy of original sin.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII split across PDF 86–87 / pp. 74–75; foeminae/umbrae restored.

title: Circumcision a seal of faith's righteousness — promise covers women and pre-day-eight males (Rom. 4; Lombard)
english: With Paul we call circumcision a seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4), not a rite that by outward application wiped original sin away.
Adults — men and women — were set right by faith in the divine promises.
Abraham's promise, I will be your God and of your seed, covered women as well as men.
By that promise God remitted original sin to covenant infants who died before reason, circumcised or not — including girls and boys before day eight.
Male circumcision sealed the promise for the whole household.
Even Lombard (and Gregory) taught Bellarmine that women and pre-circumcision infants were saved by faith — their own or their parents' — without a bodily sacrament.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX PDF 87 / p. 75; Sigillum justitiae fidei / Ero Deus tuus restored from Rom. 4 and Gen 17 sense; Lombard ref normalized.

title: Bellarmine's OT silence example flips to NT instances — Mary's perpetual virginity first
english: Bellarmine offers that Old-Testament silence as a specimen of something necessary yet unwritten.
He then piles New-Testament instances of faith-matters he says Scripture cannot teach.
First: Mary always a virgin against Helvidius — Church-wide belief, he says, with no Scriptural witness.
translator_notes: OCR: XX PDF 87 / p. 75; Helvidii restored.

title: Mary virgin in bearing Christ is of faith — perpetual virginity pious, not a salvation article (Basil)
english: Faith requires Mary's virginity in bearing Christ our Savior.
Basil: what comes after does not belong to the reason of the mystery — to pry is curiosity.
We piously hold her perpetual virginity and count Helvidius rash.
We will not rank it among articles of faith or press it as necessary to salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: XXI PDF 87; Basil Greek restored to match Latin gloss (ad rationem mysterii); Helvidium/perpetuo restored.

title: Pascha on Sunday vs fourteenth moon — indifferent rite; Victor vs Irenaeus; Quartodecimans mislabeled heretics
english: Bellarmine's Pascha instance — Sunday, not the fourteenth moon, though Scripture is silent — has no more force.
We grant the silence; we deny the stake: the day is indifferent, a church rite, not a salvation hinge.
Second-century Rome and Asia even excommunicated each other over it.
Rome's custom may look wiser, yet both sides sinned in the heat.
Irenaeus rebuked Victor for rupturing charity over a light cause.
Fathers' catalogs list Quartodecimans as heretics, but they often brand as heresy any view they dislike — even on trivial points.
translator_notes: OCR: XXII PDF 87 / p. 75; Quartodecimani / Irenaeus / Victorem / Asiaticas restored.

title: Infant baptism can be proved from Scripture — Bellarmine refutes Anabaptists, then denies the proof
english: They next call infant baptism necessary yet unwritten — or at least not proved enough from Scripture.
We deny the silence: our theologians prove infant baptism from Scripture against the Anabaptists.
This is not the place to rehearse those arguments.
Stranger still: Rome herself routs Anabaptists from Scripture — Bellarmine boasts his baptism arguments cannot be escaped (On Baptism 1.9).
The same Bellarmine, attacking Scripture's sufficiency, then says paedobaptism cannot be proved from Scripture.
We appeal from partisan Bellarmine to Bellarmine elsewhere convinced by the truth.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIII PDF 87–88 / pp. 75–76; paedobaptismum / Anabaptistas / libr. 1 de sacram. Bapt. cap. 9 restored.

title: Rebaptism of those baptized by heretics is not simply necessary to salvation — Cyprian, Stephen, Augustine
english: Rome presses hardest the rule against rebaptizing those baptized by heretics — as if it were necessary faith we cannot deny, yet cannot prove from Scripture.
Cyprian died holding the opposite view the Church later repudiated — yet who would say that martyr fell from salvation?
Their dodge that nothing was yet defined in Cyprian's day fails: if the dogma is Apostolic tradition, a later Church decree adds nothing to Apostolic authority.
Stephen of Rome condemned Cyprian while he lived; Cyprian refused and answered him.
We share the Church's settled practice — no rebaptism of heretics' baptism — but will not urge it as simply necessary to salvation.
We hold it not by unwritten word, but because Augustine's Scripture arguments make it highly probable — and it would be shameless to reject universal practice Scripture does not oppose.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIV PDF 88 / book p. 76; haereticis/Stephano/Augustinus restored.

title: Filioque is hard, but can be proved from Scripture — Rome's own arguments against the Greeks
english: Some also press the Filioque — procession of the Spirit from the Son — as if Scripture cannot show it.
We will not list it among truths that cannot be denied without losing salvation.
We prefer Rome's reading, yet would not damn the Greeks for this alone or break communion over it.
The mystery is hard, but we deny it cannot be proved from Scripture: Spirit of the Son, sent by the Son as by the Father.
Rome herself piles Scripture texts against the Greeks — Lombard, Bessarion, Bellarmine — so she must admit either Scripture proves the Filioque or her anti-Greek case is sophistic.
translator_notes: OCR: XXV PDF 88 / p. 76; Bessarionem/Bellarminum/Lombardum restored.

title: Mosaic books presuppose immortality and prove resurrection — Christ vs the Sadducees
english: Graver still: they say Moses alone never contained all needful to salvation — immortality and resurrection are missing.
Immortality every religion presupposes: if souls die like cattle, piety is vain — eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
Moses' whole scope is religion and worship; soul-immortality is presupposed and openly drawn from that scope.
Particular Mosaic texts also prove resurrection: Christ vs the Sadducees cites I am the God of Abraham... — God of the living, not the dead.
He blames their ignorance of the Scriptures; if resurrection was only obscure then, clear distinct faith of it was not yet required for salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI PDF 88-89 / pp. 76-77; Sadducaeos/Edamus bibamus restored.

title: Legal sacrifices foreshadowing Christ were not clear faith for OT believers — revelation measures faith
english: They add: OT believers had to know legal sacrifices foreshadowed Christ's — yet Moses and the prophets do not make that plain.
Answer: Christ's real death and the types' force toward it is a Gospel mystery, silent in prior ages (as Paul says).
Apostles read it from Scripture after Gospel light and fulfillment; before, it lay in shadows — not clear to the common faithful.
Even after Christ came, Jews and even the Apostles did not yet grasp His death — Peter rebuked as Satan (Matthew 16).
Ancient saints lacked nothing needful: revelation measures faith. Obscure confused faith sufficed until the Gospel made clear distinct faith necessary.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII PDF 89 / p. 77; adumbrarent/Vade a me Satana/Matth. 16 restored.

title: Rome's hardest instance: Scripture cannot prove its own divinity — so an unwritten word seems needed
english: Harder still: they say Scripture cannot be a sufficient faith-rule because we must know which books are inspired.
Even if Scripture calls the Prophets' and Apostles' books divine, no one trusts that claim until he already trusts that Scripture is divine.
So, they argue, some unwritten word of God must teach us that Scripture is God's word — or faith has no divine ground.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII PDF 89 / p. 77; self-witness attack.

title: Reply: the self-witness objection is a sophism — even a complete written word would face the same charge
english: Answer: however showy, the argument is a mere sophism.
Rome admits God could have put His whole word in writing and ordered the Apostles to write all the Church must know — and then our thesis would be true.
Yet the same objection would still run: that this complete Scripture is inspired and these are its books is itself a faith-matter Scripture cannot prove, since nothing proves itself.
That would again demand an unwritten witness — a conclusion false under the hypothesis — so the argument that yields it is sophistic.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIX PDF 89-90 / pp. 77-78; sophisma/hypothesi restored.

title: Retorsion: Rome's Scripture-plus-tradition rule fails the same self-witness test
english: Ask Rome: if Scripture is not the whole sufficient rule, what is?
They answer: written plus unwritten word in Rome's mouth — the total rule outside which there is no other word of God.
Retorsion: that mixed rule also cannot prove what is most necessary — that Rome's Scriptures and traditions are the divine ones, and that her witness is infallible.
Scripture's self-claim and Rome's boast do not settle the point until one already believes God speaks through Rome.
So their rule demands yet another word beyond Scripture, tradition, and Rome's testimony — or faith rests on no word of God.
No faith-rule escapes a similar charge.
translator_notes: OCR: XXX PDF 90 / p. 78; retorqueo/infallibili restored.

title: Fallacy exposed: a sufficient faith-rule need not prove itself — like science's first principles
english: The sophistic fallacy assumes what is false: that a sufficient faith-rule must prove everything including itself.
No rule of faith can prove itself by its own testimony — proof is from what is better known, and a thing is not better known than itself.
Yet embracing the rule is itself necessary to faith.
A perfect sufficient rule is one that, once supposed, proves all else of faith — not one that proves itself.
Scripture's inability to prove itself by bare self-testimony does not strip its sufficiency.
Saying otherwise is like saying the sky does not cover all because it does not cover itself — or that science's first principles are no rule because principles do not prove principles.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXI PDF 90 / p. 78; fallacia/coelum/principia restored. Batch closes before XXXII.

title: Faith accepts revealed things by the word — but the word itself by innate notes
english: The objection assumes faith accepts only what another divine word proves — true for revealed things, not for the word itself.
Things revealed are believed because God testifies in his word; the word itself cannot be propped by infinite regress of further words.
Faith must finally rest in a word received for its own sake, made known by implanted signs and notes under the Spirit's light.
Scripture needs no second word to witness its divinity — it is still faith's proper object.
Rome's own faith likewise bottoms out in some word accepted by motives, not by yet another divine word.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXII PDF 90-91 / book pp. 78-79; res vs verbum / notis insitis / progressus restored.

title: Scripture proves itself by innate notes of divinity — like creation or a classic author's genius
english: Bare self-assertions in Scripture do not convince those who already doubt its authority — in that sense Scripture cannot prove Scripture.
Yet another sense holds: Scripture carries many innate notes of divinity by which it shows itself true and divine.
As heaven and earth prove God by excellence and wisdom's traces — not by a spoken certificate.
As a book claims Aristotle or Cicero by genius of doctrine and style, not by the title page alone.
Scripture's books likewise bear divine wisdom so deeply that inspiration and divine authorship appear.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIII PDF 91 / p. 79; notae/Aristoteli/Ciceroni/vestigia restored.

title: Sum of the reply: no circle, no infinite regress — Scripture known by implanted signs
english: Faith-analysis allows neither a circle nor infinite regress — the mind must stop in a word received immediately for itself.
That word is sacred Scripture (a fixed number of God-breathed books), known by implanted signs, not by another divine word's bare certificate.
Self-knowledge by innate notes does not strip Scripture's perfection as faith-rule.
A rule need not prove itself the way it proves everything else — first principles are supposed, proved at most ad hominem / a posteriori.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIV PDF 91 / p. 79; theopneustos/circulum/a posteriori restored.

title: Rome's integrity objection: Scripture's sincerity cannot be learned from Scripture alone
english: Rome adds: we must know not only that Scripture's books are Spirit-dictated, but that they remain sincere and uncorrupted in our hands.
That integrity, they say, cannot be learned from Scripture itself — so another divine word seems required.
Hence their claim that Scripture alone is not a sufficient faith-rule.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXV PDF 91 / p. 79; sinceritate/integritate restored.

title: Retorsion: tradition's integrity faces the same demand — Bellarmine's 'no new revelations' collapses
english: Same demand hits oral tradition: we must know Apostolic deliveries reached us intact across ages — yet tradition cannot certify its own integrity.
So Rome would need yet another divine word beyond Scripture-plus-tradition to guarantee both arrived uncorrupted.
That falsifies Bellarmine's claim that the Church needs no new revelations and only keeps what Apostles and Prophets delivered.
Appealing to an infallible Church's testimony does not help — whence does the Church itself learn, and on what does its faith rest?
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVI PDF 91-92 / pp. 79-80; Bellarminus lib.4 cap.9 / hodierna Ecclesia restored.

title: Further squeeze: even an infallible Pope or Council cannot prove its own legitimacy or pure decrees
english: For faith to rest sure, you need more than an infallible Pope or Council — you need certainty that this Pope and this Council are the legitimate ones.
Neither can prove its own legitimacy by its own testimony.
Even if legitimacy is granted, you still need certainty that the decrees and canons reached you uncorrupted.
So Rome's rule would demand yet another divine word beyond Scripture, tradition, papal decrees, and conciliar canons — or faith has no sure foundation.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVII PDF 92 / p. 80; Pontificem/Concilium/Canones restored.

title: Reply: the same innate notes that show divinity also show essential integrity
english: Rome is caught in its own snare — the integrity demand forces the reply their Scripture objection needs.
As Scripture needs no second word to prove its divinity, because it is the first rule known by innate signs and motives,
so it needs no second word to prove it uncorrupted and integral.
The same path that shows it divine shows it integral and sincere — at least in momentous and essential matters.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVIII PDF 92 / p. 80; laqueis/notis insitis/essentialibus restored.

title: No circle, no regress: faith reduces to an authority received immediately by the Spirit's illumination
english: In faith's proofs neither circle nor infinite regress is allowed — both are absurd.
Faith must reduce to some authority received as divine (and thus sincere) for its own sake and immediately.
The Holy Spirit's internal illumination brings us there — not by another external divine word's testimony, but by motives of another kind.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIX PDF 92 / p. 80; Spiritus sancti/circulus; batch closes before XL (sense of Scripture).

title: Rome: having Scripture is not enough — you need its true sense, hence tradition
english: Rome presses again: owning the book is not enough — faith needs Scripture's true Spirit-intended sense.
Words alone are not the rule; the sense is.
That sense, they say, cannot come from Scripture alone, because the text is often ambiguous.
Without an infallible explainer — tradition — certainty fails; therefore sola Scriptura fails.
translator_notes: OCR: XL PDF 92 / book p. 80; sensus/traditio/Sola Scriptura restored.

title: Reply: hard places exist — but saving faith does not require piercing every obscurity
english: Yes, Scripture has very hard places even the learned cannot settle.
That does not make an unwritten tradition necessary for those loci.
Faith and salvation do not require piercing every obscurity.
If they did, the Church would lack necessities — and Rome itself confesses tradition does not settle those darkest places either.
translator_notes: OCR: XLI PDF 92 / p. 80; doctissimi/genuinus restored.

title: Scripture is not so dark that necessary doctrine cannot be gathered — pastors help without replacing it
english: Whatever Scripture's obscurity, necessary faith-and-life doctrine can still be gathered certainly by an attentive, skilled reader.
Clarity is not instant ease without labor — weighing words, context, parallels, and purged affections still matter.
Pastors and teachers rightly go before the flock in private, pulpit, and writing.
God gave them to open Scripture's sense — not to replace Scripture as another divine word.
translator_notes: OCR: XLII PDF 92-93 / pp. 80-81; perito lectore/Pastores & Doctores restored.

title: The flock does not take the pastor's sense by blind obedience — but by the light of truth shown
english: Believers do not swallow a pastor's reading by blind obedience or bare office.
Once the sense is shown, the light of truth itself leads them to it.
Finding a sense is harder than recognizing it when another has demonstrated it.
Like faded handwriting: after it is read aloud, the eye begins to see the strokes for itself.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIII PDF 93 / p. 81; caeca obedientia/exolescentibus restored.

title: Need a skilled interpreter, not an infallible one — sense has light in the text itself
english: Faithful readers need a skilled interpreter — not Rome's interpreter who cannot err.
After guidance, certainty rests on the light of truth in the things themselves under the Spirit, not on the guide's or tradition's authority.
Like Aristotle or Horace: a teacher helps, but then you see the sense in the author by your own judgment.
Scripture's sense has light and proofs in the text; it is not blank until tradition or Church judgment fences it.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIV PDF 93 / p. 81; sagaci/Aristotelis/Horatii/limitet restored.

title: Sufficiency allows ordinary explanation — it denies another divine word or infallible sense-fixer
english: Some obscurity and need of explanation do not touch Scripture's sufficiency.
Sola Scriptura does not mean every believer needs no help to draw the whole faith alone.
It means: no second divine word, no second faith-rule, no infallible sense-fixer beyond Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: XLV PDF 93 / p. 81; sufficientiam/infallibili restored.

title: Rome: major doctrines are only probable from Scripture until tradition locks the sense
english: Rome lists weighty doctrines drawn from Scripture only 'somehow' — Trinity equality, Filioque, original sin, need of inward grace.
Until tradition seals the sense, they say, the mind cannot rest without doubt.
Heretics (Greeks, Arians, Pelagians) quote Scripture both ways with a show of probability.
So they demand another divine word to end controversy infallibly.
translator_notes: OCR: XLVI PDF 93 / p. 81; Filioque/Ariani/Pelagiani restored.

title: Sophistry does not erase clarity — tradition and councils face the same heretical pushback
english: Sophistry and varnish that snare the unwary do not make truth unclear for a purged, unprejudiced mind.
Otherwise nothing stays certain — not even God's existence by reason, nor mathematics against Sceptics.
Retorsion: the same dogmas are also contested from tradition and the Fathers — Arians and Pelagians claimed tradition too.
Councils do not escape: Arians set Rimini against Nicaea; Greeks oppose Rome with their own tradition, Fathers, and councils.
translator_notes: OCR: XLVII PDF 93-94 / pp. 81-82; Ariminense/Graeci/Monarchia; batch closes before XLVIII.

title: Blinded disputers do not cancel Scripture light for sincere Spirit-led readers
english: If many dispute the same proofs made every rule useless, no word of God could ever settle heresy.
Prejudice and vain sophisms can darken Scripture for the blinded — that does not cancel its light.
Sincere minds, freed from perverse affections and led by the Spirit, still gather the saving doctrine evidently from Scripture.
They hold firm, undoubted arguments in the text itself.
translator_notes: OCR: XLVIII PDF 94 / book p. 82; sophismatis/Spiritu sancto/facem praeferente restored.

title: Rome: you cannot prove from Scripture that Scripture alone is enough
english: Last objection: you claim Scripture holds all needful to faith and salvation — and no unwritten word of God.
Rome: that claim itself cannot be proved from Scripture; the usual texts are answerable.
Answer: the thesis is solidly from Scripture; earlier theses already undercut unwritten tradition and assert Scripture perfection.
Our theologians bring still more proofs and clear the exceptions.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIX PDF 94 / p. 82; perfectio/sufficientia/non scriptae restored.

title: Even without self-commendation, no rival divine word appears — duty stops at what God revealed
english: Even if Scripture never named traditions or praised its own sufficiency, we would still deny an unwritten word of God.
No such word appears; proposed divine tradition carries human marks and fails as a safe faith-foundation.
True first principles need no higher proof — and false claimants need no express biblical rebuttal if their weakness is plain.
Since no other divine word exists beside Scripture, it holds all that is necessary: men owe no more belief than God has revealed.
translator_notes: OCR: L PDF 94 / p. 82 (closes Pars III before PARS QUARTA). innitis/imbecillitatis/plura scire & credere restored; end of tract Pars III.

title: Pars IV opens: Rome next claims unwritten tradition equals Scripture
english: Pars III answered the claim that Scripture is not a full faith-rule.
Pars IV turns to Rome next move: unwritten traditions share Scripture authority.
They want those traditions received with the same piety as the written word.
We take up that equal-authority claim thesis by thesis.
translator_notes: OCR: Pars IV I PDF 95 / book p. 83; Thesibus novissimis restored.

title: Rome cites John 16 and John 21: much Jesus said and did went unwritten
english: Rome opens with John 16: I still have many things to say — you cannot bear them now.
They add John 21: the world could not hold books of all Jesus did.
Acts 1: forty days of kingdom teaching after the resurrection, yet the Gospels write little of it.
So, they say, much apostolic teaching must live in unwritten tradition.
translator_notes: OCR: II PDF 95; Joan. 16 / John 21 / Actorum 1 restored.

title: Reply: the unsaid things were Gospel mysteries the disciples could not yet bear
english: The many things of John 16 are not a blank check for later Roman traditions.
They mean the clear unpacking of Gospel mysteries the disciples could not yet carry.
Cross, resurrection, ascension, session, Gentile call, end of legal worship, New-Testament church — Christ had sketched these briefly.
Prejudice, grief, and the still-missing Spirit blocked full grasp before the Passion.
translator_notes: OCR: III PDF 95; efficacia/ascensione/sessione restored.

title: Even after Easter the Apostles were slow — but those mysteries are written in the NT
english: Acts 1 proves the point: even after Easter they still asked about restoring Israel kingdom.
Peter needed Acts 10 vision before Gentile inclusion clicked.
Christ did teach after the resurrection and by the poured-out Spirit — true.
False: that teaching stayed unwritten; the NT already holds those mysteries in substance for salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: IV PDF 95-96; Actorum 1/10; summam atque substantiam restored.

title: John 16 is no warrant for Mass, saints, or images — heretics used the same text
english: Rome may not map John 16 onto Mass sacrifice, saint-invocation, or image-worship.
Ancient heretics used the same verse to baptize their figments.
Augustine (tract on John) already called out that abuse.
So the Pontifician move repeats the old heretical color, not a new proof.
translator_notes: OCR: V PDF 96; Missae/Sanctorum/Augustinus in Joan. restored.

title: John 21: not every deed is written — enough is written for saving knowledge of Christ
english: We never claimed every deed of Jesus is in the book.
What is claimed: the whole doctrine needful for salvation is written.
John 20 sets the measure: enough signs for knowing Christ unto life.
Unwritten deeds do not open a second equal rule beside Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: VI PDF 96; Joannes cap. 20 restored.

title: Unwritten signs do not imply unwritten saving dogmas — the same limit cuts both ways
english: Rome consequence fails: unwritten signs do not prove unwritten saving dogmas.
Better inference: even miracles are certain only from Scripture, not tradition.
Same for words and doctrine — certainty stays in Scripture.
Christ measured both deeds and teaching to what suffices for saving knowledge.
translator_notes: OCR: VII PDF 96; consequentia/signa restored.

title: 1 Cor 11 traditions means the Gospel Paul delivered — not unwritten prayer rules
english: Rome third text: 1 Cor 11 — keep the traditions as I delivered them.
They hear unwritten church-prayer rules; that needs proof, not assertion.
Tradition here means the whole Gospel and precepts Paul had given — oral or written.
Much already written, more written later in Paul and the NT; leftover rites fit their age, not a second equal rule.
translator_notes: OCR: VIII PDF 96; 1 Cor 11; Corinthiis (layout) restored; batch closes before IX.

title: Rome: 1 Cor 11 — I received from the Lord what I delivered; the rest I will set in order
english: Rome's second 1 Cor 11 text: I received from the Lord what I delivered — the rest when I come.
Bellarmine leans on delivered as if it proved unwritten tradition.
He adds that Paul's later arrangements are nowhere written.
Catholics fill the gap with ordination, altar-sacrifice, and sacrament matter and form.
translator_notes: OCR: IX PDF 97 / p. 85; Coenae/tradidi/Cetera disponam restored.

title: tradidi is general — the Supper is written; the rest is free order and decency
english: Bellarmine already grants deliver is a general verb — written or unwritten.
The Supper institution Paul delivers is written in 1 Cor 11 and the Synoptics.
What he will arrange later is free order and decorum, not binding everywhere always.
1 Cor 14's general rule — all things decently and in order — is enough; particulars stay with pastors and churches.
translator_notes: OCR: X PDF 97; Matthaeo/Marco/Luca; diatagmata/decenter restored.

title: Burden of proof: Bellarmine must prove Mass and Roman sacraments, not demand our disproof
english: He may not shift the burden: we need not disprove Mass and Roman sacrament forms.
He argues; we answer — he must prove his fill-ins.
Denial of his propositions is enough until he demonstrates them.
Show that Paul ordered Mass sacrifice and those sacraments we call spurious — or drop the claim.
translator_notes: OCR: XI PDF 97; Missae/adulterina restored.

title: Cetera cum venero: lesser order left for an apostolic visit, not Mass dogma
english: His conjectures weigh nothing — and the text itself undercuts them.
After fixing Supper institution and rebuking abuses, Paul adds: the rest when I come.
That rest is lesser business needing his presence and local judgment.
Not a coded deferral of Mass sacrifice and sacrament matter and form.
translator_notes: OCR: XII PDF 97; Cetera/Corinthiacae restored.

title: If cetera were Rome's necessary rites, Paul would already have given the Corinthians all needful
english: Retorsion: if cetera meant altar-sacrifice and sacrament forms, those were still missing when Paul wrote.
But Rome calls those first necessities — while 1 Cor 1 and 15 say the Corinthians already had every word, knowledge, and saving Gospel.
Paul had given a complete faith-doctrine; he hid nothing needful.
So either those Roman traditions are not necessary, or they are not what Paul postponed.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII PDF 97-98; 1 Cor 1/15; perfectam restored.

title: Absurd: Paul writes about head-coverings yet postpones the chief part of Christian worship
english: Even without 1 Cor 1/15, the timeline is absurd.
Would Paul plant a church and omit the chief sacrificial sum of Christian religion?
Yet he writes now about men's and women's attire in the assembly.
And postpone sacrament institution — Rome's supposed chief part of worship — for later? Preposterous.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV PDF 98; praepostera/feminae restored.

title: Rome's third text: 2 Thess 2 — hold traditions by word or by letter
english: Third Rome text: 2 Thess 2 — stand and hold the traditions, by word or by letter.
They hear two equal bins: written epistles and oral-only deposits.
Both, they say, must be held alike.
So unwritten apostolic tradition stands beside Scripture.
translator_notes: OCR: XV PDF 98; 2 Thess 2; Thessalonicenses restored.

title: Reply: then oral and written both bound hearers — now only Scripture locks apostolic substance
english: True for Thessalonians then: some Gospel by voice, some by letter — equal reverence while Paul preached.
The NT canon was still unfinished — granted.
False now: that apostolic substance stayed unwritten, or that certainty comes outside Scripture.
Hearers then had Paul's living voice; after the Apostles, only their Spirit-sealed writings bind the church's perpetual need — no parallel unwritten precept bank remains.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI PDF 98; Thessalonicenses/Canon/Spiritus sanctus restored; batch closes before XVII.

title: Bellarmine: Paul taught when Antichrist would come — Augustine says we cannot know it
english: Bellarmine's press: not everything Paul taught later landed in writing.
2 Thess: you know what restrains — he had said these things when present.
The calendar of Antichrist's coming is nowhere written.
Augustine Civ. Dei 20: hearers knew by living voice; we who did not hear cannot know that point.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII PDF 98 / p. 86; Antichristus/Augustine Civ. Dei 20 restored.

title: Reply: only faith-and-salvation necessities were written — Antichrist's hour is not one
english: We never claimed every apostolic sentence is in the canon — only all needful to faith and salvation.
Nothing of that saving kind stayed oral-only.
Private revelations to some need not bind the whole church or reach parchment.
Antichrist's clock, if Paul knew it, is that private kind — Rome will not call the hour salvific.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII PDF 98; duntaxat/fidem & salutem restored.

title: Retorsion: tradition is as silent as Scripture on when Antichrist comes
english: Ask them: can the whole apostolic doctrine be had from Scripture and tradition together? They will say yes.
Then teach from tradition the Antichrist timetable Paul allegedly gave.
Tradition is as mute as Scripture here.
If that silence does not wreck their tradition-rule, it does not wreck sola Scriptura either.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX PDF 98-99; Thessalonicensibus/Proculdubio restored.

title: Paul taught that Antichrist comes before the Lord — not the date; the restrainer is in the letter
english: Paul did not teach a date — only that Antichrist comes before the Lord's return, and what delays him.
He says you know what restrains — not you know the hour of the man of sin.
The same restrainer is repeated in the letter itself until he is taken out of the way.
Oral clarity may have helped hearers; tradition still adds nothing beyond the written hint.
translator_notes: OCR: XX PDF 99; detineat/retinebit/revelabitur restored.

title: Augustine's line helps us: without the written word we cannot know the apostolic point
english: Bellarmine's Augustine citation cuts his own way.
If it is not written, we who never heard Paul cannot know it.
So Augustine denies certain knowledge of apostolic preaching from tradition alone.
Certainty rests on sacred Scripture — our claim, not Rome's oral bank.
translator_notes: OCR: XXI PDF 99; Augustinus/traditione sola restored.

title: Rome's next reason: heretics of every age rejected traditions — so contempt marks heresy
english: Beyond the texts, Rome argues from reason.
First: heretics in every age despised traditions.
So rejecting tradition is treated as a heresy-mark.
They list Valentinians, Marcionites, Donatists, Arians, Eunomians, Nestorius, Eutyches, Aerians, and more.
translator_notes: OCR: XXII PDF 99; Valentinianorum/Marcionitarum/Eutychetis restored.

title: Reply: heretics can mix true with false — rejecting tradition is not automatically heresy
english: Heresy is not every opinion a heretic holds.
False teachers can still affirm many truths.
Even shared rejection of traditions would not make rejecting them heresy.
They were heretics for perverting Scripture — not for under-valuing tradition; else we must also damn their confession that Jesus is Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIII PDF 99; amplecti/haeresin/Jesum esse Christum restored.

title: Bellarmine is wrong: many heretics sold unwritten tradition — Irenaeus and Jerome say so
english: Bellarmine's premise fails: not every heretic dumped tradition.
Some sneered at unwritten tradition while twisting Scripture; many others sold oral tradition as cover for figments.
Irenaeus: the Marcionites and Valentinians — Bellarmine's alleged tradition-foes — fled Scripture for living-voice tradition.
Jerome and Augustine: heretics forge apostolic tradition and abuse John 16 the same way Rome does now.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIV PDF 99; Irenaeus 3.2; Hieronymus in Aggaeum; Joan. 16 restored.

title: Epiphanius: heretics boasted apostolic tradition — so Rome cannot tar us with their company
english: Epiphanius: Ptolemaeus sold 'apostolic tradition by succession' to Flora.
Semi-Arians likewise boasted a father-to-son faith inheritance from the Apostles.
Worst heretics waved unwritten tradition as cover — just as Rome does.
So they cannot brand our rejection of their traditions as heretic-company.
translator_notes: OCR: XXV PDF 99-100 / pp. 87-88; Epiphanius haer. 33/73; Ptolemaeus/Flora restored.

title: Rome: unwritten tradition is natural — Jews, pagan states, Pythagoras and Socrates
english: Next Rome proof: every nation runs on unwritten custom.
Jews keep extra-scriptural traditions; Athens, Sparta, and the Gauls used unwritten law.
Pythagoras and Socrates taught much and wrote nothing.
Bellarmine: nature itself cries that unwritten tradition is necessary or most useful.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI PDF 100; Athenienses/Lacedaemonii/Caesar restored.

title: Jewish tradition is no model — Christ rebuked it as voiding God's law
english: Yes, Jews had unwritten traditions — Christ called them out for voiding God's law by them.
Isaiah applied: in vain they worship me with commandments of men.
God disapproved; Christ rebuked — no rule for the church.
Today's Moses-mouth boasts show how well oral tradition preserves truth: trifles and blasphemous dreams.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII PDF 100; Isa. 29:13 / Matt 15 pattern; Mosis restored.

title: Pagan unwritten civil law does not prove unwritten faith-rules
english: Athens and Sparta may run on unwritten civil custom — that lane is reason's.
Faith and worship come by revelation, not civic prudence.
Memory alone is not a safe vault for revealed things.
So wisdom had inspired men put them in writing for an uncorrupted church.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII PDF 100; civilem gubernationem restored.

title: Rome: if all were written, the Church would lose her privilege of secret mysteries
english: Third argument: church dignity / privilege.
Romans 3: Jews held the oracles — so the church alone holds true religion's secrets.
If everything is written, that privilege vanishes.
Heretics, Jews, and pagans would know the mysteries as well as we and our bishops.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIX PDF 100; Rom. 3; sponsi restored.

title: Reply: the church keeps written oracles — privilege is faith, not secret textbook knowledge
english: Same privilege as Israel's: the oracles are committed to the church — and they came in writing.
She is guardian and depositary of Scripture; outsiders borrow knowledge from her.
Knowing the textbook is not believing the mysteries.
A Muslim can learn the whole Christian corpus without the faithful's privilege — just as one can read the Koran without believing Muhammad.
translator_notes: OCR: XXX PDF 100; Alcoranum/Mahumetanus/depositaria restored.

title: If bare knowledge were the privilege, Rome's own theology books already destroy it
english: If privilege were mere textbook grasp, nothing should ever have been written — only perpetual oral handoff.
Rome already admits the mysteries sit clear in countless scholastic books.
Unbelievers can learn the system from those theologians even if they miss it in the Prophets and Apostles.
So their imaginary privilege dies either way — written Scripture or written Doctors.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXI PDF 100-101; chartis/Theologorum restored.

title: Rome: some Mass mysteries need silence — so they must not be written for the world
english: Last dignity argument: some mysteries demand silence.
Scripture is read by the whole world — so Rome says those secrets must stay out of it.
Unbaptized may not watch the tremendous Mass mysteries.
Therefore, they ask, how may the same things be delivered to them in writing?
translator_notes: OCR: XXXII PDF 101; Missae/silentium restored; batch closes before XXXIII reply.

title: Reply: superstition hides mysteries — Christian truth is not ashamed
english: Reply: hiding mysteries is superstition's habit — pagans barred the crowd.
Christian truth is not ashamed; Tertullian: it blushes only at being hidden.
Prudence still holds — milk for babes, solid food for the mature; do not cast pearls.
Writing the Gospel is not casting pearls: Rome's own summas and catechisms already publish every Mass mystery Bellarmine calls tremendous.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIII PDF 101 / pp. 88-89; superstitionis/Tertullianus/margaritas restored from tess+layout.
Pass B compresses the long tu-quoque on Roman summas vs Apostolic writing.

title: Name the mysteries too sublime for Scripture — image-cult is not greater than the Trinity
english: Challenge: name the mysteries too sublime for Scripture.
Creation, judgment, resurrection, incarnation, two natures, Trinity — already written.
Image-cult, saint-invocation, papal succession are not higher than Trinity and the cross.
Madness: Apostolic writing would degrade tradition, yet ordinary doctors print it daily.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIV PDF 101; closes De Scripturae plenitudine Pars IV (and the tract).
Next treatise in the 1675 folio is Demonstratur Deum esse.

title: Theology begins from God — He is its chief object
english: Theology takes its name from God — and He is its chief object.
So the right start for theological work is God Himself.
translator_notes: OCR: Thesis I PDF 102 / p.90; Ut Deus restored (scan dropped initial U).

title: Two heads about God: whether He is, and what He is
english: Two heads: AN SIT (whether God is) and QUID SIT (what God is).
Reason says start with whether He is.
translator_notes: OCR: II PDF 102; AN SIT / QUID SIT caps retained as scholastic tags.

title: First theorem: God is — eternal mind, cause of all
english: First theorem under all religion: God is.
Eternal mind — best, most powerful, most wise — cause and ruler of all.
Hebrews 11:6: the one who comes to God must believe that He is.
translator_notes: OCR: III PDF 102; Hebr. 11.6 restored.

title: God's existence is not revelation-only — nature presses it on the senses
english: This principle is not revelation-only — nature itself drums it in.
Romans 1:20: everlasting power and divinity seen in the things made.
Job: ask beasts, birds, earth, and fish — the Lord's hand made them.
translator_notes: OCR: IV PDF 102; Rom 1.20 / Job 12 restored from tess+layout.

title: Even without the Word, some knowledge of God reaches nearly all peoples
english: Even without the Word, some God-knowledge reaches nearly every people.
Almost no nation lacks some religion and some cult of divinity.
Conscience terrors drag even the most lost toward God's tribunal.
translator_notes: OCR: V PDF 102.

title: Saving knowledge is rare — yet even "atheist" nations keep a sense of deity
english: True saving knowledge is rare; most nations miss the true God.
Ephesians 2:12: without God in the world — yet a sense of deity remains.
Idolatry proves it: proud man would rather bow to stones than admit no God.
translator_notes: OCR: VI PDF 102; Greek ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ from Eph 2.12 restored.

title: World-contemplation can reach God — and His existence is demonstrable
english: World-contemplation can reach some knowledge of God — sin's darkness does not block that path for most.
Open question: are the reasons necessary or only probable?
Verdict with nearly all theologians, ours and Rome's: God's existence is demonstrable by necessary arguments.
translator_notes: OCR: VII spans PDF 102-103 page break (nostri / quam Pontificiis).

title: God is not shown a priori from causes — but a posteriori from effects
english: Two demonstration modes: from causes, or from effects.
God cannot be shown a priori from a higher cause — there is none.
He is shown a posteriori from effects — and those arguments convince, not merely persuade.
translator_notes: OCR: VIII PDF 103; closes tip before IX (examples / unique demonstration).

title: One path: from the visible world deduce the God who made it
english: Best shown by sample arguments that carry their own necessity.
From what the eyes meet in this visible world, deduce the God who made it.
One demonstration path is enough — chasing every proof would be endless.
translator_notes: OCR: IX PDF 103 / p.91; numen restored.

title: First lay principles — foundations for physical and metaphysical evidence
english: Before the proof: lay principles as foundations.
Aim at the evidence physics and metaphysics can demand.
These principles will be reused through the whole argument.
translator_notes: OCR: X PDF 103.

title: Principle 1: nothing makes itself — nothing is its own cause
english: First principle: nothing makes itself; nothing is its own cause.
Self-making would require being before being — contradiction.
What is becoming is not yet; what acts already is.
translator_notes: OCR: XI PDF 103.

title: Principle 2: nothing depends on itself — dependence is on another
english: Second principle: nothing depends on itself.
Whatever depends, depends on another.
Self-dependence would make the same thing prior and posterior to itself.
translator_notes: OCR: XII PDF 103.

title: Principle 3: no infinite regress of efficient causes — a first cause
english: Third principle: no infinite regress of efficient causes — arrive at a first cause.
If every cause had infinite superiors, infinite causes would stand outside the whole set — contradiction.
Same distance up and down: if no first cause ascending, no last effect descending.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII PDF 103; long principle restored from tess+layout.

title: Principle 4: not every being is made — some unproduced independent being
english: Fourth: not every being is made — some unproduced, independent being must exist.
Else infinite regress (already ruled out) or a circle of mutual makers.
Abraham–Isaac–Jacob circle: Abraham would mediately beget himself — absurd.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV PDF 103; Abraham/Isaac/Jacob example restored.

title: Principle 5: the first cause is not less perfect than its effect
english: Fifth: the first cause is not less perfect than its effect.
No perfection in the effect is missing from the cause — formally or more eminently.
Nothing gives what it does not have.
translator_notes: OCR: XV spans PDF 103-104; page-break quod non habet joined.

title: Two things to prove: world-bodies are not from themselves; their cause is God
english: Proof plan: two lemmas.
First: earth, sun, stars, planets are not unproduced self-beings — they have a cause.
Second: that cause can only be the highest intelligence we call God.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI PDF 104 / p.92; opens the two-step demonstration for XVII+.

title: World-bodies are composites, not simple self-beings
english: First: chief world-bodies are not unproduced self-beings.
They are composites of diverse parts — rocks, waters, earth — not simples.
What is from itself must be simple and have nothing prior; composites need a unifier.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII PDF 104 / p.92.

title: What is from itself needs nothing — but planets need the sun
english: What is from itself is self-sufficient.
Earth and planets need the sun's light and heat — they cannot stand alone.
Need of another means dependence — and conservation implies an efficient cause.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII PDF 104.

title: World-bodies aim at ends — so they are not for themselves
english: Each world-body has an end — not for itself but for another.
Aseity cannot be referred to an end or have anything prior intending it.
Parts serve the world's common good — so some mind conceived the harmony.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX PDF 104.

title: Limited diverse natures prove an efficient cause — not aseity
english: Diverse limited perfections need an efficient cause.
If all were from themselves they would be one unbounded being.
Aseity would be the fountain of all perfection — not a capped planet-nature.
translator_notes: OCR: XX PDF 104-105 page break into XXI.

title: If the parts are produced, the universe itself is produced
english: Produced parts → produced universe.
A whole of produced parts cannot itself be unproduced.
translator_notes: OCR: XXI spans PDF 104-105.

title: If the world were from itself it would be eternal — but motion and time are not
english: Aseity would mean an eternal world with no start of duration.
But this bodily world is in perpetual motion measured by time.
Motion and time cannot be from eternity — next theses prove it.
translator_notes: OCR: XXII PDF 105 / p.93.

title: Eternal solar motion yields contradiction in the Zodiac
english: Eternal sun-motion: either stuck in one Zodiac sign forever, or in all at once.
One-sign forever: infinite time covers only finite space.
All-signs at once: contradicts moving through the Zodiac.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIII PDF 105.

title: Eternal motion would require infinite human generations — impossible
english: Eternal motion → infinite past human generations.
No first human: every human begotten by a human — including the whole set.
Begetter outside the set is impossible; begetter inside would beget himself.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIV PDF 105; next XXV+ continues generation/time arguments.

title: No first human in an infinite past — contradiction
english: No human is born before another already existed.
Infinite past births: humans before any human — contradiction.
An infinite generation-order could never arrive at us.
translator_notes: OCR: XXV PDF 105-106.

title: Eternal time fails: day and night cannot both be from eternity
english: Eternal time would mean eternal day/night turnover.
What is from eternity is simultaneous — but day and night cannot be.
Night is privation of day: habit and privation cannot coincide.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI spans PDF 105-106.

title: No first day; infinite days cannot equal or sit inside infinite hours
english: Eternal time → no first day — yet a day before every day is absurd.
Infinite past hours vs days: equal would make part = whole.
Lesser infinite days inside greater infinite hours is not infinite.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII PDF 106.

title: A bounded slice of past time cannot be eternal
english: Hours matching infinite days are still bounded by today and a longer past.
A twenty-fourth of past time cannot be called eternal.
Any finite-bounded slice — and a whole of such slices — is not infinite.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII PDF 106.

title: Past infinite time was once future infinite — unreachable; Hebrews 1
english: All past was once future — infinite past was infinite future, never finishable.
Today would have been infinitely distant — unreachable.
No day / every day / some day from eternity all fail; Hebrews 1: God made the ages.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIX PDF 106-107; Hebr. 1 restored.

title: So the world has a beginning — made by the eternal mind we call God
english: Motion and time need a start — so the moving timed world does too.
Therefore the world was made by another.
Author: highest eternal mind — what all call God.
translator_notes: OCR: XXX PDF 107 / p.95.

title: Three candidate causes: chance, blind nature, or intelligent mind
english: World is made — what cause?
Three options: chance atom-clash, blind necessary nature, or intelligent best-and-powerful mind.
Next theses reject the first two.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXI PDF 107.

title: Democritus and Epicurus: chance atoms cannot yield order
english: First option: Democritus/Epicurus — world from rash atom-clash.
Chance yields mess, not constancy, order, harmony.
This universe — and each natural work — shows supreme order.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXII PDF 107; next XXXIII+ palace/watch vs blind nature.

title: Palace and watch: chance cannot build the universe-machine
english: Who credits a palace or a clock to chance scrap-heaps?
This universe outdoes any palace in art and proportion.
No machine shows more motions — more marvelous, more constant.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIII PDF 107; horologium/chalybis restored.

title: Blind necessary cause cannot birth knowers — Psalm 94
english: A brute necessary cause cannot explain knowers.
Knowing effects require a knowing first cause.
Psalm 94: He who planted the ear — shall He not hear?
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIV PDF 107; Psal. 94 / aurem restored.

title: Nature acts for ends — either intelligent, or steered by God
english: Nothing in the world is rash — nature acts for ends.
Sun, seasons, organs: each fitted to a use.
End-seeking without knowledge needs an archer — God either is or steers that nature.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXV PDF 107-108 page break.

title: Infinite marks of wisdom — not a brute cause
english: World-system and each creature show infinite marks of highest wisdom.
Proportions exact beyond human grasp.
Only a fool credits that to a brute, mindless cause.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVI PDF 108.

title: “Nature” is only the order of causes — who authored that order?
english: Ask the nature-only crowd: what do you mean by nature?
Usually: the order of causes — plant begets plant, seasons turn.
That order itself needs an author — who made heaven, sun, earth?
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVII PDF 108.

title: Matter-particles are not from themselves either
english: Some say matter bits self-sorted into the world-order — stop there.
Same proofs that bar planet-aseity bar particle-aseity.
Imperfect parts exist for wholes — not from themselves.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVIII PDF 108.

title: Matter’s division and shapes need an agent
english: Whence matter's split sizes and shapes?
Some agent must have divided and figured it.
Self-shaped bits could not differ or change — yet matter divides without end.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIX PDF 108.

title: Matter’s motion needs an external mover — God
english: Motion is not eternal — so matter-motion had a start.
Matter cannot give itself that first stir.
Who wound torpid matter into a world-system? The highest mind — God.
translator_notes: OCR: XL PDF 108; next XLI+ human-body / conclusion.

title: Blind particle-toss cannot build the human body — or the universe
english: No sober mind credits ordered universe-harmony to undirected particle-toss.
Even one human body — organs apt for many uses — bars that cause.
Blind matter-jactation cannot build this fabric.
translator_notes: OCR: XLI PDF 108-109 / book pp. 96-97; caeco animo normalized from layout OCR.

title: Conclusion: eternal mind — God is
english: Universe and its parts are not a-se — they need a cause.
Not chance, not blind self-ignorant nature.
Necessary: eternal mind, best, strongest, wisest — God. Demonstratum: God is.
translator_notes: OCR: XLII PDF 109 / book p. 97; mentem aeternam from raw OCR mentcmseterrum; tract ends.

title: From Esse Deum to Quid sit Deus — inquire with sobriety
english: Esse Deum is done — now Quid sit Deus.
Inquire into God's nature with fitting modesty and sobriety.
translator_notes: OCR: I PDF 109 / book p. 97; new lock.

title: Our mind cannot grasp what God is in Himself
english: First: confess our weakness — we cannot grasp God-in-Himself here.
1 Cor 13: mirror and enigma; 1 John 3: seeing as He is is future privilege.
If fly and ant essence escape us, much less God's.
translator_notes: OCR: II PDF 109; 1 Cor 13; 1 John 3.

title: Yet we form concepts — the divine attributes
english: We can still form limited concepts of the divine nature.
True attributions fall short of His immense perfection.
Those are the divine attributes — a faint outline of essence.
translator_notes: OCR: III PDF 109.

title: Two kinds of attributes: via affirmation and negation
english: Attributes affirm or deny — two paths to divine nature.
Give God creature-perfections eminently; strip every creature-imperfection.
Negatives teach clearer what God is not; affirmatives dimly what He is.
translator_notes: OCR: IV PDF 109-110.

title: First attribute: God's simplicity removes all composition
english: First attribute: God's Simplicity.
Not moral "simple" — physical/metaphysical vs mixed and composite.
Simplicity attributed = every composition removed.
translator_notes: OCR: V PDF 110.

title: Created compositions: extended parts; subject and accident
english: Creatures show many composition kinds.
Sensible: body parts outside parts, divisible.
Next: subject + accident — white/whiteness; virtue, vice, knowledge on a man.
translator_notes: OCR: VI PDF 110.

title: Essence vs existence composition in creatures
english: Metaphysical composition: essence ≠ existence in creatures.
Essence = what you must conceive (rational animal = man).
Winter rose-nature without a rose: creatures can be and not-be.
translator_notes: OCR: VII PDF 110.

title: Nature vs suppositum — incarnation shows the split
english: Another split: nature vs the singular that has it (Peter / humanity).
Incarnation: Christ took human nature, not a human person.
Creatures = nature + suppositum (subsistence).
translator_notes: OCR: VIII PDF 110; next IX+ genus/difference then corporeity.

title: Genus and difference — another creaturely composition
english: Last shared creature-composition: grades in essence.
Agree by genus; differ by difference.
Finite creatures = genus + difference.
translator_notes: OCR: IX PDF 110.

title: Does God's simplicity exclude all these? First: is God a body?
english: Christian School: God's simplicity bars every such composition.
First question: is God extended parts-outside-parts — a body?
Ancients who said yes: Anaximenes, Diogenes, Xenocrates, Epicurus.
translator_notes: OCR: X PDF 110; Anaximenes normalized from Artaximenes OCR.

title: Sadducees, Anthropomorphites, Tertullian on a corporeal God
english: Sadducees: no spirits — so God must be body.
Anthropomorphites gave God human members; Tertullian called God corporeal.
Augustine excuses him as meaning substance / something real.
translator_notes: OCR: XI PDF 110-111; Aug. haeres. 86.

title: Scripture: God is spirit, fills all, no bodily likeness
english: Scripture + reason: God is wholly incorporeal.
John 4: God is spirit; Ps 139 / Jer 23: He fills all — no extended body.
Isa 40 / Acts 17: no bodily likeness of God.
translator_notes: OCR: XII PDF 111; Psal. 139 (layout 139/139).

title: Image of God is spiritual — human members of God are metaphor
english: Anthropomorphites abused imago Dei into bodily members.
Image = intellect, will, grace-gifts — not limb-shape.
God's ears/eyes/hands in Scripture are metaphor for knowledge and power.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII PDF 111.

title: Philosophy: unmoved mover, immaterial products, no imperfect parts
english: Aristotle: first unmoved mover — no body moves unmoved.
He makes angels and souls — so He is still more immaterial.
Bodies have imperfect parts; a-se first being cannot.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV PDF 111.

title: No accidents in God — subject-accident composition denied
english: Second composition: subject + accident — does God have it?
Theologians say no: first independent being cannot depend as accidents do.
Perfect essence takes no add-on perfection — God is accident-free.
translator_notes: OCR: XV PDF 111.

title: Wisdom and justice in God name the essence, not accidents
english: Objection: God is called wise, just, merciful — are those accidents?
In us those names mark accidents; in God they name the essence itself.
One essence, many names — no single word holds that perfection.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI PDF 111-112; next XVII+ essence/existence.

title: In God essence cannot be cut from existence
english: Creatures: essence without existence — contingent, accidental.
God: essence cannot be conceived without existing.
First essential attribute: necessary being — to be and exist is of His essence.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII PDF 112.

title: Ego sum qui sum — Jehovah; no essence-existence composition
english: Plato's to on / ens per essentiam: exists by His essence forever.
Exod 3: I am who I am; Jehovah from havah — being proper to God.
Apocalypse: who is, was, is to come — no essence-existence split.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII PDF 112; Greek/Hebrew normalized from OCR.

title: Fourth composition: nature and subsistence in creatures
english: Fourth composition: nature vs subsistence (person/suppositum).
Peter ≠ his humanity; Gabriel ≠ angelic nature.
Concrete and abstract names split in creatures.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX PDF 112.

title: In God no added subsistence — else a quaternity
english: Divine nature is singular — no contracting difference needed.
Subsistence is not really other than essence in God.
Else quaternity (nature + three persons); perfect essence needs no add-on to subsist.
translator_notes: OCR: XX PDF 112.

title: Deus est Deitas — Gilbert of Poitiers rejected
english: In God abstract = concrete: God is Deity; goodness itself, justice itself.
John 14: I am the truth and the life.
Gilbert of Poitiers exploded — Person/nature not split names in God.
translator_notes: OCR: XXI PDF 112-113; Joan. 14.

title: God is above every genus — not univocal with creatures
english: God is above every genus — nothing univocally common with creatures.
Wise/just of God names essence; of men, a quality — analogy only.
Even substance is no shared genus: God farther from creatures than substance from accidents.
translator_notes: OCR: XXII PDF 113.

title: No proper difference — one simple essence
english: No genus → no proper difference.
Divine nature has no graded composition.
One simple essence differs through itself from all else.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIII PDF 113.

title: Act and potency — the last metaphysical composition in creatures
english: Last metaphysical composition: act and potency.
Act = whatever perfects; potency = aptness to be perfected or changed.
Every creature has both — and can still receive more change.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIV PDF 113; next XXV+ God immune from act/potency.

title: God is pure act — no passive potency
english: God has no passive potency — nothing can accrue or be stripped from Him.
Schools: He is actus purus — no mixed potency.
Whole mere perfection: whatever He can be, He is.
translator_notes: OCR: XXV PDF 113.

title: Most simple — first being, first one
english: Every composition kind removed — God is most simple.
First being = first one; perfect unity bars composition.
Composites depend on prior parts and a unifier — God has neither.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI PDF 113.

title: School axiom: whatever is in God is God Himself
english: School axiom: whatever is in God is God Himself.
Follows absolute simplicity.
Anything in God that is not God would split and compose Him.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII PDF 113.

title: All attributes one with the essence — split only in our conceiving
english: All attributes are one with each other and with the essence.
Distinction is only in our conceiving — not in the thing.
Infinite perfection forces many concepts of one sufficient reality.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII PDF 113-114; tract ends; next De Dei Perfectione & Infinitate.

title: After simplicity — highest perfection demands absolute simplicity
english: Simplicity and highest perfection are necessarily linked.
In bodies, simpler often means more imperfect — creatures need composition.
Highest perfection demands absolute simplicity — so after simplicity, perfection.
translator_notes: OCR: I PDF 114 / book p. 102; new lock.

title: Perfect = nothing lacking — absolutely or secundum quid
english: Perfect: that to which nothing is lacking.
Said two ways: absolutely, or secundum quid.
translator_notes: OCR: II PDF 114.

title: Secundum quid: complete in its own kind
english: Secundum quid: nothing lacking in its own kind.
Perfect horse / perfect plant = full for that nature.
Still miss many absolute excellences.
translator_notes: OCR: III PDF 114.

title: Simply perfect: every possible excellence — God alone
english: Simply perfect: nothing lacking; every possible excellence.
No creature — only the divine nature.
Creatures have bounded perfections; God holds them all.
translator_notes: OCR: IV PDF 114.

title: Two grounds: cause of all; uncaused from Himself
english: Highest divine perfection from two grounds.
He is cause of all.
He has no cause — through Himself, from Himself.
translator_notes: OCR: V PDF 114.

title: Effect-perfection is in the cause — Psalm 94; Isaiah 66
english: No effect-perfection missing from the first cause.
Ps 94: planter of the ear hears; former of the eye sees.
Isa 66: He who makes others bear is not barren.
translator_notes: OCR: VI PDF 114-115; Psal. 94 / Isa. 66.

title: Axiom: every creaturely excellence is somehow in God — simply simple perfections
english: Axiom: every creaturely excellence is somehow in God.
Two kinds: first, simply simple — better to have than lack.
Life, intellect, free will — no greater perfection bars them.
translator_notes: OCR: VII PDF 115.

title: Secundum quid perfections: sensitive and vegetative tied to imperfection
english: Secundum quid perfections: kind-good but locked to imperfection.
Sensitive / vegetative conflict with higher (angelic) perfection.
Absolutely: better without sense/vegetative than with them.
translator_notes: OCR: VIII PDF 115; next IX+ formaliter / eminenter.

title: Two modes: formaliter vs virtute / eminenter
english: Schools: contain a perfection formally, or by virtue / eminently.
Formal: the perfection is present by its whole nature — fire hot, water cold.
translator_notes: OCR: IX PDF 115.

title: Eminent containment: Sun and heat; angels and senses
english: Eminent: hold something better that can do all the lesser does — without its flaw.
Peripatetic Sun: not formally hot, but produces heat.
Angels: no sense-nature, yet sense-knowledge more nobly by intellect.
translator_notes: OCR: X PDF 115.

title: Secundum quid perfections in God only virtute & eminenter
english: Secundum quid creature-perfections: not formal in God.
Yet God has them all by virtue and eminently.
translator_notes: OCR: XI PDF 115.

title: Why not formal: they drag imperfection and clash in one subject
english: Formal secundum quid would import imperfection — none in God.
Human/horse/ox natures and hot/cold cannot share one subject.
If formal in God, we could predicate them — we cannot.
translator_notes: OCR: XII PDF 115.

title: Yet eminently: He made ear and eye — perceives without organs
english: Not by proper ratio — still virtute & eminenter.
No plant/animal nature formally — yet He made them.
No ears/eyes — yet He planted the ear and formed the eye.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII PDF 115-116.

title: Simply simple perfections are formal in God
english: Simply simple perfections: formal and proper in God.
Life, intellect, will, wisdom, goodness, justice — by proper form.
God is truly living, understanding, free, wise, just, good.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV PDF 116.

title: Objection: intellect and wisdom are accidents — answer by analogy
english: Objection: intellect/wisdom name accidents — none in God.
Answer: as in creatures they are imperfect accidents; as absolute concepts, formal in God.
Analogical names strip accident — sit inside the divine essence.
translator_notes: OCR: XV PDF 116.

title: Every creaturely perfection is somehow in God — as in the fountain
english: No creaturely perfection missing from God — formal or eminent.
He is first cause: all perfection flows from Him and preexists in Him.
Excellence resides in God as in a fountain.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI PDF 116; next XVII+ uncaused first being / infinitude.

title: Uncaused first being — fountain of all entity and perfection
english: Creatures' bounded perfections prove they received being from another.
First being has no cause — exists by His essence.
He is the fountain of all entity and perfection — not a measured grade.
