title: Most Reformed: no sufficient grace that is not also efficacious — elect only
english: Most Reformed deny any ‘sufficient’ grace that fails to convert in fact.
Sufficient = efficacious — no real distinction.
God’s grace efficacious in the elect alone.
So sufficient grace for conversion or avoiding sins is for the elect only — not for all.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII 1675 PDF 214.

title: Some Reformed: universal external mercy-offer counts as sufficient
english: Some Reformed today preach a universal grace common to all — enough of itself for salvation.
Asked if all get sufficient grace: they say yes.
Not as inward Spirit-work on mind/will/affections.
But as outward mercy-preaching and invitation to faith and repentance — by word or providence’s effects.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII 1675 PDF 214.

title: ‘Sufficient’ = physically possible to be saved if one will — not actual conversion alone
english: They do not mean this grace alone actually converts without further help.
It makes salvation possible — he can be saved if he will.
No ‘physical’ block to salvation.
Salvation is duly offered; mind and will can embrace it if used rightly.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX 1675 PDF 214.

title: Yet without internal grace, right use of faculties is morally impossible
english: Still: mind and will are sin-corrupted.
Without inward grace lighting the mind and bending the will, right use cannot happen.
Obeying the outward call needs that inward help.
Without it, obedience is morally impossible because of inherent vice.
translator_notes: OCR: XX 1675 PDF 214.

title: Still inexcusable — moral impossibility sits in the will’s own hardening
english: Refusal of the call is still inexcusable.
Moral impossibility sits in the will’s own hardening in evil.
That does not excuse sin — demons show as much.
Excuse only for blocks outside our will that we cannot remove however hard we try.
translator_notes: OCR: XXI 1675 PDF 214.

title: Outward offer enough for ‘God wills none to perish’ — block is perverse will
english: This common outward offer is enough to say God wills none to perish — and seriously wants all saved and converted.
Salvation is possible for all under a will-dependent condition they can meet if they will.
No external block.
Only a perverse will that spurns God’s offered means.
translator_notes: OCR: XXII 1675 PDF 214–215.

title: Internal grace still elect-only — Amyraut and Testard
english: Inward grace to embrace mercy: elect-only — not common to all.
Amyraut: particular and universal grace dissertations.
Testard, On nature and grace ch. 7 — supernatural grace and salvation’s power through it.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIII 1675 PDF 215; Amyraut; Testard.

title: Their ‘universal’ grace covers infants via parents’ possible salvation
english: Their universal grace covers infants too, not adults only.
God tied infant salvation-power to the parents’ condition.
He made every parent’s own salvation possible.
So children — as parents’ appendages — share that possible salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIV 1675 PDF 215; next XXV+ Amyraut’s third Reformed opinion.

title: Amyraut’s third Reformed view: universal inward grace too — elect still have a peculiar efficacy
english: Amyraut reports a third Reformed opinion (unnamed).
Not only universal external/objective grace unto salvation.
Also a universal inward/subjective grace — without it none can believe or convert.
Elect still have a peculiar efficacy; absolute reprobation they would drive from religion.
Taught in private papers, not print — yet widely circulated.
translator_notes: OCR: XXV 1675 PDF 215; Amyraut De Gratia Particulari.

title: Remonstrants: universal internal grace — free to use well or ill
english: Belgian Remonstrants/Arminians make universal sufficient grace a chief dogma.
God gives it so all can repent and convert if they please.
With most modern Romans: salvation offered outwardly to each.
Also inward universal action — free to use well or ill; reject, or climb by degrees to true faith and eternal salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI 1675 PDF 215.

title: Lutherans reject sufficient/efficacious split — call resists, not weak offer
english: Lutherans scrap sufficient-vs-efficacious as useless.
Yet near the Remonstrants here: all are universally called.
The call is efficacious of itself and by God’s intent.
It fails in many because they resist, refuse its efficacy, or cast grace off — not because the offer was weak (Gerhard).
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII 1675 PDF 215; Gerhard Tom. 2 de Elect. & Reprob. c.7.

title: Not yet a Roman article of faith — Reformed majority still deny universal sufficient grace
english: Rome: universal sufficient grace is not yet a binding article of faith — some still oppose.
Some Reformed today defend a universal, kind-sufficient grace.
But the commoner Reformed church opinion is against it.
What most Romans affirm for all (conversion and avoiding new sins), most Reformed simply deny.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII 1675 PDF 215–216.

title: Word-agreement with Rome hides a real split: internal vs external ‘sufficient’
english: Even Reformed who speak with Romans of universal sufficient grace still dissent in substance.
Romans mean inward/subjective grace — conversion physically and morally possible.
Those Reformed mean only external/objective grace.
With that alone and no inward grace, conversion stays morally impossible.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIX 1675 PDF 216.

title: Amyraut’s inward-universal Reformed align with recent Thomists on a further peculiar help
english: Amyraut’s inward-universal Reformed still look like recent Thomists/Dominicans.
Universal grace (even subjective) converts no one in act by itself.
Actual conversion needs a further peculiar help.
That help is not for all — only for those who actually convert.
translator_notes: OCR: XXX 1675 PDF 216; tract ends; next De Fidei justificantis natura.

title: Historical faith: bare assent that does not move to right living
english: Historical faith = bare assent to what God’s Word proposes.
Authority of God speaking — yet no move to right living, no betterment.
Simon Magus believed thus — heart not right; still in bitterness and iniquity (Acts 8).
Jewish leaders likewise: believed but would not confess Christ — loved men’s glory more (John 12).
translator_notes: OCR: I 1675 PDF 216; Act. 8; Joan. 12 (OCR 1 1).

title: Why called ‘historical’: idle contemplation, not content limited to narratives
english: ‘Historical’ is not ‘only Bible stories’.
It believes promises, doctrines, and precepts too.
The name tracks the manner: like reading unrelated history — bare gaze, no inward effect.
Idle speculation on the Word — not referred to practice.
translator_notes: OCR: II 1675 PDF 216.

title: James’s dead faith — no salvation; not worthy of the name ‘true faith’
english: James calls this dead faith — no motion or action, like a corpse.
It does not save; it worsens guilt and damnation.
Demons believe God is one and tremble — same sort of faith.
Protestants deny it the name ‘true faith’: true faith alone brings justice and salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: III 1675 PDF 216–217; James 2.

title: Scripture’s praised faith is another — true, saving, justifying
english: Scripture’s highly praised faith is another thing entirely.
John 3 / Mark 16 / Romans: believe → eternal life, salvation, justice.
Whoever has it is just before God — unlike demon/ungodly assent.
Protestants reserve ‘true, saving, justifying faith’ for this alone.
translator_notes: OCR: IV 1675 PDF 217; Joan. 3; Marc. 16; Rom. 10 (OCR to).

title: Justifying faith actually justifies — not mere remote preparation
english: Justifying faith ≠ any mere preparation for justification (near or remote).
It actually justifies — or justification always and infallibly goes with it.
Saving faith = what truly places a man in grace and salvation.
translator_notes: OCR: V 1675 PDF 217.

title: Reformed split: ambiguous word vs analogous species (Maresius / Wittich)
english: Reformed disagree on how historical and justifying faith differ.
Maresius: not genus/species — an ambiguous word’s senses (System XI.21).
Wittich (and Paraeus / Leiden): genus into analogous species (Theologia Pacifica 11.136).
translator_notes: OCR: VI 1675 PDF 217; Maresius; Wittich Theologia Pacifica.

title: Calvin and the common Catechism: sure knowledge and trust of God’s love in Christ
english: Better seen from defining justifying faith and its acts/parts.
Reformed definitions vary in wording — nearly the same sense.
Calvin: firm sure knowledge of God’s goodwill to us, on the free promise in Christ, Spirit-revealed and heart-sealed.
Common Catechism: sure persuasion/trust that the Father loves me for Jesus’ sake.
translator_notes: OCR: VII 1675 PDF 217; Calvin; vulgar Catechism.

title: Beza, Ursinus, Paraeus: persuasion and fiducia that the promises are mine
english: Beza: firm constant persuasion — God’s word true, and the free-reconciliation promises mine.
Ursinus/Paraeus: not only sure assent to all God disclosed.
Also Spirit-kindled trust through the Gospel — rest in God.
Sure that remission, eternal justice, and life are given to me too — freely, for Christ’s merit alone.
translator_notes: OCR: VIII 1675 PDF 217; Beza Ann. Rom. 1; Ursinus/Paraeus Cat. Expl. II.21; next IX+ Rivetus.

title: Rivetus and Moulin: assent plus particular fiducia — adoption’s inward witness
english: Rivetus: Spirit-wrought firm assent to revealed things — especially saving promises in Christ.
Fiducia rests in God: remission not only in general but mine; eternal justice and life for Christ’s merit.
Du Moulin (Sedan): firm assent that Gospel promises are true and particularly mine.
Spirit of adoption inwardly witnesses sonship → peace, trust, charity’s works.
translator_notes: OCR: IX 1675 PDF 217–218; Rivetus; Moulin Sedan Disp.

title: Maresius, Wendelin, Alting: gift that fiducially applies Gospel promises
english: Maresius: faith = gift that rests in Gospel promises as true/sure and applies them fiducially.
Wendelin: elect believe divine truth; firm-will receive saving promises; apply Christ and all benefits.
Alting: knowledge of God’s grace in Christ the Redeemer + fiducial grasp applied to myself singularly.
translator_notes: OCR: X 1675 PDF 218; Maresius; Wendelin; Alting.

title: Bucanus: knowledge, assent, appetite — firm trust and personal application of Christ
english: Bucanus (Lausanne): knowledge, assent, and appetite for what grace’s word promises.
Firm trust/apprehension of salvation for Christ’s sake.
Or: mind’s knowledge and approval → heart’s desire and grasp.
True believers each apply crucified Christ and His benefits (word and sacraments) to themselves.
translator_notes: OCR: XI 1675 PDF 218.

title: Ames, Wittich, Mestrezat: heart’s rest in God — hunger for justice; refuge to mercy
english: Ames: faith = heart’s rest in God as author of life/eternal salvation.
Will-act embracing the good the intellect approves (Marrow I.3); virtue leaning on God’s faithfulness (I.27).
Wittich: hunger and thirst for justice + heart’s rest in God as salvation’s fountain.
Mestrezat: justifying faith = penitent sinner’s refuge to God’s mercy in Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: XII 1675 PDF 218; Ames Medulla; Wittich; Mestrezat.

title: Vermigli, Musculus, Placeus: firm assent that draws fiducia, hope, charity
english: Vermigli: firm sure assent to God’s words, Spirit-breathed unto salvation.
‘Firm’ means efficacy that pulls fiducia, hope, charity, and good works along (as this life allows).
Musculus: constant heart-assent to what the word narrates or promises.
Placeus (Saumur): tenacious efficacious persuasion — especially remission and eternal-life promises in Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: XIII 1675 PDF 218; Vermigli; Musculus; Placeus.

title: Zanchi: generic living/dead split — then a stricter fiducia in the promises
english: Zanchi’s broad definition: God-given virtue persuading us the whole preached Word is God’s — law and Gospel.
He splits that into living (love-efficacious) and dead.
Living = justifying; so justifying faith = Word-assent efficacious through love.
Narrower later: firm undoubted assent to promises of remission, justice, eternal life in Christ — Spirit-excited fiducia.
translator_notes: OCR: XIV 1675 PDF 218–219; Zanchi Tom. 4.

title: Public confessions: Thorun Polish Declaration and English Confession on saving faith
english: Public Reformed confessions outweigh private doctor lists.
Toruń 1645 Polish Declaration IV.8: justifying faith fiducially embraces and applies the Gospel promise with a contrite heart — then efficacious through charity.
English Confession (~same time) ch. 14: believe all God reveals; obey, tremble, embrace promises.
Chief acts: accept and receive Christ; rest in Him alone for justification and eternal life by the covenant of grace.
translator_notes: OCR: XV 1675 PDF 219; Thorun 1645; English Confession ch.14.

title: Why definitions vary: whole essence vs the differentia from historical faith
english: Varied definitions are not random conflict.
Some sketch the whole essence (shared with historical + what is proper).
Others mark only the differentia from historical faith.
One property or another in the wording — both belong; combine, don’t oppose.
translator_notes: OCR: XVI 1675 PDF 219; next XVII+ complete vs minimal faith.

title: Complete persuasion vs the minimum without which true faith cannot stand
english: Some define justifying faith by its complete/perfect state — firm sure persuasion of being in grace and of remitted sins.
Yet weak faith can subsist for a time without that full persuasion.
Others define by the minimum without which true faith — however small — cannot stand.
Hunger and thirst for justice; heart's rest in God. Acts of faith come next.
translator_notes: OCR: XVII 1675 PDF 219; complete vs minimal definitions.

title: Two marks: practical assent, and particular application of the promises
english: Reformed: two things mark living/justifying faith off from historical/dead.
Historical = theoretical — sticks in the theoretical intellect.
Justifying = practical assent — recalls belief to practice; moves will and affections.
Historical: only general assent to promises; justifying: applies them to each believer one by one.
translator_notes: OCR: XVIII 1675 PDF 219.

title: Justifying faith includes historical virtue — as rational soul includes lower life
english: Justifying faith differs from historical yet includes all its virtue — perfect vs imperfect; higher degree.
Analogy: rational soul to sensitive/vegetative — embraces lower powers and adds reason.
It also believes all God teaches (as historical faith does).
Above that: brighter theoretical light, deeper practical penetration, sharper sense, firmer assent; refers revelation to life and applies it personally.
translator_notes: OCR: XIX 1675 PDF 219; diversam (not eversam).

title: Object of saving faith: all revealed things — principally the Gospel promises
english: Next: object, parts, and acts of justifying faith.
Object commonly: all God revealed in His word — faith refuses none when proposed.
Proper and principal object: Gospel promises.
Mercy and grace through Christ offered to all who truly believe and repent.

title: Rivetus: special object of justifying faith — Evangelical promise of Christ the Mediator
english: Rivetus (Leiden Synopsis): faith in breadth embraces notitia, assent, fiducia toward all revealed unto salvation.
Yet as justifying it has a special object.
That object: the Evangelical promise of Christ the Mediator — what marks it off from other senses of faith.
It justifies/saves insofar as it apprehends and embraces Christ’s merit revealed in the Gospel word.
translator_notes: OCR+vision: XXI 1675 PDF 220; Rivetus Disp. de Fide th. 9–10.

title: Maresius and Alting: adequate object the whole Word — proper object Christ/Gospel
english: Maresius: adequate object = God’s Word; proper/special/proximate = doctrine of Christ and remission in His blood (XI.36).
Alting: generally/adequately = whole Word; specifically/properly = Gospel / Christ the Redeemer in Gospel and Sacraments.
The rest of the Theologians agree — no need to pile more citations.
translator_notes: OCR+vision: XXII 1675 PDF 220; Maresius; Alting.

title: Promises as object not only in general — but applied to me by sure fiducia
english: Reformed warn: Gospel promises are object not only as generally true.
Also as pertaining to this and that person one by one — apprehended and applied by faith.
Rivetus: knowing that Christ suffered is not enough; nor assent that He suffered for all.
Need sure fiducia: remission given to me privately for Christ’s merit; received into grace; applied fiducially to myself.
translator_notes: OCR+vision: XXIII 1675 PDF 220; Rivetus on particular application.

title: Wendelin: proper object — Christ for me and special mercy applied by faith
english: Wendelin (Chr. Theol. II.24, th. 11): proper/principal/proximate object = Evangelical promise of sins expiated by Christ’s death.
Penitent believers received into grace for Christ crucified apprehended by faith.
Each applies that promise to himself in particular — thus believes unto salvation.
Explanation: Christ crucified for us/me/you + free remission by His blood — special mercy applied by faith.
translator_notes: OCR+vision: XXIV 1675 PDF 220; next XXV+ Paraeus/Ames on quae/qua.

title: Paraeus and Ames: generic vs specific object — quae justificat and qua justificat
english: Paraeus: generic object = all God revealed; specific = promise of special mercy.
Ames: object of faith which justifies vs by which it justifies.
Which-justifies spans the whole Word; by-which restricts to the promise of mercy.
Special mercy follows faith — it does not precede it.
Faith justifies by fleeing to Christ for particular remission, not by believing sins already remitted.
Proper object as such: Christ Himself, not a bare proposition.
translator_notes: OCR+prior vision: XXV 1675 PDF 220; Paraeus; Ames Bell. Enerv.

title: Trelcatius: intellect’s object divine truth — will’s object singular grace in Christ
english: Trelcatius (Leiden): object of faith by intellect vs by will.
Intellect: divine truth. Will: singular grace promised in Christ Jesus.
Both bounded by God’s word — faith’s adequate object.
In that Word: crucified Christ with all benefits — principal, first, proximate, proper object.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVI 1675 PDF 221; Trelcatius Inst. Loc. Comm.

title: Three acts commonly: knowledge, assent, and fiducia applying the promise
english: Most Reformed: three acts/parts of justifying faith.
1. Notitia — know God’s word at least as needed for salvation.
2. Assensus — assent to all God revealed.
3. Fiducia — believer specially applies the general promise-word to himself.
Ursinus/Paraeus Cat. Expl. 21; Wendelin; Tilenus; Trelcatius.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVII 1675 PDF 221.

title: Musculus: believe about God, believe God, believe in God
english: Musculus: three degrees/parts — explained differently.
1. Believe certain things about God, Christ, and the Spirit.
2. Believe God — credit His word as infallible Word of God.
3. Believe in God — direct all hope to Him; depend with firm trust on His goodness.
translator_notes: OCR: XXVIII 1675 PDF 221; Musculus Loci de Fide.

title: Bucanus: knowledge of Christ, double judgment, heart’s apprehension
english: Bucanus: three constituting parts — with a distinctive twist.
1. Knowledge of crucified Christ and His benefits.
2. Consent / double judgment: general approval of Word-truth about Christ; special self-adjudgment that Gospel promises are mine.
3. Heart’s apprehension — will embraces what the mind judged true, holy, good, saving, and peculiarly ours.
translator_notes: OCR: XXIX 1675 PDF 221; Bucanus Loc. 29 q.6.

title: Perkins: five degrees from Gospel knowledge to special Spirit-persuasion
english: Perkins (Golden Chain 16): five degrees in faith’s rise.
1. Spirit-illumined Gospel knowledge → general assent.
2. Hope of pardon — remissible even if not yet felt remitted.
3. Hunger for grace offered in Christ.
4. Access to the throne of grace — apprehend Christ; find mercy.
5. Spirit-impressed special persuasion applying Gospel promises to myself.
translator_notes: OCR: XXX 1675 PDF 221; Perkins Armilla Aurea 16.

title: Ames: five concurrents — faith properly in pious affection, rest, and apprehension
english: Ames: five things concur in divine faith.
Knowledge of what God attests; pious affection toward God; assent; rest in God; choice/apprehension of the good shown.
Knowledge required but does not constitute faith; assent is an effect.
Faith properly = pious affection + rest in God + apprehension of the proposed good.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXI 1675 PDF 221; Ames Medulla I.3.

title: Wittich: antecedent, essential, and accidental acts — remission-fiducia not of the essence
english: Wittich: antecedent / essential / accidental (corroborated-only) acts.
Antecedent: knowledge of revelation.
Essential: general+special assent (Christ sufficient for me if I flee); sincere love of Christ; fiducia of sure help in straits.
Accidental/corroborated: fiducia of obtained remission; solid joy; peace of conscience.
Remission-fiducia is not of justifying faith’s essence — effect of fuller faith.
Weak believers may hunger for justice without yet persuading themselves of remission.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXII 1675 PDF 221–222; Wittich Theol. Pac. 11.138; next XXXIII+ Perkins/Ames on implicit faith.

title: Perkins: assurance of remission is faith’s perfection, not its essence — weak implicit faith
english: Wittich is not alone: certainty of obtained/coming remission is complement of saving faith, not essence.
Perkins (Reformed Catholic, implicit faith q.6): weak sons of God may not distinctly say ‘I believe my sins remitted’.
Yet they have true implicit faith — like leaves/flowers latent in a dry grain; God accepts it unto salvation.
Catechisms that define faith only as complete persuasion of God’s love miss lower true degrees.
Mustard-seed: weak faith believes sins remissible and hates condemnation — without yet daring full ‘remitted’ certainty.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIII 1675 PDF 222; Perkins Reformed Catholic; Granum sinapis.

title: Ames and Pierre du Moulin the son: full certainty is supreme degree, not essential form
english: Ames: particular intellectual assurance of grace already possessed can be falsely absent for a time while true faith lies latent.
Not all justified are at once certain of justification (Bell. Enerv. VI).
Pierre du Moulin the son (Canterbury): full fiducia that ‘my sins are remitted’ = supreme degree, not essential form.
Essential form: embrace Christ’s merits; appropriate them; seek salvation nowhere else — Belgic Confession art. 22.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIV 1675 PDF 222; Ames Medulla; P. du Moulin fils; Belgic 22.

title: Pierre du Moulin the father: this fiducia is commanded and to be sought — weak sight still sees the way
english: Pierre du Moulin the father taught the same before his son.
Those not yet at this degree of fiducia are not struck from the roll of the faithful.
God does not give that degree to all at once or in the same measure.
It is commanded, to be sought, and grown by prayer and good works.
First unfeigned faith may be smoky — bleared eyes still see the way (bronze serpent).
translator_notes: OCR: XXXV 1675 PDF 223; Fide justif. II.39; bronze-serpent allusion.

title: English Confession 1647: saving faith and assurance of being in grace are distinct
english: English Confession (1647) separates saving faith from certainty of being in grace.
Ch. 18: that certainty is not so of faith’s essence that a true believer cannot lack it.
He may await it and struggle with many difficulties before sharing in it.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVI 1675 PDF 223; English/WCF ch.18; year 1647 (OCR often 1641).

title: Public Confessions agree — Wendelin: love also belongs among faith’s acts
english: Not only Wittich: private doctors and public Reformed Confessions agree.
Full remitted-certainty belongs to corroborated faith.
Wendelin too: sincere love of God/Christ among faith’s acts.
Though parts are notitia/assensus/fiducia, love still belongs — will as well as intellect.
Augustine: to believe in Christ is to love Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVII 1675 PDF 223; Wendelin Christ. Theol. II.24.

title: Chamier: faith is in the will — to believe in God is to love God
english: Chamier: same argument — faith in the will, not intellect alone.
Every love is a will-act; faith is love; therefore faith is a will-act.
True faith believes in God = loves God (Augustine).
translator_notes: OCR: XXXVIII 1675 PDF 223; Chamier Panstratia.

title: Cocceius with Wittich: faith a species of love — vs those who keep love only as effect
english: Wittich cites Cocceius: faith = a species of love of God as expiator and healer.
Faith connected with charity — Christ’s charity poured in the heart; who believes loves.
Opposed: Maresius, Baron, Bucanus, du Moulin, Saumur — faith in intellect alone.
They grant love is born from true faith and inseparable as effect — but not an act elicited as faith itself (lest faith = charity).
translator_notes: OCR: XXXIX 1675 PDF 223; Cocceius; opposing intellect-only party.

title: All agree notitia is included — not philosophical science, but some grasp of what is proposed
english: Amid disagreement on acts, all agree: notitia of things to be believed is included in / required for saving faith.
Not philosophical scientia through causes, nor accurate grasp of mode and reason.
Divine mysteries: known that they are by revelation; cause/mode often unknown.
Notitia here = some apprehension of what the Word proposes for assent.
translator_notes: OCR: XL 1675 PDF 223; next XLI+ explicit vs implicit knowledge.

title: Explicit knowledge of chief articles required — pure church-trust without grasp condemned
english: Not every believer must distinctly know all Scripture contains.
Measure of knowledge differs — pastor/doctor more than a private believer.
All need some express explicit knowledge of the chief articles.
Blind church-trust with no distinct grasp of articles = condemned ‘implicit’ faith.
Enough: know the chief saving heads expressly; believe the rest at least in general.
translator_notes: OCR: XLI 1675 PDF 223–224.

title: Chief articles suffice for faith — yet every believer must press on in the Word
english: Explicit knowledge of a few chief heads suffices for faith — but not as a pious rest-stop.
Each must press on in saving doctrine according to calling.
Colossians: abound in the word; Hebrews 5: leave milk for solid food.
Fostering people’s crass ignorance under ‘implicit faith’ is grave error.
translator_notes: OCR: XLII 1675 PDF 224; Col. 2–3; Heb. 5.

title: Fiducia as faith’s formal act — or only its inseparable effect (Garissol)
english: Most Reformed: fiducia = proper formal/specific act and primary part of faith.
Others: fiducia is faith’s offspring/effect — not faith’s act properly.
Garissol (Montauban): fiducia coheres inseparably with faith but is effect, not faith itself.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIII 1675 PDF 224; Garissol Cat. Expl. §18.

title: Beza, du Moulin, Faius: fiducia differs from faith as effect from cause
english: Beza on Eph. 3: fiducia differs from faith as effect from cause — do not swap the names.
Du Moulin: faith ≠ fiducia; fiducia = inseparable fruit/effect.
Faius (Geneva): liberty of access and Abba-cry fiducia are effects of faith.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIV 1675 PDF 224; Beza Eph. 3; du Moulin; Faius.

title: Zanchi: generic faith ≠ bare fiducia — yet justifying faith nearly is fiducia
english: Zanchi: faith in general ≠ mere fiducia — faith also regards the law and whole Word.
Yet justifying faith is trust, or differs little from it.
Justifying faith = firm undoubted assent to promises of remission, justice, eternal life in Christ — Spirit-excited.
Fiducia = most sure persuasion we shall obtain what God freely promised.
translator_notes: OCR: XLV 1675 PDF 224–225; Zanchi Tom. 4.

title: Wittich: fiducia as rest in God is of the essence — remitted-certainty may be lacking
english: ‘Fiducia’ is used in several senses — apparent verbal disputes often hide real agreement (or reverse).
Wittich’s essential fiducia = heart’s rest in God as salvation’s author.
Rest in Christ as sufficient Savior for those who flee = of faith’s essence.
Persuasion of remitted sins (past/future) can be lacking — such believers are weak.
Learned from Widmar (Maresius’s colleague).
translator_notes: OCR: XLVI 1675 PDF 225; Wittich Theol. Pac. 11.139.

title: Ames: believe-into-God fiducia — general assent causes it; special remitted-assent is its effect
english: Ames: primary essential act = believe-into-God fiducia (choose/lean on the sufficient means).
Not bare persuasion of a future good.
General Word-assent ≠ saving faith (can be lifeless).
Special ‘God is my God in Christ’ flows from faith — not faith’s first act.
General assent → causes fiducia; special remitted-possession assent ← effect of fiducia.
Particular intellectual assurance can be absent while true faith lies latent.
translator_notes: OCR: XLVII 1675 PDF 225; Ames Medulla I.3.

title: Ames on faith of special mercy: unto Christ before justification — of mercy already given after
english: Ames (Bell. Enerv.): ‘faith of special mercy’ in two senses.
1. Apprehend/lean on Christ unto mercy through Him — precedes justification; most properly justifies.
2. Apprehend mercy as already given — follows justification; does not justify in that respect.
Apprehension = arriving/reaching Christ, not bare intellect-grasp.
Many still describe justifying faith by the latter assurance-act.
translator_notes: OCR: XLVIII 1675 PDF 225; Ames Bell. Enerv.; Contarini; next XLIX+.

title: Ames: proper object of justifying fiducia is Christ — not the proposition ‘my sins are remitted’
english: Ames: the fiducia that leans on Christ is faith’s proper formal justifying act.
Its proper object = Christ / God’s mercy in Christ — not a proposition or axiom.
Not ‘my sins are remitted through Christ’ as the immediate object.
After justification, another act may reach that proposition’s certainty.
Explains why some speak as if that remitted-proposition were faith’s proper object.
translator_notes: OCR: XLIX 1675 PDF 226; Ames.

title: Davenant: lean-on-Mediator fiducia justifies — felt assurance is its daughter
english: Davenant (Salisbury, Dort): ‘fiducia’ names two things.
1. Lean-on/embrace-Christ act — justification always follows, with or without felt remission at once.
2. Full vivid sense of obtained remission/favor — daughter of justifying faith, after exercises.
Proper formal act: apprehend the promise and fiducially rest on the Mediator.
Not bare notitia, general assent, or mere conditional promise-grasp — those prepare; lean-on-Mediator is the last accompanying act.
translator_notes: OCR: L 1675 PDF 226; Davenant Determ. q.37.

title: Du Moulin the son: fiducia of refuge justifies — fiducia of sense follows
english: Pierre du Moulin the son: twofold fiducia.
Fiducia of refuge — flee to God / lean on Him (Ps 31; Isa 50) — instrument and essential form.
Fiducia of sense — Spirit-witness that God is reconciled and life is ours — born from the former (Eph 3:12).
Promises belong to those coming hungry to Christ, not to those who already possess Him.
Sense-fiducia presupposes justification — cannot cause it.
Direct act justifies; reflex sense may lag — many justified without yet feeling they have Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: LI 1675 PDF 226–227; P. du Moulin fils; Ps 31; Isa 50; Eph 3:12.

title: Mestrezat and Perkins: refuge/access justifies — special persuasion is perfection
english: Mestrezat: justifying faith = penitent’s refuge to God’s mercy in Christ.
Perkins’s fourth degree (access to the throne, apprehend Christ) = fiducia of refuge — justification follows at once.
Fifth/special Spirit-persuasion applying promises = fiducia of sense — follows justification; perfection, not essence.
translator_notes: OCR: LII 1675 PDF 227; Mestrezat; Perkins degrees.

title: Walaeus: justifying fiducia is a will-act receiving Christ — not intellect’s remitted-assent
english: Walaeus faces the objection: if faith = trust of remitted sins, justification can’t be faith’s effect.
Answer: first justifying act is receiving Christ with His merit unto coming remission — not believing sins already remitted.
Will’s fiducia from general Gospel assent — precedes special remitted-assent.
Proper object = Christ and His merit, not the remitted-proposition.
Agrees with Ames.
translator_notes: OCR: LIII 1675 PDF 227; Walaeus Loci.

title: English Confession: receive and rest in Christ — assurance of grace is not faith’s essence
english: English Confession 1647: chief acts = accept/receive Christ; rest/lean on Him alone for justification, sanctification, life (14.2).
Separates saving faith from certainty of being in grace (ch. 18).
True believers may long lack that certainty — so sense-fiducia is not faith’s formal essence.
Essence: lean-on/rest-in-Christ fiducia unto mercy.
translator_notes: OCR: LIV 1675 PDF 228; English/WCF 14.2, 18.

title: Wendelin: fiducia as persuasion we are counted just — required beyond general assent
english: Other Reformed: proper specific act = persuasion I am accepted and given life for Christ’s merit.
Wendelin: fiducia = third/principal part — apply general Gospel promises; persuaded we are reputed just and heirs.
Respect of this fiducia: faith called saving/justifying.
God justifies none who do not trust in Christ and firmly believe sins remitted for His merit.
Notitia or general assent alone does not suffice.
translator_notes: OCR: LV 1675 PDF 228; Wendelin I.24 th.15.

title: Rivetus and Sohn: certain fiducia that remission and life are granted to me in particular
english: Rivetus: sure fiducia — remission not only in general but mine; eternal justice and life for Christ’s merit.
Sohn (Heidelberg): chief part of justifying faith = apply the grace-promise to myself.
Not only others — I too have God propitious; rest and rejoice in God through Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: LVI 1675 PDF 228; Rivetus; Sohn; next LVII+ Paraeus/Baron.

title: Paraeus: sure fiducia — remission, justice, and life granted to me in particular
english: Paraeus: faith = sure fiducia resting in God.
Sure that remission, eternal justice, and life are given not only to others in general but to me/you in particular.
From God’s mercy for Christ’s merit alone.
translator_notes: OCR: LVII 1675 PDF 228; Paraeus on Bell. Justif. I.4 App.

title: Baron of Aberdeen: four senses of fiducia — persuasion, rest, fortitude, peace
english: Baron (Aberdeen): four senses of fiducia to clear ambiguity.
1. Firm intellectual persuasion — redeemed by Christ’s blood; sins remitted; future deliverance and glory.
2. Inward rest in God’s goodwill — depend wholly on it.
3. Spiritual fortitude against temporal/spiritual evils.
4. Peace/serenity of conscience — quiet from servile fear.
translator_notes: OCR: LVIII 1675 PDF 228; Baron Aberdeen.

title: Baron’s first sense grounds the rest — yet omits the refuge-fiducia of Ames and Wittich
english: Baron: first-sense fiducia (apply promises) founds rest, fortitude, and peace.
Le Blanc: he still misses refuge-fiducia — flee/lean on Christ to become a partaker, not rest as already one.
Refuge-fiducia is born from solid Gospel assent but precedes special ‘already mine’ assent.
Baron’s first sense = special remitted-assent; his second = rest as already persuaded — not simple fleeing to obtain.
translator_notes: OCR: LIX 1675 PDF 228–229; Baron vs Ames/Wittich/Moulin.

title: Baron: senses 2–4 are effects — only first-sense fiducia is faith’s proper act
english: Baron on ‘Is fiducia an act of faith?’ — two assertions.
Senses 2–4: not faith’s act but faith’s effect/consequent.
Sense 1: true proper act of saving faith — even its chief specific act.
translator_notes: OCR: LX 1675 PDF 229; Baron Phil. Theol. ancill. Ex. 3 art. 18.

title: Baron: instrumental act is fiducia of pardon to be obtained — not already obtained
english: Baron art. 20: object — remitted already, or to be obtained?
Instrumental justifying act = fiducia of pardon to be obtained — not of pardon already gotten.
One who prays for remission, trusting he is among those for whom Christ died, obtains remission.
No need to make already-obtained-pardon fiducia the instrumental cause.
translator_notes: OCR: LXI 1675 PDF 229; Baron Ex. 3 art. 20.

title: Baron’s reconciliation: two fiducial acts — one before justification, one after
english: Already-obtained-pardon fiducia can be a saving-faith act — but not the instrumental cause (it follows justification).
Object of fiducia: both remission to-be-obtained and already-obtained.
Two acts: before (instrumental cause) / after (effect).
Before: persuasion of Christ’s satisfaction for me + remission to be obtained.
After: persuasion of remitted sins + perseverance to life’s end.
Not all acts of justifying / special-mercy faith precede justification.
translator_notes: OCR: LXII 1675 PDF 229; Baron reconciles art. 18 & 20.

title: Wendelin: special-mercy faith — future, present, and past remission as object
english: Other Reformed also split special-mercy fiducia into acts before/after justification.
Wendelin: before the act, not ‘already remitted to me’; rather ‘will come to me’.
In the justifying act: believes sins are being remitted — receives remission (Acts 26).
After: past application + future remissions.
Special object = remission future, present, and past.
translator_notes: OCR: LXIII 1675 PDF 229–230; Wendelin I.24 th.11; Acts 26.

title: Leiden Censure: present-tense remitting fiducia justifies — past-tense follows
english: Leiden Censure (Rivetus): justifying fiducia ≠ already-perceived remission.
Formal act: believe sins are remitted to me now (present), not past/future as such.
General truth + personal ‘this promise is mine and received’ — then remission and fiducia are simultaneous.
‘I will be justified if I believe’ alone does not justify — need present reception of justice.
Past-tense belief follows justification.
One faith, three acts: disposing / properly justifying / conscience-pacifying.
translator_notes: OCR: LXIV 1675 PDF 230; Leiden Censure Remonstrant Conf. XI; Rom. 4:7; next LXV+ Maresius.

title: Maresius: threefold faith-act — disposing, formally justifying, consoling
english: Maresius (System, locus 11, Th. 57): a threefold act of faith must be marked in justification.

Disposing act: I believe Christ has merited remission for his own, and that my sins will be remitted if I repent and rest in his merit — with law-bred misery and the hunger of Matt. 5:6 setting the guilty under an absolving sentence yet to be heard.

Formally justificatory act: by the Spirit of adoption the absolving sentence is spoken into me now — present remission of past and future weakness-sins, never imputed to condemnation, innocence from Christ's imputed righteousness, and certain eternal life; simultaneous with actual justification.

Consolatory act: past-tense confidence that all sins were already remitted and condemnation is gone (Rom. 8:1), with trust that absolution stretches to daily falls sought in the Lord's Prayer — this follows justification.
So faith is saving condition three ways: before, with, and after justification.
translator_notes: OCR: LXV 1675 PDF 230; Maresius System. loc. 11 Th. 57.

title: Paraeus: special-mercy fiducia — before, in, and after justification
english: Paraeus: special-mercy fiducia in the repenting sinner precedes justification by nature-order — as in the Publican who first cries for mercy, trusting pardon will come.
It accompanies the justifying act (sins are remitted to me now) and follows it (sins have been remitted — he goes home justified).
Special object: Gospel promise in future, present, and past tenses to me/you/him believing in the Son.
Before the act (by nature, not time): will be remitted; in the act: are remitted; after: have been remitted.
translator_notes: OCR: LXVI 1675 PDF 230-231; Paraeus on Bell. Justif. I.10.

title: Rivetus and Baron: past-remission persuasio is faith’s fruit, not its justifying instrument
english: Rivetus (and Baron’s stronger wording): faith defined as sure fiducia that remission is granted not only in general but to me in particular — even called saving faith’s chief specific act.
Yet their mind is not that past-tense persuasion (“sins have been remitted”) is the act by which we are justified.
They describe faith that way because such persuasion is a property true faith is apt to produce, and belongs to its perfection.
It is a real act of justifying faith (vs dead/historical), precious for peace and piety — but it follows justification; it is not the instrument.
translator_notes: OCR: LXVII 1675 PDF 231; Rivetus; Robert Baron.

title: Why define justifying faith by the consequent act — Ames on contested certainty
english: Why define justifying faith by an act that does not justify but follows justification already done?
Because the later act presupposes the earlier, shows faith’s perfection more clearly, and most consoles believers.
Above all: the believer’s certainty of his own grace was the flashpoint with Roman doctors.

Ames (Bellarmine Enervated V.2): one faith both applies mercy in Christ and makes that application sure; enemies of grace attack that certainty — so many describe justifying faith by it, though sense of it may for a time be parted from faith.
translator_notes: OCR: LXVIII 1675 PDF 231; Ames, Bellarmino Enervato V.2.

title: Alting: sins deleted two ways — decree/death of Christ, and efficacious application
english: Some Reformed seem to grant that the justifying act is persuasion that our sins are already deleted and remitted through Christ.
No clash, they say, in God remitting because we believe them remitted — if “deleted” is heard two ways.
First: as to God’s decree and Christ’s death already undergone from that decree.
Second: as to efficacious application — Christ giving remission, believers receiving it by faith.
Alting: remission is given and applied while with sure fiducia we embrace Christ, persuaded that by decree his death has blotted out and expiated our sins.
translator_notes: OCR: LXIX 1675 PDF 231; Alting Loci communes II, Controv. 2.

title: Chamier: sins remitted before we believe — yet that faith does not justify
english: Chamier: sins remitted to us before we believe; faith later than justification.
Yet the faith that sins are already remitted does not justify — it is wrought in, and required of, the already-justified.
No one of sound reason is justified without this faith; no one has this faith who is not justified.
Panstratia Catholica XIII.6.
translator_notes: OCR: LXX 1675 PDF 231; Chamier Panstratia XIII.6.

title: Molinaeus: justification from eternity — faith gives the sense of it
english: Du Moulin (Sedan): justification is from eternity — part of the election decree — unlike regeneration, which begins in time.
Sense of justification is given to believers at a certain time; regeneration’s start is first sparks of faith and first motions of repentance.
On his hypothesis: sins remitted before the sinner believes.
Faith justifies only inasmuch as through faith we have the sense of justification.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXI 1675 PDF 231; Molinaeus De Justif. & Fide I.54.

title: Molinaeus: fiducia is faith’s inseparable fruit — hope, security, quiet joy
english: Du Moulin sets fiducia apart from that persuasion: fiducia rises from it as justifying faith’s perpetual companion — not faith itself, but faith’s effect, without which faith is not true.
Fiducia = firm hope, constancy, security, tranquillity against terror and trembling.
In his words: terrors shaken off, will quieted in peace, joy poured out, the believer calling on God with familiar liberty.
Faith is one thing, fiducia another — its inseparable fruit: once the mind firmly assents that Gospel promises are for me, that quiet joy follows by the Spirit of adoption.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXII 1675 PDF 231-232; Molinaeus De Justif. & Fide II.19.

title: Beza and Garissolius: fiducia is faith’s inseparable effect — verbal clash only
english: Beza, Garissolius (and du Moulin with them): fiducia is not a part of faith but its inseparable effect — coheres with faith, yet is distinct from it.
Those who make fiducia faith’s chief part mean by the name that sure persuasion of God’s grace toward me and that Gospel goods are peculiarly mine.
Beza’s side grants that persuasion as part of faith, but reserves “fiducia” for the quiet, liberty, and constancy that rise from it.
Same thing; only the wording differs.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXIII 1675 PDF 232; Beza; Garissolius; Molinaeus.

title: Reformed consensus: justifying faith specially applies the Gospel — schools differ how
english: Common Reformed consent: justifying faith specially applies the general Gospel word and grace-promises to each believer.
Schools differ on what “application” means.
Many reduce it to the judgment that Gospel goods are peculiarly mine, and that I am and will be partaker of them.
So du Moulin, Ursinus, Paraeus, and Tilenus.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXIV 1675 PDF 232; Molinaeus; Ursinus; Paraeus; Tilenus.

title: Baron: two applicative acts — mind’s persuasion and will’s ardent love
english: Baron: the regenerate apply Christ’s merit and God’s mercy by two acts, not one.
First: sure mind-persuasion on God’s testimony — Christ has fully satisfied for our sins; remission, eternal justice, and life are given to us too, freely, for Christ’s merit alone.
Second: ardent love — the will embraces grace, looking for fuller sense now and clear vision hereafter.
Both required for fiducia (firm persuasion + desire); yet the first is fiducia’s formal essence, the second only concomitant — so grace is chiefly applied by the prior act.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXV 1675 PDF 232; Baron, Phil. Theol. ancill. Exerc. 3 Art. 19.

title: Bucanus: apply Christ by mind’s judgment and heart’s desire — with Wendelin and Chamier
english: Bucanus: Christ is applied not by mind’s judgment alone but also by the heart’s desire and apprehension.
Faith = from mind’s knowledge, approval, and special judgment, the will’s desire and grasp by which each privately applies crucified Christ with his benefits offered in Word and Sacraments.
Same line as Baron for all who count love and desire among justifying faith’s acts — Wendelin, Chamier, and others.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXVI 1675 PDF 232; Bucanus; Wendelin; Chamier.

title: Perkins to Ames: post-justification persuasion vs pre-justification refuge-fiducia
english: More carefully: after justification the believer applies promises by sure persuasion that the goods are his.

Before justification the repenting sinner applies them by refuge-fiducia — fleeing to God’s glory and mercy in Christ, seeking and longing with the whole heart, resting on God’s goodness, expecting liberation and saving good from God through Christ alone.
So Perkins, Davenant, Wittich, Ames — and that refuge-motion is what they mean by fiducia as faith’s chief part.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXVII 1675 PDF 232-233; Perkins; Davenant; Wittich; Ames.

title: Living faith applies the whole Word practically — not Gospel promises only
english: Some: the application that marks living saving faith vs historical/dead is not limited to Gospel promises — though those are its chief object.
True faith applies grace-promises and the rest of God’s Word, each in its own way.
Practically: refer everything in the Word to one’s own action and use.
Promises → judge highest good and blessedness there; redemption mysteries → seek consolation and conscience-peace; precepts → resolve to live by them.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXVIII 1675 PDF 233.

title: English Confession: faith differently affected by each part of the Word — chiefly receiving Christ
english: The mid-century English Confession seems to share that whole-Word application sense.

By this faith the Christian believes whatever God reveals, on God’s speaking authority, and is differently moved by each part: obeys commands, trembles at threats, embraces promises for this life and the next.
Chief saving acts: accept and receive Christ, and rest in him alone for justification, sanctification, and eternal life.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXIX 1675 PDF 233; English Confession (~1640s).

title: Placeus, Vermigli, Musculus: essential act is practical assent — especially to Gospel promises
english: On that line, saving faith’s proper essential act = practical assent to the whole Word, specially to Gospel promises.
Placeus (Saumur): tenacious, efficacious persuasion of what God reveals — specially remission and eternal life through Christ.
Vermigli: assent so strong it draws fiducia, hope, charity, and good works as present weakness allows.
Musculus: consenting heart-assent to what the Word narrates or promises.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXX 1675 PDF 233; Placeus Salmur.; Vermigli; Musculus.

title: Historical vs saving faith — bare theoretical assent vs practical applying faith
english: Common Reformed judgment: historical faith and saving/justifying faith must be sharply distinguished.
Historical: bare simple assent to God’s Word — from the Spirit, but stuck in theoretical intellect, not moving will or affections.
Saving: lights the mind and moves practice — will and affections; refers the Word to the believer’s use; specially applies God’s promises.
Historical faith only idly contemplates what it believes as if it did not touch him.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXI 1675 PDF 233.

title: Same genus or mere homonym? — a philosophical quarrel, not a theological one
english: Reformers quarrel: are historical and justifying faith species under one genus (univocal or analogical), or only homonyms?
Le Blanc: the question is merely philosophical — once the real difference is clear, Theology need not care which school-word names it.
If we keep school usage: nothing blocks calling them species of one genus — common name and common thing: assent to God revealing, from the Spirit’s light.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXII 1675 PDF 233.

title: Why Reformed definitions of justifying faith diverge — omit the common, mark the difference
english: Reformed definitions of justifying faith diverge for two reasons.
First: many omit what it shares with historical faith and mark only the difference — so they skip the assent justifying faith still gives to the whole revealed Word.
Second: some define from one property, others from another.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXIII 1675 PDF 233-234.

title: Calvin, Beza, catechisms: define faith by persuasion of God’s goodwill — Molinaeus, Maresius, Alting
english: Calvin, Beza, and popular catechisms define faith from the fiducia/persuasion of God’s grace and goodwill that saving faith carries.
Calvin/Beza: firm certain knowledge of divine goodwill, founded on grace promised in Christ, revealed and sealed by the Spirit.
Short catechism: sure trust that the Father loves me for Christ.

Near them: du Moulin (firm assent that Gospel promises are true and peculiarly mine); Maresius (gift resting in and fiducially applying those promises); Alting (knowledge plus fiducial apprehension of grace in Christ the Redeemer).
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXIV 1675 PDF 234; Calvin; Beza; Molinaeus; Maresius; Alting.

title: Ames, Wittich, Mestrezat: define faith by refuge-fiducia fleeing to mercy in Christ
english: Another definitional path: faith = the refuge-fiducia by which the repenting sinner flees to God, adheres, and leans on him for mercy through Christ.
Ames: heart’s rest in God as author of life/eternal salvation — freed from every evil, gaining every good.
Wittich: hunger and thirst for righteousness plus heart-rest in God as salvation’s fountain — committing the soul in straits and temptations.
Mestrezat: the repenting sinner’s refuge to God’s mercy in Christ.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXV 1675 PDF 234; Ames; Wittich; Mestrezat.

title: Neither side denies the other’s act — assent, refuge, and consequent persuasion cohere
english: Those who omit whole-Word assent in the definition still confess it is included or required.
Grace-persuasion definers do not deny prior refuge-fiducia fleeing to God for mercy.
Refuge-fiducia definers do not deny consequent persuasion of God’s love and goodwill.
The acts cohere; definitions spotlight different moments.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXVI 1675 PDF 234.

title: Do not define justifying faith by the consequent persuasion — or by refuge alone
english: Ill-formed: defining justifying faith as sure persuasion that God’s goodwill and Gospel goods are ours.
That persuasion follows justification already done; weak faith can briefly stand without it.
Unreasonable to define justifying faith by an act that presupposes justification — and can be parted from faith — rather than by the act through which we are justified.
Also unreasonable to pin the definition on one act when several necessary acts concur — including those who mention only refuge-fiducia fleeing to God for grace.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXVII 1675 PDF 234.

title: Prefer fuller definitions — English Confession 1647: whole Word, chiefly receiving Christ
english: Le Blanc prefers fuller, clearer definitions of justifying faith.

English Confession 1647: saving faith believes whatever God reveals, on God’s speaking authority, and is differently moved by each part — obeys commands, trembles at threats, embraces promises for this life and the next.
Chief acts: accept and receive Christ, and rest in him alone for justification, sanctification, and eternal life, by the covenant of grace.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXVIII 1675 PDF 234; English Confession 1647.

title: Placeus preferred — tenacious efficacious persuasion; Vermigli, Musculus, Le Blanc’s own formula
english: Le Blanc ranks Placeus’s definition most convenient, full, and brief: tenacious efficacious persuasion of what God reveals — specially remission and eternal life through Christ.
“Persuasion of revealed truth” marks what it shares with historical faith; “tenacious and efficacious” marks what sets justifying faith apart.
Vermigli: firm certain Spirit-breathed assent strong enough to draw fiducia, hope, charity, and good works.
Musculus: constant heart-assent to what the Word narrates or promises.
Le Blanc’s own: firm, practical, fiducial assent to all God reveals — specially Gospel promises.
translator_notes: OCR: LXXXIX 1675 PDF 234-235; Placeus; Vermigli; Musculus.

title: Generic object = whole Word; special object = Gospel promises — as saving, not as exclusive
english: Most Reformed: adequate/generic object of faith = the whole Word; proper/special = Gospel promises.
Not that promises belong only to justifying faith — historical faith also believes them true, as it believes the histories.
Promises are “proper” because faith as saving and justifying is specially conversant about them.
So: whole Word is object of the faith that justifies; Gospel promises are the object whereby it justifies.
translator_notes: OCR: XC 1675 PDF 235.

title: “Proprie” means chiefly, not uniquely — covenant faith embraces mysteries too (Rom. 10)
english: “Proprie” here = chiefly/principally, not uniquely — justifying faith is not only about promises.
Faith saves as condition of the gracious covenant (living faith working through love), not as perfect law-keeping.
Moses: do and live; Gospel: believe and be saved — and that faith also covers precepts and dogmas (e.g. the Resurrection).
Rom. 10: heart-belief and mouth-confession — so justifying faith includes assent to Gospel mysteries, not grace-promise alone (though that remains chief).
translator_notes: OCR: XCI 1675 PDF 235; Rom. 10.

title: “Special mercy” as object — prefer saying grace-promises fiducially applied
english: “Special mercy is justifying faith’s proper object” means: unlike historical faith, it applies divine-mercy promises personally — before justification trusting sins will be remitted, after believing they have been.
The phrase is obscure and open to slander.
Le Blanc prefers (with many): principal object = grace-promises apprehended with practical fiducial assent and applied to oneself — same substance, clearer words.
translator_notes: OCR: XCII 1675 PDF 235 (printed CXII in OCR).

title: Notitia is prerequisite, not a constitutive part of faith — against Bucanus, with Ames and Wittich
english: Reformed disagree on faith’s parts/acts.
Notitia (apprehension of what is to be believed), apart from assent: constitutive part (Bucanus) or only prerequisite (Ames, Wittich)?
Le Blanc sides with Ames/Wittich: you cannot rightly believe without some notion, but faith does not consist in that notion.
Bare notitia can sit in profane minds — even atheists know what Christians are told to believe — without a spark of faith.
translator_notes: OCR: XCIII 1675 PDF 235-236; Bucanus; Ames; Wittich.

title: Assent belongs to faith’s essence — Ames departs from common Reformed doctrine
english: Some (Ames) doubt whether assent is faith’s formal essential act — calling assent an act of faith but locating faith itself in certain will-acts.
Le Blanc: Ames leaves common Reformed (and all Christian schools’) doctrine that assent belongs to faith’s essence.
To believe the Gospel as one ought is nothing but due assent — and Paul names believing God raised Jesus as a saving-faith act.
translator_notes: OCR: XCIV 1675 PDF 236; Ames.

title: Love: not formal when faith is precise; essential when faith means faith working through love
english: Is love a formal essential act of faith? Chamier, Wendelin, Wittich, Cocceius say yes; others no.
Le Blanc distinguishes: take faith precisely (apart from hope and charity) → love belongs to charity, not as faith’s formal act.

Take faith as the aggregate “faith working through love” (how most Reformed take it here) → intellect and will together; sincere love of God and Christ is essential — living faith cannot be conceived without it.
translator_notes: OCR: XCV 1675 PDF 236; Chamier; Wendelin; Wittich; Cocceius; Paraeus.

title: Four senses of fiducia — rest in God, grace-persuasion, fortitude, conscience-quiet
english: Reformed speak variously of fiducia: some call it faith’s primary proper act; others only faith’s offspring/effect — and the name itself shifts.

Four acceptations Le Blanc repeats: (1) reclining on God as salvation’s fountain; (2) firm persuasion of obtained grace, pardon, and reconciliation; (3) spiritual fortitude against life’s evils; (4) conscience-quiet / spiritual security against servile fear.
translator_notes: OCR: XCVI 1675 PDF 236.

title: Fiducia as fortitude or conscience-quiet — fruits only, not constitutive acts
english: Fiducia as spiritual fortitude (sense 3) or conscience-quiet against servile fear (sense 4) is only faith’s fruit and effect.
Not a constitutive part or faith’s act properly so called.
All Reformed doctors agree here.
translator_notes: OCR: XCVII 1675 PDF 236.

title: Refuge-fiducia: not formal when faith is precise; included in living faith’s aggregate
english: Refuge-fiducia (leaning on God / fleeing to him for life and salvation) follows the same rule as love.
Take faith precisely (apart from other virtues) → not faith’s formal act.
Take faith as living faith working through love’s aggregate → this fiducia is included as a part.
translator_notes: OCR: XCVIII 1675 PDF 236.

title: Grace-persuasion fiducia: primary essential act, or only perfection’s fruit?
english: Chief quarrel: second-sense fiducia = firm persuasion that I have obtained grace and that Gospel goods are mine.
Baron, Rivetus, Ursinus, Paraeus, Wendelin (and others): define faith by it; call it primary, chief, specific saving act — as if saving faith could not stand without it.

Perkins, Ames, Davenant, Wittich, Widmar, young du Moulin, English Confession 1647: it belongs to faith’s perfection, not inmost essence; proper to corroborated, not weak, faith; many truly justified lack it.
So: accidental/secondary/reflex act — better called faith’s fruit than its chief act.
translator_notes: OCR: XCIX 1675 PDF 236-237; Baron–Wendelin vs Perkins–Eng. Conf. 1647.

title: Le Blanc holds the latter — grace-persuasion presupposes faith already in the heart
english: Le Blanc’s earlier theses already took the Perkins–Ames side — and he still holds it.
Persuasion that I am reconciled and received into grace is secondary/accidental, not primary/essential.
Without special revelation it is only the conclusion of a syllogism: living faith working through love → reconciled; I find such faith in myself → therefore reconciled.
So the persuasion presupposes faith already in the heart — it cannot be faith’s essence.
translator_notes: OCR: C 1675 PDF 237; Le Blanc’s prior theses.

title: Pious doubters still belong among the faithful — do not drive them to despair
english: Experience: many godly people trust God’s Word and promises, flee to him, and plead for mercy — yet are not sure grace is already theirs, anxious about whether their faith and repentance are sincere enough.
No reason to cast them out of the truly faithful.
Console them: the faith by which they flee and thirst is itself the faith to which God promised remission and salvation.
To demand certainty of obtained grace as if without it there is no true faith is to pave the way to despair.
translator_notes: OCR: CI 1675 PDF 237.

title: Even Baron’s line admits grace-persuasion follows justification — it is not the justifying act
english: Separate question: which act is the one through which faith justifies?
Oddly, even those who call past-tense redemption/remission persuasion faith’s chief specific act (Baron, Rivetus, Wendelin, Ames, Paraeus) still admit it is not the act by which faith justifies.
It follows justification already done — they teach both at once.
translator_notes: OCR: CII 1675 PDF 237; Baron; Rivetus; Wendelin; Ames; Paraeus.

title: Against Chamier: believing sins already remitted cannot be the justifying act
english: Chamier (and some): justify by the act of believing sins are already remitted — Le Blanc: wholly false.
That fiducia presupposes justification already done.
They concede a man is justified and sins remitted before he believes — against all Scripture: wrath remains on the unbeliever; faith and repentance are conditions of promised remission.
The justified are in grace and accepted for eternal life — yet without faith one cannot please God, and still serves sin.
Absurd to justify by what only follows justification.
translator_notes: OCR: CIII 1675 PDF 237; Chamier.

title: Chamier’s ‘all the justified have this faith’ proof proves too much — election parallel
english: Chamier’s escape: faith “justifies” because every justified person eventually has this faith, and no one has it who is not justified.

Le Blanc: that proves too much — by the same logic we could say we are elected to grace through faith and good works, since every elect person eventually has them, and no one has them who is not elect.
translator_notes: OCR: CIV 1675 PDF 237-238; Chamier.
